en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Names of Buddhas, Volume One.

Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the World-Honored One...
Surrounded by the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
I shall proclaim for you the names of all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present."

If good sons or good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite the names of the Buddhas, these people will enjoy peace and security in the present life, remain far removed from all calamities, and extinguish all their transgressions; in the future, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If a son or daughter of good family wishes to extinguish all transgressions, they should bathe thoroughly, put on new and clean clothes, kneel with palms joined, and speak these words:

“Homage to the Buddha Akṣobhya of the East. Homage to the Buddha Prathamacittotpādabhadra of the eighty-sixth kalpa. Homage to the Buddha Arciṣmat. Homage to the Buddha Vimalanetra. Homage to the Buddha Abhaya. Homage to the Buddha Acintya. Homage to the Buddha Dīparāja. Homāge to the Buddha Raśmipramukta. Homage to the Buddha Prabhāvyūha. Homage to the Buddha Mahājayottama. Homage to the Buddha Mahārthasiddha. Homage to the Buddha Bhūtadarśin. Homage to the Buddha Dṛḍharājapuṣpa. Homage to the Buddha Mahāmaitrīduḥkhaparitrātṛ. “I take refuge in the Buddhas of the East, such as these, who are immeasurable and boundless.”

“Homage to the Buddha Samantapūrṇa of the southern quarter; homage to the Buddha Vīrarāja; homage to the Buddha Dhṛtiparākrama; homage to the Buddha Mati; homage to the Buddha Yaśasvara; homage to the Buddha Akṣayadarśanātmabhāva; homage to the Buddha Siṃhasvara; homage to the Buddha Amoghadarśin; homage to the Buddha Cāritramati; homage to the Buddha Sarvacaryāviśuddha; homage to the Buddha Vyūharāja; homage to the Buddha Mahāparvatarāja. I take refuge in the Buddhas of the southern quarter, such as these, who are immeasurable and boundless.”

“Namo to the Buddha Amitāyus of the Western Quarter; Namo to the Buddha Siṃha; Namo to the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa; Namo to the Buddha Gandhapāṇi; Namo to the Buddha Bhīṣmasvara; Namo to the Buddha Gaganagañja; Namo to the Buddha Ratnaketu; Namo to the Buddha Vimalanetra; Namo to the Buddha Priyadarśana; Namo to the Buddha Ratnagiri; Namo to the Buddha Prabhārāja; Namo to the Buddha Candrodayaprabha. I take refuge in all such infinite and boundless Buddhas of the Western Quarter.”

“Homage to the Buddha Difficult to Conquer of the northern quarter! Homage to the Buddha Moonlight! Homage to the Buddha Sandalwood! Homage to the Buddha Sovereign! Homage to the Buddha Golden-Colored King! Homage to the Buddha Sandalwood Moonlight! Homage to the Buddha Universal Eye-Seeing! Homage to the Buddha Universal Illumination Eye-Seeing! Homage to the Buddha Wheel-Hand! Homage to the Buddha Stainless! We take refuge in these and all other such immeasurable and boundless Buddhas of the northern quarter.”

“Namo to the Buddha Bhūmipariśodhana of the southeast; namo to the Buddha Īśvara; namo to the Buddha Dharmeśvara; namo to the Buddha Dharmamati; namo to the Buddha Dharmacintin; namo to the Buddha Nityadharmamati; namo to the Buddha Nityasukha; namo to the Buddha Sucintita; namo to the Buddha Susthita; namo to the Buddha Subāhu. I take refuge in all such infinite and boundless Buddhas of the southeastern direction.”

"Homage to the Buddha Nārāyaṇa of the southwest; homage to the Buddha Dragon-King Virtue; homage to the Buddha Jewel Sound; homage to the Buddha Earth Sovereign; homage to the Buddha Human King; homage to the Buddha Wondrous Sound; homage to the Buddha Wisdom; homage to the Buddha Wondrous Fragrance Flower; homage to the Buddha Heavenly King; homage to the Buddha Constantly Pure Eye. I take refuge in these and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddhas of the southwest."

“Namo to the Buddha Candrānanābha of the northwest; namo to the Buddha Candraprabha; namo to the Buddha Candradhvaja; namo to the Buddha Śūramgama; namo to the Buddha Sūryānanābha; namo to the Buddha Sūryagarbha; namo to the Buddha Sūryaprabhālaṃkāra; namo to the Buddha Puṣpakāya; namo to the Buddha Padmagarbha; namo to the Buddha Padmabhrū; namo to the Buddha Siṃhasvararāja; namo to the Buddha Supratiṣṭhitamati. I take refuge in all such infinite and boundless Buddhas of the northwest.”

“Homage to the Buddha Śāntendriya in the northeast; homage to the Buddha Śānti; homage to the Buddha Mahāsena; homage to the Buddha Viśuddhajaya; homage to the Buddha Viśuddhasvararāja; homage to the Buddha Viśuddhadevapūjita; homage to the Buddha Suvinīta; homage to the Buddha Nirmāṇa; homage to the Buddha Sumati; homage to the Buddha Sumatidhara. I take refuge in all such infinite and boundless Buddhas of the northeast.”

“Homage to the Buddha True Practice of the lower direction; homage to the Buddha Swift Action; homage to the Buddha Wisdom; homage to the Buddha Firm King; homage to the Buddha Vajra-Array; homage to the Buddha Lion; homage to the Buddha Swift as a Monkey; homage to the Buddha Abiding in Reality; homage to the Buddha Accomplished Merit; homage to the Buddha Attained Merit; homage to the Buddha Well-At-Ease; homage to the Buddha Celestial Vajra. I take refuge in all such immeasurable and boundless Buddhas of the lower direction.”

“Homage to the Buddha Immeasurable Victory in the Upper Direction; homage to the Buddha Cloud King; homage to the Buddha Cloud Virtue; homage to the Buddha Immeasurable Renowned Name; homage to the Buddha King of the Body of Hearing; homage to the Buddha Great Virtue; homage to the Buddha Great Sumeru; homage to the Buddha Subduer of Māra. We take refuge in these and all other immeasurable and boundless Buddhas of the upper direction.”

“Namo to the future Samantabhadra Buddha; namo to Maitreya Buddha; namo to Avalokiteśvara-Svayambhū Buddha; namo to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Buddha; namo to Gaganagañja Buddha; namo to Vimalakīrti Buddha; namo to Arthasiddha Buddha; namo to Satyaghoṣa Buddha; namo to Mahāsāgara Buddha; namo to Akṣayamati Buddha; namo to Akṣayagarbha Buddha. I take refuge in all such infinite and boundless Buddhas of the future.”

“Good son! If a person receives, maintains, reads, and recites the names of these Buddhas, they will enjoy peace and security in the present life, remain far removed from all calamities, and eliminate all transgressions; in the future, they will ultimately attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

“Homage to the Buddha Vimalaprabha; homage to the Buddha Pratibhānalaṃkāravicaya; homage to the Buddha Vimalacandradhvajaśrī; homage to the Buddha Puṣpārāja; homage to the Buddha Mahāprabha; homage to the Buddha Ratnottama; homage to the Buddha Abhayadarśin; homage to the Buddha Sarvabhayatrāsāpagata; homage to the Buddha Siṃhavikrāntabalasamudgata; homage to the Buddha Prabhāsarāja. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family recites, studies, and contemplates these names of the Buddhas for ten days, they will certainly be freed from all karmic obstructions.”

"I take refuge in these and other immeasurable and boundless Pratyekabuddhas.
Having paid homage to the Three Jewels, I shall next perform repentance.
Now, one who wishes to perform prostrations and repentance must first revere the Three Jewels."
The reason for this is that the Three Jewels are the true friends and fields of merit for all sentient beings.

If one can take refuge in them, immeasurable sins will be extinguished and immeasurable blessings will grow; they can enable the practitioner to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of liberation.
Therefore, we, the disciples [Name] and others, take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space;

we take refuge in all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space; we take refuge in all Great Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space; and we take refuge in all Noble Sanghas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.

“Disciple! The reason for your repentance today is that, speaking truly, since beginningless time while remaining in the stage of an ordinary person, regardless of whether one is noble or base, one’s offenses have been immeasurable. Whether sins were produced through the three karmas, or transgressions arose from the six sense organs; whether they originated from internal, perverse reflections, or from defiled attachments triggered by external objects—thus, even up to the increase of the ten evil deeds and the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction.”
Although the characteristics of these offenses are indeed immeasurable, when stated in broad terms, they do not exceed three.
What are these three? First, the hindrance of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa); [the second is the hindrance of karma; the third is the hindrance of maturation].
Second is the obstacle of karma;
third is the obstacle of retribution.
These three types of dharmas can obstruct the Noble Path, as well as the superior and wondrous blessings of humans and devas.

Therefore, the sutras designate these as the three obstacles. For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the practice of skillful repentance; once these three obstacles are eliminated and extinguished, the six sense organs, the ten evil deeds, and even the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction will all become completely pure.
"Therefore, disciples! Today you should cultivate this superior and sublime resolve to repent for the three obstructions.
If you wish to extinguish the offenses of these three obstructions, what kind of mind must you employ to cause these offenses to be eliminated?"
First, one must give rise to seven kinds of mental states as a preliminary means; only then can these offenses be extinguished.
The first is shame and remorse.
fourth, the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Fifth, to regard enemies and kin with equanimity;
sixth, to mindfully repay the Buddha’s kindness;
seventh, to contemplate that the nature of offenses is empty.

"First, regarding shame and remorse: I reflect that I and Śākyamuni Tathāgata were once both ordinary beings; yet while the World-Honored One has already attained the Way for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, we have instead remained immersed in the six sense-objects, wandering through birth and death with no prospect of escape. This is truly something for which one should feel ashamed, remorseful, abashed, and disgraced before the world."

"The second fear is this: being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one's actions of body, speech, and mind are constantly associated with transgressions. By reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of life, one ought to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts to undergo immeasurable suffering; this is truly something to be startled by, to be afraid of, to be terrified of, and to be fearful of."

"Third, regarding detachment: one should contemplate that within birth and death there is only impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity; it is as illusory as a bubble upon water, arising and ceasing rapidly; its coming and going and cyclic wandering are like the turning of a wheel; and the eight sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death torment one incessantly, with not a moment's respite."

All of you together should simply observe your own bodies from head to foot; therein there are but thirty-six things: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, bags of pus, nasal mucus, saliva, the two internal organs of the raw and the cooked (stomach and small intestine), the large and small intestines, the spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, stomach, mesentery, fat, grease, sinews, membranes, veins, arteries, marrow, and the nine orifices through which excrement and urine constantly flow.
"This body is a collection of manifold sufferings; everything within it is impure. What wise person would take pleasure in this stinking fleshly body?"
"Since birth and death contain such various evil dharmas as these, they are truly to be dreaded and weary of.
Regarding the fourth [reason] for generating the bodhicitta, the Sūtra says:
'One should delight in the Buddha-body; the Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body.'"

The body of the Tathāgata is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom; it is born from the six pāramitās; it is born from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; it is born from the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment; and it is born from all such various merits and wisdom.

"Those who wish to attain this body should resolve upon bodhicitta, seeking the fruit of *sarvajñā*—the all-knowing wisdom characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and should purify buddha-fields and bring sentient beings to maturity, without being stingy with their body, life, or wealth."
"Fifth, regarding equanimity toward enemies and kin: one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, free from the notion of 'other' or 'self.

Why is this so? If one perceives an enemy as distinct from a relative, that is discrimination. Because of discrimination, various attachments and perceptions arise; with attachments and perceptions as conditions, various afflictions are produced; with afflictions as conditions, various evil karmas are created; and because of evil karma as a condition, bitter fruits of suffering are obtained."

"Sixth, regarding repaying the Buddha's kindness through mindfulness: throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, the Tathāgata sacrificed his head, eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, hands, feet, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures; for our sake, he practiced various ascetic austerities. This kindness and this virtue are truly difficult to repay."
"Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] on the crown of one's head or upon both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, one could never repay [his kindness].

Those of us who wish to repay the grace of the Tathāgata should, in this world, practice with courageous diligence, endure toil and suffering, and without begrudging body or life, establish the Triple Gem, propagate the Mahāyāna, and extensively transform sentient beings so that they may all enter the Right Path.

"Seventh, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses: they possess no real characteristic and arise from causes and conditions; they exist through inversion. Since they arise from causes and conditions, they can likewise be extinguished by means of causes and conditions."
That which arises from causes and conditions was produced without cause through associating with evil friends;
that which ceases through causes and conditions is precisely today’s cleansing of the mind through repentance.
"The characteristics of this offense are neither within, nor without, nor in between; thus one knows that this offense is fundamentally empty."

"Having generated these seven kinds of minds, one contemplates the Buddhas and worthy sages of the ten directions. With hands joined in prayer and palms pressed together, one lays bare one's innermost sincerity; through shame and remorse, one reforms oneself, exposing one’s heart and liver and washing clean one’s intestines and stomach. When one repents in this manner, what transgression is there that will not be extinguished?"
Furthermore, what obstacles would not be dissolved?
If you instead remain thus indolent and lax, allowing your thoughts to run wild, it is merely a waste of effort to toil at worldly affairs;

what benefit is there in this? Moreover, human life is impermanent, like a flickering candle; if one breath does not return, one immediately turns to dust and earth. The retributions of suffering in the three miserable realms must be borne by the body itself; they cannot be avoided by entrusting oneself to money, wealth, or treasures. In the profound and dark abyss, there is no hope for pardon; one must alone endure this suffering, with no one to take it upon themselves.
Do not say, "In this present life I have committed no such offenses, therefore I cannot repent with utmost sincerity.
As it is said in the sutras:
"For an ordinary person, every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step is nothing but offense."
Furthermore, throughout past lives, one has fully accumulated immeasurable evil karma that pursues the practitioner like a shadow follows a form.

If one does not repent today, these evils will deepen daily; therefore, the Buddha did not permit the concealment of one's flaws, whereas the purification of prior offenses through repentance is what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* esteems. Thus, we know that long-term immersion in the sea of suffering is truly due to self-concealment.
Today we openly confess and repent, not daring to conceal anything.
As for what are called the "three obstructions":
The first is called the obstacle of afflictions;
the second is named the obstacle of karma;
the third is the obstacle of retribution.
These three kinds of phenomena depend upon one another: because of afflictions, one gives rise to unwholesome karma; by reason of the conditions of unwholesome karma, one obtains bitter fruits.
Today, with a sincere heart, you should first of all repent for the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, these afflictions have been variously rebuked by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones who have entered into the principle; they have also designated these afflictions as enemies.
Why is this? Because they are able to sever the life-root of the wisdom of sentient beings;
furthermore, these afflictions are designated as "thieves," for they are able to plunder the various wholesome dharmas of sentient beings.
These afflictions are also designated as "fierce rivers," for they can sweep sentient beings into the great ocean of suffering within birth and death;
they are also designated as "fetters and shackles," for they bind sentient beings in the prison of birth and death so that they cannot escape;
and they are also designated as being like "pythons," for they devour the *tathatā* buddha-nature of sentient beings.

Therefore, the six realms are interconnected and the four modes of birth never cease; evil karma is inexhaustible and the fruits of suffering do not end. You should know that all of this is the fault and affliction of the defilements.
Today, with this superior mind of goodness, I take refuge in the Buddha: Homage to the Buddha Śubhavyūha of the East; Homage to the Buddha Ratnākara of the South;

Homage to the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa of the West; Homage to the Buddha Lakṣaṇaguna of the North; Homage to the Buddha Jālinīprabha of the Southeast; Homage to the Buddha Upari-jñāna of the Southwest; Homage to the Buddha Puṣpavatsa of the Northwest; Homage to the Buddha Vairocana-prajña of the Northeast; Homage to the Buddha Guṇaprabhāsa of the Nadir; Homage to the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa of the Zenith. I pay homage to all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions.

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, while receiving retribution within the six realms of existence—whether as humans or devas—this mind-consciousness has constantly harbored ignorance and delusion, filling the breast with their abundance."

Whether by means of the three poisons one commits all manner of transgressions, or by means of the three outflows one commits all manner of transgressions, or by means of the three perceptions one commits all manner of transgressions, or by means of the three feelings one commits all manner of transgressions, or by means of the three sufferings one commits all manner of transgressions, or conditioned by the three provisional designations one commits all manner of transgressions, or through craving for the three realms of existence one commits all manner of transgressions—such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless, vexing and disturbing all beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth. Today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent.

"Furthermore, disciples! From beginningless time until this day, we may have committed all manner of offenses due to the four abodes of consciousness; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four floods; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four graspings; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four attachments; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four conditions; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four great elements; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four bonds; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four nutriments; or committed all manner of offenses due to the four modes of birth. Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless, causing affliction and turmoil for all sentient beings throughout the six realms. Today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent."

"Furthermore, disciples! From beginningless time until this day, we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsa-bhūmi*); or all manner of transgressions due to the five faculties of sensation (*pañca-vedanendriya*); or all manner of transgressions due to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*); or all manner of transgressions due to the five forms of stinginess (*pañca-mātsarya*); or all manner of transgressions due to the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*); or all manner of transgressions due to the five mental states (*pañca-citta*). Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, causing turmoil for all four modes of birth within the six realms. Today, we openly confess them, taking refuge and repenting."

"Furthermore, disciples! From beginningless time until this very day, we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*); we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*); we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six perceptions (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā*); we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six feelings (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*); we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six volitional formations (*ṣaḍ-saṃskāra*); we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six cravings (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā*); or we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six doubts (*ṣaḍ-vicikitsā*). Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, causing turmoil for those in the six realms of existence and all four modes of birth. Today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent."

From beginningless time until this very day, we may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven outflows (*āsrava*), or all manner of transgressions due to the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), or all manner of transgressions due to the eight inversions (*viparyāsa*), or all manner of transgressions due to the eight impurities (*mala*), or all manner of transgressions due to the eight sufferings (*duḥkha*). Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless; they have disturbed and vexed all beings of the four modes of birth within the six realms. Today, we openly confess them, taking refuge and repenting."

From beginningless time until this very day, one may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine afflictions (*nava-nīvaraṇa*), or all manner of transgressions due to the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*), or all manner of transgressions due to the nine superior objects of perception (*nava-adhyālambana*), or all manner of transgressions due to the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*), or all manner of transgressions due to the ten envelopments (*daśa-paryavasthāna*), or all manner of transgressions due to the eleven pervasive latent tendencies (*ekādaśa-anuśaya*), or all manner of transgressions due to the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), or all manner of transgressions due to the sixteen false views (*ṣoḍaśa-dṛṣṭi*), or all manner of transgressions due to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), or all manner of transgressions due to the twenty-five notions of self (*pañcaviṃśati-ātman*), or all manner of transgressions due to the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, due to the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*)—both those abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—which blaze fiercely day and night, one opens the gates of the outflows (*āsrava*) and commits all manner of transgressions.

Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless; they vex and disturb the worthy and holy ones as well as those of the four modes of birth. Pervading the triple world and extending throughout the six realms, there is nowhere to hide and nowhere to escape. Today, having come before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, I feel shame and remorse, confessing and repenting for them all.

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this confession of all afflictions such as the three poisons, in every birth and lifetime, attain the clarity of the three types of wisdom, the brilliance of the three forms of omniscience, the cessation of the three sufferings, and the fulfillment of the three vows."

May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance of all afflictions such as the four consciousnesses, vow that in every birth and life we shall broaden the four immeasurable minds, establish the karma of the four reliances, extinguish the four evil destinies, and attain the four fearlessnesses.

“May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit arising from this confession of the five hindrances and all other afflictions, pray that in birth after birth we may cross over the five realms of existence, establish the five faculties, purify the five eyes, and perfect the five aggregates.”

"May we disciples, by virtue of the merit arising from this confession of the various afflictions such as the six cravings, in every birth and lifetime, be fully endowed with the six supernormal powers and fulfill the karma of the six perfections; may we not be deluded by the six sense objects and constantly practice the six sublime conducts."

"May we disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance of all afflictions—the seven outflows (*āsrava*), the eight impurities, the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and so forth—vow that in every birth and lifetime we shall sit upon the flowers of the seven purities (*saptaviśuddhi*), wash away the dust with the eight waters, possess the nine knowledges of abandonment, and fulfill the practices and vows of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). By virtue of the merit produced from this repentance of the eleven pervasive afflictions, the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and all other afflictions, may we vow that in every birth and lifetime our minds shall be constantly washed by the understanding of the eleven emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), that we shall be able to freely turn the wheel of the twelve modes of conduct, that we shall be fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and that all immeasurable merits shall be perfectly complete."
The *Tripiṭaka Combined Volume: Sūtra on the Retribution of Offenses*. This sūtra consists of twenty-eight chapters; this single chapter is circulated as an abridgment.

**Mahāyāna Lotus-Padmavati-Ratnagati Question-and-Answer on the Retribution of Śramaṇas, Chapter One.** At that time, the light of the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment in Magadha did not appear; its flowers withered and fell before the Buddha. The entire great assembly was struck with alarm and doubt, and they said to one another:
"Why have the flowers of this Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment fallen?"
The great assembly of bodhisattvas all gave rise to doubt and were not at ease.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnapani came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why have all the flowers of the Bodhi tree fallen?"

The radiance and color of its flowers were not as they usually are, and the entire great assembly gave rise to doubt and confusion. "We pray only that the World-Honored One will explain this for us, so that the doubts of all the Great Beings seated here may be entirely removed."

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi; his countenance was majestic and radiant, and light issued forth from every pore of his body as he spoke to the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa: "Listen well!
I shall now explain this for you.
Why is it that the flowers of the Bodhi tree have fallen and lost their luster?
As previously stated, because śramaṇas commit evil deeds and fall into states of suffering to undergo retribution without end, the flowers of the Bodhi tree thus lose their luster and fall.
Bao Da stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
that you will explain for me the places where the retribution for such evil-conduct śramaṇas is experienced.”

"In the eastern direction there is a great mountain called Cakravāḍa. In the dark and obscure places within that mountain, where the light of the sun and moon as well as the light of fire cannot reach, it is called 'Hell'."
Within that hell, there are wicked śramaṇas who undergo such punishments; you should go there and ask those sinners: "By what causes and conditions have you been born in this place?"
"What kind of conduct did he practice to incur such a retribution?
"We possess no majestic power; how could we possibly go there?
We pray that the Buddha, out of great compassion, will extend his divine regard toward us, so that we may behold the Avīci Hell in the eastern direction."
"You need only go now, and you shall be able to see it.
Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi prostrated before the Buddha and departed; the dragon then flew through the void, circling with sovereign ease.
At that moment, the great earth shook, and precious lotus flowers rained down from the sky, falling in a flowing cascade.

At that time, in a single thought-moment, Bodhidatta traveled to the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) in the eastern direction. Those mountains were shrouded in dense gloom and steeply towering; on all four sides of the mountains there was not a single blade of grass or tree, and the majestic radiance of the sun and moon could not reach them at all.
As Bao Da proceeded forward along the road, there were thirty-six kings on both sides who presided over the hells;
these kings were named King Gaṅgā-jina, King Pāṅgi-tu, King Viśāla-netra, King Āndhula,
King Vyāghra-netra-darśana, King Uṣṇa-śabda-kalyāṇa, King Mahā-vivāda-pāṭha, and King Raktapāyin.
The King of Ghosts, King Anadra, King Dadada, King Dataro, King Kiliśa,
King Anhula, King Ratnaśīrṣa, King Suvarṇavṛkṣaśrī, King Mahāghoṣa, King Śakuntamūrdhan, King Vyāghranayana, King Dantapāda, and King Samānaghoṣa.
Equaling King Return-to-the-Head, King Headed-in-Garments, King Seeing-the-Head, King Vast-Peace,
King Vast-Concentration, King Head-of-Kings, King Establishing-Righteousness, King Establishing-Vision, King Maṇila, King General-Superintendent,
King Section-Vision, King Evil-Eyes, Good King, Dragon-Mouth King, and Ghost King.
The thirty-six kings, including King Nanshan and the others, saw Bodhisattva Baoda from afar; they all joined their palms together, stepped forward to pay homage, and said:
"How do the causes and conditions lead one into this place of suffering?
It is like sandalwood growing amidst *eranda* weeds.
"I have heard the Tathāgata, the Honored One among the people of the three realms, say:
'In the east there is the Cakravāḍa mountain; that mountain is dark and obscure, such that the light of the sun and moon cannot illuminate it.'"
"I have heard this, and therefore I have come to you, O kings, to enter the hells before those who commit various crimes.
Among you kings, who is able to go with me before the Great King to witness the suffering of these offenders?"
At that time, King Gaṅgājin immediately accompanied the Bodhisattva Ratnabhadra to the Great King.

Then, the Great Ghost King saw the Bodhisattva Ratnabhadra approaching from the gate from afar; his countenance was radiant and his bearing composed. He immediately descended from his seat, went forward to pay homage, and said:
"How strange it is that this evil place has suddenly produced sandalwood trees amidst a forest of eranda!
At that time, Bodhidatta stepped forward to take his seat and asked the King of Ghosts:"
"How many hells are there currently in this eastern region?
The King of Ghosts replied, "Within these mountains there are immeasurable hells; currently, in this one direction alone, there are thirty-two śramaṇa hells."
"What are the names of the thirty-two hells?
The Iron Car, Iron Horse, Iron Ox, and Iron Donkey Hells; the Iron Garment Hell; the Iron Pellet Hell;
the Hell of Molten Copper Poured into the Mouth; the Flowing Fire Hell; the Iron Bed Hell; the Plowing Field Hell;
the Severed Head Hell; the Burnt Feet Hell; and the Iron Spike Hell.
The hells are: the Iron Pellet-Eating Hell, the Flying Knife Hell, the Fire-Brand Hell,
the Flesh-Tearing Hell, the Body-Inflaming Hell, the Fire-Ball-Upright-Mouth Hell, the Dispute Hell, the Rain-of-Fire Hell,
the Flowing-Fire Hell, the Excrement-and-Urine Hell, and the Hooked-Penis Hell.
The Fire-Elephant Hell, the Hell of Bleating Cries, the Hell of Iron Spikes, the Hell of Being Buried Under Collapsing Debris,
the Hell of Burning Hands and Feet, the Hell of Copper Dogs with Hooked Teeth, the Hell of Flaying Skin and Drinking Blood, the Hell of Dissecting the Body,
the Hell of the Iron House, the Hell of the Iron Mountains, and the Hell of Flying Flames.
At that time, the King of Ghosts replied to Bodhidatta:
"The names of the hells where one undergoes punishment are such as these."
In the first fascicle of the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, according to the *Kaiyuan lu* (Kaiyuan Era Catalogue), under the section "Spurious Works that Confuse the Authentic," it states:

"The aforementioned scripture is commonly known among the laity as the *Mātṛka-rākṣasa-buddhanāmasūtra*. It appears to have been compiled in recent times by taking the twelve-fascicle version translated by Dharmaruci and rearranging its contents."

Following the extraction of the titles of various sutras from among them, the names of pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats were then taken to constitute the sequence of the Three Jewels; in total, there are thirty-two items.

After the ritual worship of the Three Jewels, there is always a section for repentance; yet following this repentance, the spurious scripture of the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa is cited and placed at the end, thereby intermingling vulgar, worldly language with the words of the Sages.
Upon investigating those who compiled it, they were entirely mediocre and ignorant. For instance, as stated in the fourth fascicle:

"The *Dharmakṣema Zhuanjing* (Biography of Dharmakṣema’s Translation of the Sūtras). This biography is listed among the *Fǎbǎo* (Treasures of the Dharma), yet it is actually the record of the travels of the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Dharmakṣema to India; it is by no means a sūtra. To place it among the *Fǎbǎo* is an egregious error.
Furthermore, as it says in the ninth fascicle:
This is the name of a single person, chanted in two parts.
These are the names of two individuals, joined together as one.

Such errors and delusions are indeed numerous; as the ignorant masses imitate and practice them, they are transmitted together as perverse and reckless views. Fearing that, unless these are pointed out and clarified, they will defile the True Teaching, I have therefore recorded this account.
The *Zhenyuan lu* states: "This scripture intersperses vulgar, worldly language with the words of the Sage;

although the original text is authentic, because it contains such spurious interpolations, it has been subjected to this critical evaluation and included in the 'Record of Spurious Works that Confuse the Authentic,' and thus may not enter the canon."

This matter of approval and rejection had persisted for several hundred years until the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, when the *Mahābuddhanāmasūtra* was officially promulgated. Ma Chengzhai, General of the Left and Right Gate Guard Armies and Director of the Office of Palace Attendants, submitted a memorial stating:
"The aforementioned scripture has not yet been included in the catalog of the Tripiṭaka; by Imperial Decree, it should be ordered that the relevant authorities include it in the catalog."

Now, regarding errors within this work, I request that what is divided be unified and what is unified be separated; for all such matters, I humbly ask for correction. May it accord with the expectations of those below and fulfill the will of Heaven above, so that it may be included in the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings of the Zhenyuan Era) and transmitted as belonging to the Liang dynasty, appended to the records of that period.
"I have now examined the National Edition of the Tripitaka; within the volumes for the *Hui* and *Han* sections, there is also this scripture in eighteen fascicles.
Comparing this thirty-fascicle version with that edition, although the number of fascicles differs, the wording and meaning are entirely identical."
The repentance texts are otherwise identical; however, this sutra repeats [the passage] twice while that one repeats it thrice.
Furthermore, there are minor differences, such as the presence of the "Pseudo-Sutra of Precious Attainment" (Bǎodá wèijīng) here where it is absent there.
"This apocryphal scripture originally had two titles:
one was the *Mahāyāna-padma-hayagrīva-rākṣasa-sūtra*, which corresponds to the ancient sixteen-fascicle version;
the other was the *Ratnapāla-bodhisattva-questions-on-retribution-of-monks-sūtra*, which lacks the character 'answer' (答)."
This thirty-fascicle version has been combined under this title, yet the character "dá" (answer) has been falsely added.

The *Zhòngjīng mùlù* (Catalogue of All Scriptures), compiled by the śramaṇa Fǎjīng and others during the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, as well as the various catalogues of the Great Tang, all list this *Bǎodá jīng* as a spurious and false work.

Regarding the present *Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas*, previous cataloguers did not record it as either authentic or spurious; the *Kaiyuan Lu* classified it among the false and delusive. To now combine this with the spurious *Sūtra of Precious Attainment* is to add delusion upon delusion.

"The scriptures had not been in the land of Jin for long when those fond of novelty mixed sand with gold; since there was no comprehensive standardization, how could one distinguish the genuine from the counterfeit?"
When a farmer leaves the grain and the weeds together, Hou Ji sighed over it;
when gold and jade are sealed within the same casket, Bian He felt shame for it;
when the Jing and Wei rivers are mixed and dragons and snakes advance side by side, how could one not feel ashamed?

Now, I have listed those works which I consider not to be the Buddha’s sutras in order to demonstrate to future scholars that they are base and contrary to the truth; thus, I have placed this scripture at the very beginning.

The compilers of the catalogues have earnestly requested this; how could the national canon be recorded twice over? Those eighteen fascicles of sutras appear to be those included by imperial decree within the *Zhenyuan lu*, differing only slightly in their division of fascicles.
Later generations, seeing this thirty-fascicle version, mistook it for a different scripture and thus incorporated it.
Now, if one wishes to delete and correct it, then that eighteen-fascicle version—which lacks the spurious *Bao da* (Precious Penetration) section—may be preserved after slight rectification.

However, these thirty fascicles of sutras have been widely circulated in our country for a long time; it is common for people here to rely upon them to cultivate merit. If they were suddenly deleted now, it would surely provoke public resentment, yet it is likewise unreasonable to preserve both. Therefore, in deference to public sentiment, I shall preserve these while deleting those, recording the intentions of the ancients to inform you, O refined and upright gentlemen. As for the places where errors occurred regarding divisions and combinations, I have corrected them accordingly.
As stated in the twelfth fascicle: "Namo Kūṭila-Nanda.
These are the names of two sages; the scripture has erroneously combined them, so they are now divided into two.
"Namo Piṇḍola, Namo Pāṭala. This is the name of a single arhat;
the scripture erroneously divided it, so it is now combined into one.
There are many such instances that cannot be recounted in full. "Alas!

The Great Sage Ānanda was not far removed from the Buddha and was the compiler of the Sūtra-piṭaka; yet when he sought to correct the verse regarding the water-crane of a single monk, the monks ultimately refused to comply—how much more so, then, for me, a mere ordinary person?"
Is the era of the Buddha already so distant?
Are the scriptures and the Dharma transmitted only from afar?

Yet, regarding a canon that has flourished throughout the entire nation for a long time, you suddenly arise alone to edit it, while desiring that the sentiments of the multitude not be provoked against you.
It is like a cicada angrily brandishing its forelegs to stop a chariot, wishing that it not be crushed; this is still insufficient as a metaphor for its impropriety.
Knowing in one's heart that [the teachings] are false and delusive, yet lacking the power to correct them—such is the extent of the decline in the Dharma of the Final Age.

How lamentable! There is but one principle: since the grievance lies in the falsification and confusion of the authentic, if one clearly recognizes that among the titles of various sutras, the names of various arhats, and the texts of repentance, there are places where these were compiled by humans and contain errors, one should correct them according to the original texts of the holy teachings.

One should delete the spurious *Sūtra of Bǎodá* and title it the *Interpolated Sūtra of Repentance and Buddha Names*, so that when people see its name they may distinguish between the host and the guest, just as in the case of various annotated sutras with interlinear commentaries. If it were circulated in this manner, it might perhaps be acceptable for the world.

"I take refuge in these and all other immeasurable and boundless Pratyekabuddhas.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, I shall next perform repentance.
Now, as for what is called repentance, its essence is to reform the past, cultivate the future, extinguish evil, and promote good."
Living in this world, who can be without transgression?

Even those who have studied the Way still give rise to afflictions when their mindfulness lapses; even Arhats manifest karmic actions of body and speech through the movement of residual habits—how much more so, then, for ordinary people, who could possibly be without fault?

However, the wise perceive this first and are thus able to repent and reform; the foolish conceal their faults, causing them to spread like creeping vines, so that through long habituation they remain in the "long night" with no hope of awakening.

If one can, with a sense of shame and remorse, reveal and repent their transgressions, it will not only serve to extinguish their offenses, but will also increase immeasurable merit and establish the wondrous fruit of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.

"If one wishes to practice this dharma, one should first externally solemnize one's physical demeanor to reverently gaze upon the sacred image, and internally arouse a spirit of respect by focusing the mind on the object of contemplation, reaching a state of earnest sincerity and giving rise to two kinds of mental states."

What are these two? First, one reflects: "This life of mine is difficult to preserve forever; it may perish in a single morning, and I do not know when this body might be restored. If I do not encounter the Buddhas and the worthy sages, and should suddenly fall into the company of evil friends to commit various sinful karmas, I shall surely fall again into the deep pits and perilous realms.

Second, one reflects: "In this life, although I have encountered the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and become a disciple of the Buddha—wherein the duty of a disciple is to perpetuate the lineage of the Sages and abide in the wholesome dharmas of purity in body, speech, and mind—yet now we openly commit evils and conceal them, saying that others do not know and that they do not see. We hide them in our hearts, remaining arrogant and shameless; this is truly the height of folly and delusion in the world."

Furthermore, there currently exist the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Bodhisattvas of the great stages, and the celestial immortals; how could they ever fail to behold with their pure divine eyes the evil deeds we commit? Moreover, the spirits of both the hidden and the manifest record our transgressions and merits without the slightest error.

"Now, regarding those who have committed offenses, after their lives have ended, the ox-headed jailers record their spirits and bring them before King Yama to interrogate and determine their right and wrong."

At that time, all one's enemies and adversaries will come forward as witnesses, each saying, "In the past, you slaughtered my body, roasting, boiling, steaming, and grilling it," or saying, "In the past, you plundered all my wealth and property and separated me from my kinsmen."
"Now I have finally found your weakness.
Since you are here before me as living evidence, how could you dare to deny it? You must simply accept your past misdeeds with a willing heart.
As clarified in the sutras, within the hells, no one is punished unjustly."

If, during one's lifetime, the mind feels remorse for the various transgressions previously committed, then all the signs of the places where those evils were created will manifest before them, each saying:
"In the past, you committed such a crime in my presence; how can you now seek to conceal it?"
Thus, there is no place of concealment for those who commit evil deeds.

Thereupon, King Yama gnashes his teeth in reproach and consigns them to hell; for kalpas and throughout the years, they have no means of escape. This matter is not far off, nor does it concern others; it is precisely my own body that acts and my own body that receives the retribution.

Although father and son share the utmost intimacy, when the ultimate moment arrives, there is no one who can take another's place. While our bodies are currently at rest and free from various ailments, each of you should exert yourselves, contending with your very lives to cultivate great fear; for when death is about to arrive, regret will be of no avail. Therefore, disciples, with the utmost sincerity, we take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions.

“Homage to the Buddha Pure Light Destroying Doubt in the East; homage to the Buddha Virtue Free from Sorrow in the South; homage to the Buddha Supernatural Power of the Flower Adornment in the West; homage to the Buddha Pure Moon Palace in the North; homage to the Buddha Destroying All Darkness in the Southeast; homage to the Buddha Great Compassion Beholding Sentient Beings in the Southwest; homage to the Buddha Emitting Radiance of Fragrance in the Northwest; homage to the Buddha Ocean of Immeasurable Virtues in the Northeast; homage to the Buddha Severing All Doubts below; homage to the Buddha Free from All Sorrow above. I take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions.”

From time immemorial until this very day, we have accumulated ignorance that obscures the mind and eyes; following the nature of secondary afflictions, we have created sinful karma across the three periods of time. Whether it was through indulgence in and attachment to defiled objects giving rise to the affliction of greed, or through hatred and anger harboring malice as an affliction, or through dullness, confusion, and stupor failing to comprehend as an affliction, or through the pride of self-exaltation and arrogance as an affliction, or through doubt regarding the Right Path and hesitation as an affliction, or through slandering cause and effect as the affliction of false views, or through failing to recognize dependent origination and clinging to a self as an affliction, or through being deluded about the three periods of time and grasping at annihilationism or eternalism as an affliction, or through associating with evil dharmas and giving rise to the affliction of adherence to views, or through following perverse teachers and creating the affliction of adherence to precepts, even down to the various afflictions of the fourfold attachments and arbitrary conceptualizations—today, with utmost sincerity, we take refuge and repent.
"Furthermore, disciples, from time immemorial until this day, we have harbored the affliction of stinginess by guarding and clinging to things with firm attachment;
the affliction of dissipation by failing to restrain the six sense-faculties; the affliction of impatience through malicious conduct of mind;
the affliction of indolence through laxity and lack of diligence; and the affliction of discursive thought through the agitation of mental deliberation."
The afflictions: the affliction of delusion and ignorance when encountering sensory objects; the affliction of "self" and "other" arising from the eight worldly winds;
the affliction of a crooked mind that flatters and seeks praise; the affliction of being obstinate, difficult to approach, and unharmonious;
the affliction of being quick to anger, difficult to please, and harboring much resentment; and the affliction of jealousy, entanglement, and perverse stubbornness.
The afflictions of vexation, which are fierce, perilous, violent, harmful, deceitful, and poisonous; the afflictions of deviating from the two truths and clinging to signs;

the afflictions that give rise to perversions regarding suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path; the afflictions that follow along with the flow of the twelve links of dependent origination within birth and death;
and even the *āveṇika-avidyā-vāsabhūmi* (the ground of beginningless ignorance) and the *catur-vāsa* (four abodes) of afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The earth is structured by the fruits of suffering and afflictions within the three realms;

such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, vexing and disturbing the worthy and holy ones across the six paths and four modes of birth. Today, we openly confess before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, taking refuge and repenting.

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this confession of all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, in every birth and lifetime, break the banner of arrogance, exhaust the waters of craving and desire, extinguish the fires of anger, shatter the darkness of ignorance, uproot the source of doubt, and tear apart the net of false views. May we deeply realize that the three realms are like a prison, the four elements are like venomous snakes, the five aggregates are like hostile thieves, and the six sense bases are like an empty village where craving feigns intimacy. May we cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to sever the source of nescience, proceeding directly toward Nirvana without ceasing or resting, with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in accord with every thought-moment, and the ten *pāramitās* ever manifest before us."

In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning Retribution for Śramaṇas by Padmaprabha-ratnagati*, Padmaprabha-ratnagati immediately entered the hells. Climbing to the top of a high tower, he looked around in all four directions and saw the sinners, each entering from one of the four gates while wailing and crying out as they approached him.
One enters iron chariots, iron oxen, iron donkeys, and iron horses; these four minor hells constitute one single hell.
Why are they called the Iron Chariot, Iron Horse, Iron Ox, and Iron Donkey Hells?

This hell is fifteen *yojanas* in circumference and breadth. Within it stands an iron city one *yojana* high, where fierce fires blaze with brilliant intensity, burning iron chariots that glow with scorching heat. Inside, there is an iron ox whose body is likewise [burning]; its head, horns, hair, and tail are all like sharp blades, and from within its hair, fire burns while smoke and flames issue forth together.
As for the iron horses, their bodies, manes, and tails have bristles as sharp as the edge of a sword, and from their manes and tails, fire burns while smoke and flames issue forth together;
the iron donkeys are also exactly like this.
Within that hell there are iron spikes as sharp as the points of awls; these iron spikes lie scattered and strewn across the ground, their tips ablaze with a fierce and raging fire.
At that time, within the northern gate, there were five hundred śramaṇas who cried out with the sound of sheep; fire issued from their mouths and eyes as they uttered these words:
"Why must we now undergo such suffering?"
The hell-wardens, yakṣas, and horse-headed rākṣasas grasp three-pronged iron forks with their hands; thrusting them toward the backs of the offenders, they pierce through to emerge from their chests.
Furthermore, iron chains come to entwine their arms, and these chains burst into flames, burning the arms of the sinners.

Furthermore, there are iron collars that shackle the throats of the offenders; these collars have eight corners as sharp as the points of awls, and their fierce, blazing smoke and fire burn the offenders' necks.

At that time, the offenders roll about on the ground and refuse to move forward; the horse-headed rākṣasas seize iron clubs in their hands and strike them upon their heads, so that the offenders' bodies are shattered like fine dust.

Furthermore, hungry ghosts come to eat their flesh, and hungry dogs come to drink their blood; when the horse-headed rākṣasa stamps the ground and cries, "Live!", the sinner immediately comes to life.
At that time, the iron ox bellowed and ran across the ground; the ox bellowing, it came toward the sinner, who, being pressed and squeezed, rolled over and fell to the ground.
The horse-headed rākṣasa seized an iron fork in his hand and impaled him upon a cart.
The sinner leaps up, only to fall again onto an ox; the ox’s hair points upward and pierces him, entering through his belly and exiting through his back.

He leaps again onto a horse, and the horse’s hair likewise pierces him like sharp awls; as the horse shakes its tail, his body is instantly crushed and mangled, yet in a brief moment he returns to life.
At that time, an iron horse raised its hooves and kicked him repeatedly until his body was crushed like dust, yet in a moment he returned to life.

He then mounted an iron donkey, which immediately began to leap and kick; the sinner fell to the ground, and the donkey became violently enraged, raising its hooves and trampling him repeatedly until he died, only to return to life in a moment.
For one day and one night, they undergo immeasurable suffering.

"These śramaṇas received the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha, yet they disregarded the future and cared only for the present. Having violated the pure precepts, they committed evil deeds and kept impure things; they traveled by carriage, horse, or donkey to pursue worldly livelihoods, lacking a heart of kindness and compassion, and failing to maintain dignified deportment while receiving the faithful offerings of others.
Due to these evil causes and conditions, they have fallen into this hell for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas."

"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next proceed to repentance.

All of you, let your bodies and minds be tranquil right now; being free from flattery and hindrances is precisely the time for generating good and extinguishing evil. Furthermore, each of you should give rise to four kinds of contemplative practices as the preliminary means for the extinction of offenses."
Third, observing one’s own body; fourth, observing the body of the Tathāgata. Regarding the first observation of causes and conditions:

one knows that these transgressions of mine stem from ignorance and unwholesome reflection; lacking the power of right observation, I failed to recognize my faults. Having distanced myself from virtuous friends—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—I followed the path of Māra along treacherous and deviant tracks. I was like a fish swallowing a hook without knowing its peril, like a silkworm making a cocoon to entangle and bind itself, or like a moth rushing into a flame to burn and rot itself.
For these reasons, one cannot emerge by oneself.

Second, regarding the contemplation of karmic retribution: all evil and unwholesome deeds result in the endless fruits of suffering as one transmigrates through the three periods of time; one sinks into the vast ocean of the great night of boundlessness, devoured by the rākṣasas of the afflictions.

The future cycle of birth and death is obscure and boundless; even if one were to obtain the retribution of becoming a Cakravartin King, ruling over the four continents with sovereign power of flight and possessing the seven treasures, one would still inevitably fall into the evil realms after the end of life.

Even those who have attained the fruits of the four formless absorptions—the most exalted state within the three realms—will, once their merit is exhausted, become worms in the head of an ox; how much more so for others who lack merit and yet remain indolent, failing to diligently practice repentance?
This is also like holding a stone and sinking into a deep abyss; it is extremely difficult to seek deliverance.

"Third, I contemplate my own person: although I possess the true cause—the nature of numinous awareness—it is shrouded by the dense forest of the darkness of afflictions; lacking the power of the enabling cause, it cannot be made manifest."

I should now give rise to the supreme mind, shatter the heavy obstacles of ignorance and perversion, sever the false causes of birth-and-death suffering, manifest the great luminous wisdom of the Tathāgata, and establish the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

"Fourth, one contemplates the body of the Tathāgata: unconditioned, quiescent, and luminous, transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations; it is replete with all virtues, profound and eternally abiding.
Although he manifests entry into parinirvāṇa through skillful means, his compassionate rescue and reception of beings have never for a moment ceased."
To give rise to such a mind may be called an excellent ford for extinguishing transgressions and an essential practice for removing obstacles.
Today, with a sincere heart, we prostrate and take refuge in the Buddha.

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, you have nurtured afflictions that grow ever deeper, ever thicker, ever more abundant, and ever more luxuriant. They shroud the eye of wisdom so that nothing may be seen; they sever all wholesome roots so that they cannot continue; and they give rise to obstacles such that you do not see the Buddha, do not hear the True Dharma, and do not encounter the Noble Sangha."
The afflictions that give rise to obstructions: the obstruction of afflictions whereby one does not perceive the wholesome and unwholesome karmic actions throughout all past and future worlds;

the obstruction of afflictions whereby one receives the retributive fruits of human, celestial, or noble status; the obstruction of afflictions whereby one attains the meditative concentrations, blessings, and pleasures of the form and formless realms;
and the obstruction whereby one fails to attain mastery over supernatural powers, such as flying, ascending, becoming invisible, or manifesting.
The afflictive hindrances to going everywhere to the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions to hear the Dharma;

the afflictive hindrances to learning the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) and the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); the afflictive hindrances to learning the causes and conditions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity (*maitrī-karuṇā-muditopekṣā*);

the afflictive hindrances to learning the meaning of the seven expedient means and the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*); and the afflictive hindrances to learning the stages of warmth, summits, and patience (*uṣmagata-mūrdhan-kṣānti*) within the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

The afflictive hindrances: the afflictive hindrance regarding the foremost dharmas of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation; the afflictive hindrance regarding the realization of emptiness, equality, and the Middle Way;

the afflictive hindrance regarding the manifestation of signs while practicing the Eightfold Noble Path; the afflictive hindrance regarding the non-manifestation of signs while practicing the Seven Factors of Enlightenment;
the afflictive hindrance regarding the contemplation of causes and conditions within the factors of enlightenment; and the [hindrance] regarding the eight...
One removes the afflictive hindrances regarding the nine liberations and emptiness; one removes the afflictive hindrances regarding the training in the ten knowledges and samādhis;

one removes the afflictive hindrances regarding the training in the three clarities, the six supernormal powers, and the four unhindered knowledges; and one removes the afflictive hindrances regarding the training in the six perfections and the four immeasurables.

The afflictive hindrances in learning the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to extensively transform others; the afflictive hindrances in learning the Mahāyāna mind and the four great vows; the afflictive hindrances in learning the ten clarities and the ten practices; and the afflictive hindrances in learning the ten dedications and the ten vows.

The afflictive hindrances to clear understanding on the first, second, third, and fourth stages; the afflictive hindrances to various knowledges and views on the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages; the afflictive hindrances to the dual illumination practiced on the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages; and likewise, up to the supreme afflictive hindrances that obstruct the study of the one million *asaṃkhyeya* practices of the Buddha-fruit—such hindrances to practice are immeasurable and boundless.

Today I come before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly, with utmost sincerity and prostration, to confess with shame and remorse, praying that all [obstacles] may be extinguished.
By virtue of this confession, may all afflictive obstacles within the various modes of conditioned existence be forever exhausted without remainder."

May the disciples, wherever they may be born, attain mastery over their rebirth and not be turned about by the power of karmic fetters; through the supernormal power of *ṛddhi*, may they reach all the pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions in a single thought-moment to gather and transform sentient beings; may they penetrate without obstruction the profound realms of various meditative concentrations as well as all forms of knowledge and vision; may their minds universally encompass all phenomena, and may they possess inexhaustible eloquence while remaining unstained by attachment.

Having attained mastery over the mind and mastery over the Dharma, with mastery in wisdom and mastery in skillful means, they bring these afflictions and the habitual tendencies of ignorance to a final and eternal end so that they no longer continue; the untainted noble path shines forth as brightly as the sun.

In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning Retribution for Śramaṇas*, at that time, Bodhisattva Padmaratnadatta entered yet another hell, named the Hell of Iron Garments (*Ayas-kavaca*).

That hell is sixteen yojanas in length, breadth, and circumference. Within that hell are iron spikes as sharp as the points of awls, spread across the entire ground; smoke and flames blaze forth, and iron garments burn with fire, their burning brilliance wandering throughout the prison.
In the midst of the eastern gate were eight hundred śramaṇas, who looked up toward heaven, beat their breasts, and cried out loudly, saying these words:
"By what sin have we now come to enter this place?"
He rolled over and fell to the ground, unable to move forward again.
The horse-headed rākṣasa seized a three-pronged iron fork with his hand and thrust it through his back; it emerged from his chest, and flames burst forth from his entire body.
The horse-headed rākṣasa grasps an iron hook with his hand and thrusts it toward the skeleton; if the iron hook makes contact, flames erupt simultaneously.
The sinner writhes about and refuses to come forward, whereupon the horse-headed rākṣasa seizes an iron mallet with his hand and hews at the head.

Furthermore, iron dogs come to devour their flesh, and hungry ghosts come to drink their blood. Within that hell, iron garments come tumbling down to clothe the offenders; some are placed upon their heads, some upon their feet, and as they cover their entire bodies, flames erupt. For one day and one night, they undergo immeasurable suffering.
Bao Da asked the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa,
"Why do these śramaṇas, who were once sinners, undergo such punishments?

"These śramaṇas, who are sinners, received the pure precepts of the Buddha but failed to protect their dignified deportment; they abandoned the robes of the True Dharma and instead wore secular clothing rather than the Dharma-robes. Because of these evil causes and conditions that violate the pure prohibitions of the Buddha, they have fallen into this hell."
Upon hearing this, Bao Da wept bitterly and said: "How can you,
a son of the Śramaṇas, who is called one who has transcended the three realms,
fail to exercise self-restraint and fall into such an evil path?"
Why did you not exercise self-restraint, so as to undergo such great suffering?
How may one attain peace and security?
Such a person is called one who has attained liberation.
After Bodhidharma had spoken this verse, he departed.

“With the Tathāgata Jvalanolkā as the foremost,
and the Tathāgata Abhayadarśin as the foremost—
with these and other such foremost Buddhas, I pervade the ten directions with my physical, verbal, and mental actions, simultaneously paying homage, praising, and making offerings to them all.”

Regarding the profound realms of the Dharma taught by those Buddhas—the immeasurable realm, the inconceivable realm, the infinite realm, and so forth—I shall pervade the ten directions with my physical, verbal, and mental actions to pay homage, offer praise, and present offerings.

Regarding those Buddha-worlds, I—with my entire body, speech, and mind—pervade the ten directions to prostrate with my head at the feet, praise, and make offerings to the assembly of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas and the assembly of non-retrogressive Śrāvakas.
