"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we shall next perform repentance.
'Disciples! Having briefly completed the repentance for the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), we shall now proceed in order to repent for the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*')."

Indeed, karma is able to adorn and embellish every realm of existence, wherever they may be; therefore, one should contemplate seeking liberation from the world. That the retributions of the six paths are diverse and the forms and species of beings differ from one another—know that all these are produced by the power of karma.
"Therefore, among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of karma is most profound; ordinary people frequently give rise to doubts and delusions regarding it. Why is this so?"
We observe in the world that those who practice virtue encounter misfortune and adversity, while those who commit evil meet with success and fortune at every turn;
thus, it is said that in this world there is no distinction between good and evil.
Those who calculate in this manner are all unable to penetrate deeply into the principles of karma.
Why is this so? For it is stated in the sūtras that there are three kinds of karma.
First, retribution in the present life;
second, retribution in the next life; [and third, retribution in subsequent lives].
Third is retribution in a future life.
Regarding karma that yields retribution in the present life: one performs good or evil deeds in the present and receives the retribution in this very body.
Regarding karma that yields retribution in the next life: one performs good or evil deeds in this life and receives the retribution in the life to come.

Regarding karma that ripens in subsequent lives: it may be that good or evil deeds performed during immeasurable past lives are experienced either in this very life, or their retribution is experienced only in immeasurable future lives, both present and yet to come.

That those who previously committed evil appear to experience well-being in the present is because the maturation of wholesome karma from past lives—whether as a result in this life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*) or a subsequent result (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*)—is ripening; thus, there is this fruit of happiness in the present. How could it be related to the performance of various evil deeds in the present that one receives a favorable retribution?

When a person who practices virtue experiences suffering in the present life, it is because the retributive effects of evil karma from past lives—whether ripening in this lifetime or in subsequent lifetimes—have matured; since the power of their current roots of goodness is weak and cannot dispel them, they receive this bitter retribution. How could this possibly be related to performing good deeds in the present that would invite such an evil retribution?
How is this known to be so?
We see in the present world that those who perform wholesome deeds are praised by others and respected by others; therefore, we know that they will surely bring about pleasant fruits in the future.

Since one possesses such evil karma from the past, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct one to draw near to virtuous friends and practice repentance together; for a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is of complete benefit in the attainment of the Way.
Therefore, we disciples today take refuge in the Buddha with utmost sincerity: Namo to the Buddha Immeasurable Freedom from Defilement in the East;

Namo to the Buddha Tree-Root Flower King in the South; Namo to the Buddha Lotus Sovereign in the West; Namo to the Buddha Vajra Capable of Destruction in the North; Namo to the Buddha Supreme in the Meaning of *Siddhānta* in the Southeast; Namo to the Buddha Sovereign King of the Golden Ocean in the Southwest; Namo to the Buddha Sovereign King of Boundless Dharma in the Northwest; Namo to the Buddha Unobstructed Fragrant Elephant King in the Northeast; Namo to the Buddha Banner of Unobstructed Wisdom in the Nadir; Namo to the Buddha Supreme King of Ambrosia in the Zenith. We take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space.
"Disciples, from time immemorial until this day, we have accumulated evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and committed sins that fill the heavens and earth.
Through discarding one body and receiving another, we were neither aware nor cognizant of our actions;
we may have committed the grave and dense entanglements of the five heinous crimes and the karma of the Avīci hell, or we may have become icchantikas who sever all roots of goodness."
The karma of lightly misrepresenting the Buddha’s words and slandering the Vaipulya sutras; the karma of destroying the Triple Gem and subverting the True Dharma;
the karma of disbelieving in sin and merit while giving rise to the ten non-virtuous actions; the karma of delusion and ignorance that turns one away from the truth and the correct path;

the karma of filial impiety toward one's two parents and perverse rebellion; the karma of treating teachers and elders with contempt and lacking in ritual respect; and the lack of trust between friends.
They commit unrighteous deeds, or perform acts that constitute the four grave offenses, the six grave offenses, or the eight grave offenses which obstruct the Path of the Sages;
they violate the five precepts and break the eight observances; they frequently neglect and transgress the five categories and seven groups of offenses;
and they commit light or heavy defiled offenses against the Upāsaka precepts.
"Or, the Bodhisattva precepts may not be pure as prescribed for their practice; the preliminary and concluding expedients may defile the holy conduct (*brahmacarya*);
there may be the karma of indolence regarding the six monthly fasts; the practice may not be constantly cultivated during the three long fasts of the year;
the three thousand dignified demeanors may not accord with the Dharma; and there may be the karma of subtle transgressions regarding the eighty thousand rules of discipline."
They cultivate the karma of body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; yet throughout the eight royal seasons of spring and autumn, they commit various karmas of transgression.
They practice sixteen kinds of evil non-virtuous disciplines (*akuśala-asaṃvara-karma*); they have no karma of compassion toward suffering sentient beings;
they have no karma of pity, mindfulness, or mercy; they have no karma of rescue, salvation, or protection; and their minds harbor jealousy and envy, lacking the means to deliver others.
Karma that is unequal toward the objects of enemies and kin; karma of indulgence in the five desires without weariness or renunciation;
or karma of dissipation arising from food, clothing, gardens, groves, ponds, or pools; or the commission of various sinful karmas through unrestrained passion in one’s prime of life;
or wholesome *sāsrava* (outflowing) karma dedicated toward the three realms of existence, which obstructs supramundane karma—as [in the case of]...
These karmas are immeasurable and boundless; today we openly confess them before the Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Sangha of the ten directions, taking refuge and repenting.

“May we disciples, by virtue of the merit and goodness arising from this confession of the sins of the *ānantarya* [immediate retribution] and other transgressions, vow that in every birth and lifetime we shall extinguish the five heinous crimes and eliminate the delusions of the *icchantika*. From this day forth until we reach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), we swear never again to commit such light or heavy offenses. We shall constantly practice the supramundane, pure, and wholesome dharmas; we shall diligently uphold the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) and guard our majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), like one crossing the ocean who cherishes a life-preserving float. We shall always take the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) as our foremost practice. May the categories of morality, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*) ever further increase and become luminous. May we swiftly accomplish the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Tathāgata, the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the three types of mindfulness, and the constant delight in wondrous wisdom and the eightfold self-mastery.”
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Regarding Retribution for Śramaṇas*, as told by Padmadhara (Bao-da), he further entered the Hell of Molten Copper Poured into the Mouth.
Why is it called the Hell of Molten Copper Poured into the Mouth?

That hell is twenty-four yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded by iron walls and covered with an iron net, where flames blaze intensely and smoke and fire burn together without ceasing, while jagged iron spikes are strewn across its ground.

The ground is ablaze with fire reaching up to the iron netting; it penetrates from top to bottom and from bottom to top. Smoke and flames burn fiercely, scorching and boiling the offenders. Within that hell, there flows a great iron pool, from which glowing embers and fiery smoke issue forth; these blazing iron embers pour down like flowing water, drenching the mouths of the offenders.
At that time, within the southern gate there were fifty śramaṇas, from whose mouths and eyes flames issued forth as they cried out these words:
"How is it that we must now undergo such suffering?"
He rolled about on the ground, refusing to rise.

The horse-headed rākṣasa seized him with a three-pronged iron fork, trampling the ground and thrusting it at him; from the prongs of the fork, flames burst forth together, burning the sinner’s heart until he died in an instant and was restored to life in an instant.
Furthermore, iron hooks come to hook their tongues; iron clubs come to strike their heads; and flying blades come to flay their flesh.

The horse-headed rākṣasas lead the śramaṇas into the river of flowing fire. The horse-headed rākṣasas hold iron winnowing baskets in their hands, scoop up glowing iron sparks, and pour them toward the mouths [of the beings]. The iron pellets enter through the mouth and exit from the back; smoke and flames blaze forth simultaneously from the six orifices of the mouth and eyes, with the iron pellets falling in continuous succession without pause.
Bao Da asked the horse-headed rākṣasa,
"What sins did these śramaṇas commit to suffer such torment?

"These śramaṇas do not uphold the Buddha's precepts and do not fear the retribution of suffering; they greedily seek gain, offerings, fame, and renown, their hearts lacking shame or remorse, yet they claim to maintain pure conduct while having transgressed the four grave prohibitions."

Having previously accepted the faithful offerings of others, one greedily craves food and drink; though laypeople’s gifts are heavy and extremely difficult to digest, one claims, "I can digest them. Ignorant of the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, and the principle of dependent origination, such a person is like the great ocean, never knowing contentment.
"By these causes and conditions, they shall fall into the suffering of hell for thousands of millions of kalpas; when they are reborn as humans, they will be mute and unable to speak.
Upon hearing this, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi wept with sorrow and spoke these words:
"How is it that those who have attained liberation now undergo such suffering?"
How is it that one who has crossed the ocean sinks back into the great sea?
How is it that one who possesses great wealth and status falls back into poverty and distress?
How is it that one who has received the pure precepts commits transgressions without fear?
"Will one fall back into the path of wrong views?
Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi spoke this verse and departed.

"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next perform repentance.
'Disciples! We have now repented of all karmic actions through their general characteristics; we shall now proceed to repent of each one individually according to its specific characteristics. "
Whether collectively or individually, whether coarse or subtle, whether light or heavy, whether spoken or unspoken—may all such categories of afflictions be extinguished through this mutual accord.

As for the specific confession (*viśeṣa-pratikramaṇa*), first confess the three transgressions of the body, then the four of the mouth, and subsequently prostrate in repentance for all remaining obstacles in their proper order.

Regarding the three karmas of the body, the first is killing. As clarified in the sutras, one may take oneself as an analogy: do not kill, do not wield the rod. Although there is a distinction between humans and animals, the fact that all cherish life and fear death is the same for them all.

If one investigates these sentient beings from time immemorial, they may have been one's own parents, brothers, or members of the six types of close kin; yet, due to the causes and conditions of karma, they have transmigrated through the six realms, passing through birth and death, changing forms and receiving retributions until they were no longer recognized, and now you give rise to malice by devouring their flesh, severing the seed of great compassion.
"Even if one obtains leftover food, one should regard it as if eating the flesh of one's own child during a time of famine; how much more so should one refrain from eating this fish and meat?"
"To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase the flesh of sentient beings with money—both are evil karmas;
upon death, one falls into the Raurava Hell."
Thus we know that the sins of killing and eating [flesh] are as deep as rivers and seas, and more grievous than hills and mountains.
Yet from time immemorial, we disciples, failing to encounter virtuous friends, have all engaged in these karmic acts.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that the sin of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo suffering.

If they are born among animals, they may receive the bodies of tigers, dogs, jackals, wolves, hawks, or falcons; or they may receive the bodies of venomous snakes, vipers, scorpions, and the like, constantly harboring evil intentions; or they may receive the bodies of deer, bears, brown bears, and so forth, constantly filled with terror.
If one is born among humans, one will receive two kinds of retributive results:
second, having one's life cut short.
Since there are such immeasurable and various evil retributions for killing and devouring,
therefore, disciples, today you must come before me with bowed heads and, with utmost sincerity, take refuge in the Buddha.

“Homage to the Buddha who Extinguishes All Fears in the East; homage to the Buddha Moon-Sun-Lamp-Light in the South; homage to the Buddha Awakened Flower Light in the West; homage to the Buddha Who Has Set Forth Merit in the North; homage to the Buddha Who Dispels the Darkness of All Delusions in the Southeast; homage to the Buddha Unborn Sovereign in the Southwest; homage to the Buddha Great King of Great Supernatural Powers in the Northwest; homage to the Buddha Void and Undefiled Mind in the Northeast; homage to the Buddha Identical Form Void-Non-Existence below; homage to the Buddha Superior Vaidūrya Treasury above. I take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions.”

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, since this mind-consciousness has existed, we have constantly harbored cruel poison and lacked a heart of compassion. Whether through greed we committed killing, or through hatred, delusion, or pride; whether by employing evil means, vowing to kill, wishing to kill, or using incantations to kill; whether by breaching lakes and ponds, burning mountains and forests for hunting or fishing; or by setting fires driven by the wind, releasing hawks and dogs to harass and harm all sentient beings of the six realms—such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless. Today, with a sincere heart, we take refuge and repent."

"Or they use snares, traps, spears, halberds, bows, and crossbows to shoot and strike birds and wild beasts; or they use nets, weirs, and hooks to scoop up and filter aquatic creatures such as fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, shrimp, clams, and bivalves that dwell in the water, leaving those on land, in the water, and in the air with no place to hide or flee. Or they raise chickens, pigs, cattle, sheep, dogs, swine, geese, and ducks for their own kitchens or to sell for slaughter, causing their cries of distress to end before their feathers and fur have fallen out or their scales and shells have been destroyed. Their bodies and heads are severed, their flesh and bones crushed to pieces, and they are flayed, split, butchered, roasted, boiled, and grilled—inflicting cruel and agonizing suffering upon these innocent beings."

One merely seeks momentary gratification for the mouth, yet the flavor obtained is extremely meager—no more than what passes the three-inch root of the tongue—whereas the retribution for such sins will persist through eternal kalpas.

For such transgressions as these, today with utmost sincerity, I take refuge and repent. Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, I may have raised armies to invade and conquer, engaging in strife and contention;

opposing two ranks of troops, we have mutually slaughtered one another, or have killed others myself, or incited others to kill, or rejoiced upon hearing of killings. I may have practiced butchery and slicing, served as an executioner, or slaughtered the lives of others, committing acts of unbearable cruelty. I may have indulged in fits of rage, brandishing halberds and grasping blades, cutting, piercing, or pushing beings into pits and ditches; drowning them in water, blocking their burrows, destroying their nests, or crushing them with earth and stones; or using chariots and horses to trample and crush all sentient beings.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we reveal them, take refuge, and repent.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, we have irrigated dry fields, caused abortions and miscarriages, destroyed eggs and nests, used poisons and sorcery to injure and kill sentient beings, and plowed the earth and dug the ground to plant gardens and orchards.
They raise silkworms and boil cocoons; they raise cats and allow them to seize and kill mice, resulting in excessive injury and slaughter.
Or they strike and beat mosquitoes, gadflies, horseflies, bees, scorpions, and wasps; they pinch and crush fleas and lice.

Or they burn away refuse and clear ditches and channels, causing the wrongful harm of all living beings. Or they consume fruits and grains, or water and vegetables, thereby killing many creatures in vain.
In birth, one may burn various insects by lighting firewood or leaving lamps and candles unattended;
or consume sauces and vinegar without checking for moving life; or pour hot water to kill insects and ants.
In this way, throughout the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—one constantly injures and kills subtle beings, whether flying in the air or dwelling upon the ground.
Because our ordinary consciousness is obscured, we have failed to perceive and remain ignorant; today we reveal these faults, take refuge, and repent.

From time immemorial until this very day, we have used various evil means to afflict sentient beings—such as using whips, staves, shackles, fetters, and stocks; pressing them down, interrogating them, beating and throwing them; trampling them with hands and feet; binding and tethering them; or depriving them of water and grain. In all such ways, we have caused suffering through these diverse and wicked expedients.
Today, with utmost sincerity, we turn toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages; we take refuge and repent.

"We pray that by the merit arising from this repentance for the sins of killing and so forth, may we, throughout all our future lives, attain adamantine bodies with inexhaustible lifespans; may we forever be free from enmity and hatred, harboring no thought of killing; and may we attain the stage of regarding all sentient beings as one's only child. Should we encounter those in peril or urgent distress, may we not spare our own bodies or lives, but employ skillful means to rescue and liberate them. Thereafter, we shall preach the subtle and wondrous True Dharma, so that all sentient beings—upon seeing our forms or even shadows—shall receive peace and happiness, and upon hearing our names or voices, their terrors shall be entirely dispelled."
In the *Mahāyāna-padma-ratna-bodhi-praśnottara-vipāka-śramaṇa-sūtra*, Bodhi entered the Hell of Flowing Fire shortly thereafter.
Why is it called the Hell of Flowing Fire?

That hell is two hundred yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded by iron walls with an iron net covering it above. Fierce fires blaze intensely, their smoke and flames piercingly bright; iron spikes and sharp-edged weapons are strewn across the ground, and within the hell, streams of fire and rising smoke and flames coexist.

In the midst of the Western Gate, six hundred offenders were crying out with loud voices; their entire bodies were ablaze with flames that burned most fiercely and intensely. These sinful śramaṇas cried out these words:
"For what sin have we now come to this place?"
He leaped and writhed, yet refused to move forward.

The rākṣasa at the horse's head slapped his own ears, causing fire to erupt from his mouth and eyes; he seized a sharp blade and struck toward the [practitioner’s] head. Furthermore, hungry dogs came to devour his flesh, hungry ghosts came to drink his blood, and flying birds came to feast upon his marrow.

The horse-headed rākṣasa seizes his arm and drags him along; fire blazes from his hands, and as soon as it occurs, burning flames pour over his body, scorching and rotting him throughout. For one day and one night he undergoes immeasurable suffering, dying and being reborn a thousand times, ten thousand times, a hundred thousand times.
Bao Da asked the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa,
"By what causes and conditions have these śramaṇas incurred such retribution?
The Horse-Headed Rākṣasa replied to Bao Da:

"These śramaṇas received the pure precepts of the Buddha but did not maintain them with purity; they accepted the faithful offerings of others—willow twigs for cleansing, water for rinsing, and fragrant baths—and wandered through the world carrying alms bowls to beg for food. While possessing the outward form of a śramaṇa, they lacked shame and remorse; by these causes and conditions, they have fallen into this hell."
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with sorrow and shed tears, then spoke these verses:
"How is it that one who is unbound Is cast back into the prison cell?"
How is it that one who has emerged from birth and death, returns again to the three evil realms?
How is it that one who encounters a floating log, having beheld the light, returns once more to darkness?
How is it that a blown-out fire suddenly flares up again with fierce intensity?
"The person of pure conduct and liberation now endures great suffering.
Having spoken this verse, Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi departed.

"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next perform repentance. Disciples!
We now repent for the karma of stealing. As it is said in the sutras:"
"If an object belongs to another and is guarded by another, one should not take even a single blade of grass or a single leaf from it without being given; how much less so should one steal?
Yet sentient beings, seeing only the benefits of the present, seize through various unrighteous means, thereby causing themselves to suffer these calamities and consequences in the future."
"The sin of stealing can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo suffering.
If they are born among animals, they take on the forms of oxen, horses, donkeys, mules, camels, and the like, using their physical strength, blood, and flesh to repay the debts of their past lives."

"If one is born among humans as a slave or servant to others, their clothing does not cover their body and their food does not suffice for their life; they suffer the hardships of poverty and destitution until human dignity is nearly extinguished.
Since robbery and theft entail such bitter retributions, therefore, disciples!

Having arrived here today, I prostrate and take refuge in the Buddha: Namo to the Buddha Destroyer of All Afflictions in the East; Namo to the Buddha Sovereign of Wondrous Sound in the South; Namo to the Buddha Great Cloud Radiance in the West; Namo to the Buddha Sovereign King of Clouds in the North; Namo to the Buddha Adorned with Unconditioned Causes in the Southeast; Namo to the Buddha Transcending All Mara Realms in the Southwest; Namo to the Buddha Seeing No Fear in the Northwest; Namo to the Buddha Adorned with All Virtues in the Northeast; Namo to the Buddha Lotus Treasury Radiance in the Upper Direction; Namo to the Buddha Sovereign King of Wondrous Abiding in the Lower Direction. I take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, we have perhaps stolen the wealth and treasures of others, seizing them by force with blades raised; or we have taken them by coercion, relying on our own physical strength; or we have relied on official authority or feigned power, using high stocks and heavy shackles to unjustly oppress the virtuous and good, swallowing bribes and perverting the upright into the crooked."

For these reasons, one becomes ensnared in the net of bodily laws; or, subjecting oneself to corrupt governance, one misappropriates the wealth of others—encroaching upon the public for private gain or encroaching upon the private for public benefit, harming others to profit oneself or profiting others at one's own expense, depriving them while enriching oneself with both mouth and heart full of stinginess; or, one steals and embezzles rents and assessments, surreptitiously evades customs duties, and conceals or hides public taxes and levies so that they are lost to the state.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, I take refuge and repent.

"Whether it be taking without being given the property of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; or property belonging to scriptures and images; or property for the maintenance of stupas and temples; or property intended for offerings to the resident monastic community (*saṃgha*); or property designated for the *cāturmahārājakāyika* (universal) monastic community; or stealing and misusing such items; or refusing to return them out of reliance on one's power; or lending them oneself to others; or engaging in fraudulent exchanges, omissions, or falsehoods; or confusing and intermingling the property of the Three Jewels; or using the property of the monastic community—such as grain, rice, firewood, ginger, fermented soybeans, sauce, vinegar, vegetables, fruits, money, silk, bamboo, wood, brocade, banners, canopies, incense, flowers, oil, and candles—according to one's own whims and desires; or promising to give property to the Three Jewels but deceivingly failing to do so; or using it oneself or giving it to others; or plucking flowers or fruit from a Buddha image to use for the monastic community’s garlands; or using the wealth of the Three Jewels for private personal gain."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we reveal and repent them.

From time immemorial until this day, whether acting as friends, associates, preceptors, teachers, fellow students, parents, brothers, or members of the six types of kinship, we have lived and resided together. Regarding the hundreds of necessities for life, we have deceived one another; or, among neighbors and close relatives, we have shifted fences and expanded walls, encroaching upon and seizing lands and houses, or altered boundaries and exchanged properties.
I have plundered fields and gardens, using public office to serve private ends, seizing the dwellings and shops of others as well as their cultivated lands and wild tracts.
Such offenses are immeasurable and boundless; today I reveal them, take refuge, and repent.

From time immemorial until this very day, we have perhaps besieged cities and broken towns, burned villages and destroyed stockades; we have stolen and sold free citizens or enticed away the servants of others. Or again, we have unjustly oppressed the innocent, causing them to be mangled by blades and their bodies bound in fetters; their family estates were scattered and their kin separated, parted across different cities with life and death forever severed."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we reveal and repent of them.

From time immemorial until this day, whether engaged in trade as merchants or managing shops and markets, we have used light scales and small measures, reducing weights and dimensions; we have stolen fractions of a grain and deceived others regarding the *gui* and *he*; we have exchanged coarse goods for the fine and short items for the long, employing hundreds of clever deceptions in the hope of gaining even a hair’s breadth of profit.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent. Furthermore, disciples!

From time immemorial until this day, we have breached walls and leaped over fences, waylaid travelers and plundered them; we have resisted debts and interest, violated agreements, and practiced deception through face and word. We have unlawfully seized and robbed the beings of the four modes of birth—gods, ghosts, spirits, birds, beasts, and others—or falsely relied upon divination and physiognomy to take people’s wealth and treasures. Thus, even to the extent of seeking profit through profit, we have pursued evil gains and excessive desires without satiety or contentment.

Such offenses as these are immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be fully described; today, having arrived before the Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly of the ten directions, I take refuge and repent.

“May we disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance for the sins of robbery and so forth, in every birth and every life obtain wish-fulfilling jewels; may the seven treasures and exquisite garments rain down constantly, along with ambrosia of a hundred flavors and various medicinal decoctions; and may whatever is required according to our wishes arrive as soon as it is thought of.”

All sentient beings are without the characteristic of theft or plunder; all are able to have few desires and know contentment, neither indulging nor being stained by worldly things. They always delight in the practice of giving and the path of urgent relief, regarding their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains as they would spit or snot, dedicating these acts toward the fulfillment of the dāna-pāramitā.
In the *Mahāyāna Padma-ratna-bodhi-praśna-vyākaraṇa-sādhana-śramaṇa-sūtra*, Bodhi entered the Iron Bed Hell shortly thereafter.
What is meant by the Iron Bed Hell?

This hell is fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth; it is surrounded by iron walls and covered above by an iron net. Fierce flames blaze intensely throughout the entire prison, while iron spikes and iron tongs are strewn across its ground. Smoke and fire erupt violently, blazing fiercely in all four directions. Within it stands an iron bed upon which sharp blades are fixed, as keen as the points of awls; fire issues from them, with continuous, intense flames burning together.
In the midst of the eastern gate were seven hundred śramaṇas, pointing their fingers toward the sky and crying out:
"Alas! For what sin have we now come here?"
He leaps and rolls about, crying out in a loud voice.

The horse-headed rākṣasa seizes him with a three-pronged iron fork and thrusts it through his waist until it emerges from his navel; he is then laid upon an iron bed and stabbed upward with a sharp blade so that it pierces both his belly and back. He dies a thousand times and revives a thousand times, dying ten thousand times and reviving ten thousand times. Day and night he undergoes immeasurable suffering, and when he finally emerges from hell to be born among humans, his sense faculties are incomplete.
Bao Da asked the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa,
"What karmic actions did this śramaṇa perform to receive such punishment?

"These śramaṇas have received the pure precepts of the Buddha, yet they do not seek the unsurpassed path of the Buddha in the future; instead, they seek only fame and profit in the present, violating the four grave prohibitions and the eighty thousand rules of decorum."

Craving offerings of faith like fire finding grass, they know no satisfaction; they sit upon the beds and seats of others improperly; they sleep together with laypeople according to the ways of the laity; they sit upon the Buddha’s throne and tread upon the seats where their teachers sat; and they lie beneath the cool shade of their teachers’ statues—for these causes and conditions, they fall into this hell.
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with grief and said:
"The Sun of Wisdom has fallen into the great ocean; though it had already attained the gates of liberation, it is once again bound.

I take refuge in these and all other such immeasurable and boundless Pratyekabuddhas.”
"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next perform repentance.
Disciples! With a sincere heart, we repent for the sins of greed and desire."
"It is solely because they are shut in by craving within the prison of delusion that sentient beings are submerged in the river of birth and death, unable to emerge.

Due to these causes and conditions of the five desires, sentient beings have wandered through birth and death since time immemorial. The bones accumulated by each and every sentient being within a single kalpa would equal Mount Vipula at Rājagṛha; the milk they have drunk from their mothers equals the waters of the four oceans; and the blood shed from their bodies exceeds even this.

When parents, brothers, and the six classes of kinsmen and relatives pass away, the tears shed by their weeping are as vast as the waters of the four oceans. Therefore it is said: "Where there is craving, there is birth; where craving is exhausted, there is cessation. Thus one knows that craving is the root of birth and death.

"The sin of sexual desire can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo suffering; if they are born as animals, they receive the bodies of pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, and the like; if they are born among humans, their wives will not be chaste and virtuous, and they will obtain a retinue that does not accord with their wishes. Since sexual desire possesses such evil karma," [it must be abandoned].
"Therefore, disciples! Today, with a sincere heart, we prostrate ourselves and take refuge in the Buddha.

Homage to the Buddha Lion’s Roar King in the East; Homage to the Buddha Great Cloud Treasury in the South; Homage to the Buddha Immeasurable Life in the West; Homage to the Buddha Red Lotus Light in the North; Homage to the Buddha Stainless Lapis Lazuli in the Southeast; Homage to the Buddha Supreme Subduer in the Southwest; Homage to the Buddha Virtue Born from Scattered Flowers in the Northwest; Homage to the Buddha Mind Like Space in the Northeast; Homage to the Buddha King of Stainless Renown in the Nadir; Homage to the Buddha Pure Ocean of Wisdom in the Zenith. We take refuge in all the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space."

We, the disciples, from time immemorial until this very day, have either taken the wives or concubines of others, seized the women of others, violated those of pure integrity, defiled *bhikṣuṇīs*, and disrupted the *brahmacarya* of others through immoral coercion; we have looked upon them with turbid minds and evil glances, making lewd jests and taunts; or we have brought shame upon the families of others, tarnishing the reputations of the virtuous and good; or we have committed impure acts toward men of the five types of persons.
Such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we take refuge and repent. "Disciples!

From time immemorial until this day, some have received female bodies whose minds are like wild horses, constantly dissolute and never for a single moment settled, always harboring deviant thoughts and perpetually giving rise to desires."
Or, while at a monastery or assembly hall, they have no intention of listening to the Dharma but instead constantly gaze with greedy eyes;

or, out of lust for śramaṇas, they corrupt other men, showing no reverence for the Buddha-Dharma and indulging their lewd passions at will, thereby causing their minds to drift upon the great ocean, darkly losing the shore;
or they defile the three robes and dharma-garments of the Saṅgha.
Or within the courtyards and halls of monasteries, they engaged in impure conduct, groping and touching one another.
For such measureless and boundless transgressions as these, we today repent with a sincere heart and a sense of shame.
From time immemorial until this day, we have sometimes taken female form and constantly harbored lustful desires;
or we have violated and usurped the husbands of others, deluding various men."

Or they may employ talismans, incantations, or sorcery to afflict the wives of others; when people have little merit, they become possessed by malevolent spirits, and various disease-demons take advantage of this situation, leading them to death as they fail to encounter a skilled physician.

Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we disclose and repent them. With utmost sincerity, we prostrate ourselves and take refuge in the Triple Gem to perform this confession.

From beginningless time until this very day, I have either allowed my eyes to be captivated by forms—becoming stained with attachment to dark and yellow, red and purple, or by precious playthings and jeweled ornaments;
or I have grasped at the characteristics of men and women, whether tall or short, black or white, and their various postures, giving rise to improper thoughts;
or I have greedily craved pleasant sounds from the *gong* and *shang* scales, stringed instruments, pipes, and the singing and music of courtesans.
Or they may give rise to improper thoughts upon perceiving the sounds, voices, speech, weeping, or laughter of men and women;
or they may give rise to improper thoughts upon smelling famous perfumes such as musk, orchids, saffron, and storax;

or their tongues may crave fine flavors—fresh, delicious, sweet, and rich—and since the flesh and blood of sentient beings nourish the four great elements, they may further loathe the root of suffering and give rise to improper thoughts.
Or, regarding the body, one may give rise to improper thoughts toward flowers, brocades, silks, gauzes, and all fine, smooth textures or magnificent garments of the seven treasures;
or, regarding the mind, one may have many distracted thoughts that turn away from the Dharma. When these six types of thoughts arise, the commission of transgressions is most severe.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we take refuge and repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Holy Assembly.

"We pray that by the merit arising from this repentance of our sins of lust and other transgressions, may our disciples, in life after life, be born spontaneously without passing through a womb; may we be pure and radiant, with the marks and signs of excellence shining brilliantly; may our six sense-faculties be clear and bright, sharp and discerning; may we thoroughly understand that affection and attachment are like shackles, and view these six sensory objects as illusions and transformations; may we develop a resolute weariness toward the realms of the five desires, such that even in dreams no perverse thoughts arise, and we can never be moved by internal or external conditions."
"By the merit of repenting for the faculty of the eye, may this eye see through to the pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions without dualistic marks;

by the merit of repenting for the faculty of the ear, may this ear constantly hear the True Dharma preached by the Buddhas and Sages of the ten directions, and practice in accordance with the teachings;

by the merit of repenting for the faculty of the nose, may this nose constantly smell the fragrance of the Accumulated Fragrance and enter the fragrance of the stage of Dharma, abandoning the impure stench of birth and death."

By the merit of repenting the faculty of the tongue, may this tongue always partake of the food of the joy of Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna, never craving the flavors of the flesh and blood of sentient beings;

by the merit of repenting the faculty of the body, may this body wear the robes of the Tathāgata and don the armor of patience, reclining upon the bed of fearlessness and sitting upon the seat of the four dhyānas;

by the merit of repenting the faculty of the mind, may this mind achieve the ten perceptions and master the five sciences, deeply contemplating the truth of the two truths and the principle of the equality of emptiness, giving rise to the ten sublime practices through skillful wisdom, entering the flowing stream of Dharma with each thought increasing in clarity, and manifesting the Tathāgata’s great patience of non-arising.
In the *Mahāyāna Padma-ratna-bodhi-praśna-vyākaraṇa-sārdhula-śramaṇa-sūtra*, Bodhi entered yet another hell shortly thereafter, named the Hell of the Fire-Elephant.

Within that hell, there spontaneously appears an elephant; its body is exceedingly large, and its body is ablaze with fire from which smoke and flames issue forth; its mouth and eyes are likewise ablaze with fire.

When the sinner sees this, he is so terrified that he wails and weeps, refusing to move forward. The yakṣa jailer impales him upon an elephant; as the elephant leaps and bounds, the sinner falls to the ground, where a blazing fire consumes his body. Day and night, he dies and is reborn a thousand times, ten thousand times, even a hundred thousand times. Upon emerging from hell, if he is born among humans, his body will be incomplete: he will be a eunuch, one with both sexual organs, a non-male, or a barren woman.
Bao Da asked the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa,
"What sins did these śramaṇas commit to suffer such retribution?

"These śramaṇas have received the pure precepts of the Buddha yet do not maintain them with purity; they engage in sexual conduct and lack proper decorum. With impure bodies, they enter the image-chapels of the Buddha and gaze upon the images with lewd intent, touching and defiling them without shame or remorse."
"By these causes and conditions, one falls into hell and undergoes such retribution.
Having heard this, Bodhidharma wept with sorrow and departed.

"Homage to the Buddha Sumerudīparāja in the eastern direction; homage to the Buddha Mahāpuṇya in the southern direction; homage to the Buddha Aparimitabala in the western direction; homage to the Buddha Bodhimaṇḍaruciraguṇa in the northern direction; homage to the Buddha Sarvabuddhakusuma in the southeastern direction; homage to the Buddha Aparimitapratibhāna in the southwestern direction; homage to the Buddha Padmottararāja in the northwestern direction; homage to the Buddha Sarvadaurmanasyavinodana in the northeastern direction; homage to the Buddha Prabhāketurāja in the downward direction; homage to the Buddha Vidyutpradīpaketudhvaja in the upward direction. “Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, we have engaged in false speech, double-tongued talk, harsh words, and frivolous chatter; we have spread emptiness as existence and existence as emptiness; we have said we saw what we did not see and said we did not see what we saw; we have said we heard what we did not hear and said we did not hear what we heard; we have said we knew what we did not know and said we did not know what we knew; we have deceived the worthy and hoodwinked the sages, such that our words and deeds were in total discord.”

They praise themselves, claiming to have attained superhuman states, saying: "I have attained the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, and the sixteenfold contemplation of ānāpāna; I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna up to arhatship; I am a pratyekabuddha and a non-retrogressive bodhisattva. They claim that devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits come to them, as do whirlwinds and earth-spirits, all arriving at their abode. When these beings question them, they provide answers to manifest wonders and delude the masses, seeking worldly fame and profit.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we reveal them, take refuge, and repent. Furthermore, disciples!

From time immemorial until this day, we have engaged in slanderous speech to incite strife and foment discord between others; we have practiced double-tongued treachery and malicious gossip, whispering what we hear from one side to the other and reporting what we hear from the other side to this side. We have alienated others’ retinues and broken their marriages and kinships; we have exhausted others with our talk, speaking of their long and short comings to ruin their virtuous friendships. We have caused those who were close and intimate to become estranged, and those who were old friends to turn into enemies.

Or they engage in frivolous speech, speaking untruths that fail to accord with the Way; they slander their sovereign and father, disparage their teachers and elders, ruin the loyal and virtuous, and suppress those who surpass them. They act as intermediaries between two states, fanning discord on both sides; their words are flowery and deceptive, always empty and artful. Their mouths agree with their hearts in falsehood, following many such paths: praising someone to their face yet reviling them behind their back; reciting heterodox scriptures and transmitting deviant, evil teachings; or using harsh and abusive language, speaking with coarse and violent words; or calling upon Heaven, pointing at the Earth, and invoking ghosts and spirits.

Thus, the various offenses produced by verbal karma are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I take refuge and repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages.

"May we disciples, by virtue of the merit arising from this confession of offenses committed through verbal karma and the like, in every birth and lifetime possess the eight qualities of vocal resonance and the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence; may we always speak words of harmony and benefit, with voices so pure and elegant that all delight in hearing them, and may we skillfully understand the various dialects and languages of sentient beings."

If one speaks according to the occasion and the proper limit, causing those who hear it to attain understanding and realization, they shall transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, opening the eye of wisdom.
In the *Mahāyāna-padma-ratna-buddhadatta-praśna-vipāka-śramaṇa-sūtra*, after a short while, Ratna entered a hell of severed tongues.
What is called the Hell of Tongue Extraction?

This hell is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded by iron walls and covered by an iron net. At its gates stand copper dogs ten yojanas in height, with fire issuing from their mouths and eyes.

In that hell, there naturally appear blades as sharp as the points of awls, and fierce fires blaze with intense heat. At the four corners of the iron city dwell great venomous serpents that gape their mouths wide; from their mouths and eyes, flames issue forth to burn the offenders. The yakṣa wardens support a massive iron plow and furrow the tongues of the offenders.

At that time, within the northern gate, there were five hundred sinners who, upon seeing the departed souls within the prison, were struck with such terror that their hearts shattered; they rolled about on the ground, refusing to move forward, each saying:
"By what transgression have I now entered this place?"
The horse-headed rākṣasa seizes an iron club with his hand and strikes them on the head, so that their bodies are ground to dust.
Furthermore, hungry ghosts come to devour their flesh, and hungry dogs come to gnaw their bones; yet, blown by the "clever wind," they are restored to life in an instant.

The horse-headed rākṣasa grasps an iron hook with his hand; aiming for the back, he thrusts it through until it emerges from the chest. Wherever the hook makes contact, fire blazes forth along its path, penetrating through both left and right so that the body and mind are utterly consumed.

The yakṣa wardens pull out the tongues of the offenders; these tongues become exceedingly broad and long, spreading throughout the hell, where iron plows furrow them. Wherever the plows enter, blood flows in torrents, and from the blood, fire immediately erupts. Within this, blades with upward-pointing edges pierce the offenders, and thus they undergo hundreds of varieties of painful retribution.

Furthermore, there are iron axes that hack the tongues of the offenders, shattering them inch by inch until they form a mountain of flesh; for one day and one night, they undergo immeasurable suffering, dying ten thousand times and living ten thousand times, dying a thousand times and living a thousand times.
Bao Da asked the Hayagrīva Rākṣasa,
"What karma did these sinners commit to suffer such torment as this?

"These sinful persons received the pure precepts of the Buddha but failed to uphold them; they used double-tongued speech and foul abuse to slander others, disparaged the virtuous, spread falsehoods as truth, and employed myriad forms of malevolent incantations. Due to these causes and conditions, they have fallen into this hell, where they shall remain for thousands of millions of kalpas without any prospect of release."
In the future, if they escape [that state], they will constantly be born as animals such as owls, hawks, and crows; the sounds they produce will be unpleasant for people to hear.
If they are born among humans, for hundreds or thousands of lifetimes they will be deaf, blind, and mute, their breath will always be foul, and they will be loathed by others.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva Baoda wept with sorrow and spoke in verse: "How tragic!
Beyond measure, They have entered the path of false views."
How is it that one who has reached the other shore, returns to drown in the great ocean?
How is it that one who has understood birth and death, turns instead to the delusions of ignorance?
How is it that one who has attained liberation, is once again ensnared by the wicked?
"How can those who have left the world speak such non-contradictory words?
Bodhisattva Bao Da spoke this verse and departed.

I take refuge in these and all other immeasurable and boundless Pratyekabuddhas."
"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next perform repentance.
Disciples! We have already finished repenting for the three actions of the body and the four actions of speech.
Next, one further repents of all obstacles between oneself and the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.

Therefore, the sutras state that a human body is difficult to obtain, the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear, the assembly of monks is difficult to encounter, faith is difficult to give rise to, the six sense faculties are difficult to possess in full, virtuous friends are difficult to find, and the mind of dread is difficult to arouse.

Now, having together planted roots of goodness in the past, we have obtained this human body with its six sense faculties complete; furthermore, having encountered virtuous friends, we have been able to hear the True Dharma. Yet, in the interim, each of us has failed to apply ourselves with wholehearted diligence. I fear that in the future we shall sink long into myriad sufferings, with no time of emergence in sight.
Therefore, on this day, you should with utmost sincerity and shamefulness prostrate yourself and take refuge in the Buddha:

"Homage to the Buddha Pūrṇacandraprabha in the East; Homage to the Buddha Vaśavartin in the South; Homage to the Buddha Anantaprabha in the West; Homage to the Buddha Vajrarāja in the North; Homage to the Buddha Siṃhasvara in the Southeast; Homage to the Buddha Gandhahastivikrīḍita in the Southwest; Homage to the Buddha Merudhvaja in the Northwest; Homage to the Buddha Ratnottamaguṇa in the Northeast; Homage to the Buddha Ratnāmbujapuṣpa in the Nadir; Homage to the Buddha Vipulaguṇasaṃcaya in the Zenith. "I take refuge in all the Three Jewels throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space."

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, our minds have been perpetually shrouded by ignorance and the hindrances of affliction have been heavy. Consequently, we have failed to show full-hearted reverence toward the physical images of the Buddha; we have treated the Sangha with contempt and maltreated our virtuous friends. We have destroyed stupas and demolished monasteries, burning images and shedding the blood of Buddhas. Or, while dwelling in magnificent halls ourselves, we have placed sacred icons in lowly and filthy locations, subjecting them to smoke, sun, wind, rain, and dew; they have been defiled by dust and excrement, ruined by crows and rats. We have shared dwellings and beds with them without ever showing them respect. At times we have left the bodies of the images exposed and never adorned them; at other times we have obstructed their radiance by shielding them from lamps and candles, or by opening and closing the temple doors."

Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we sincerely disclose and repent them. Furthermore, disciples! From time immemorial until this day, we may have handled sutra scrolls with unclean hands while engaged in the Dharma;

or we may have spoken improper, worldly talk while facing the scriptures; or we may have placed them at the head of our beds, failing to show reverence when rising or sitting; or we may have left them in chests and boxes where they were eaten by insects or decayed; or their binding cords may have fallen off and their sections become disordered; or they may have been incomplete, missing, or erroneous, with paper and ink torn or broken, yet we failed to repair them ourselves or were unwilling to circulate them.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we disclose them, take refuge, and repent.

"Whether lying on the ground while listening to the sutras, or reading and reciting while reclining on one's back; whether speaking aloud or laughing, thereby distracting others who are listening to the Dharma; or whether misinterpreting the Buddha’s words and explaining the intent of the listeners in a distorted way; whether preaching what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, or preaching the Dharma as what is not the Dharma; whether declaring what is not an offense to be an offense, or declaring an offense to be no offense; or whether describing a light offense as heavy, or a heavy offense as light."

They may excerpt passages from the beginning and place them at the end, or excerpt from the end and place them at the beginning; they may place what belongs at the beginning or end in the middle, or what belongs in the middle at the beginning or end, thus embellishing their rhetoric and establishing it as their own scripture. Or, for the sake of gain, reputation, and honor, they preach the Dharma to others; lacking a heart of virtue, they seek out the faults of other Dharma masters and engage in debate to unjustly attack them.

I did not seek the supramundane Dharma for the sake of long-term understanding; instead, I treated the Buddha’s words with contempt while honoring heterodox teachings, disparaging the Mahāyāna and praising the path of the Śrāvakas.
Such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with a sincere heart, I reveal and repent of them.

From beginningless time until this day, we may have created obstacles within the Sangha; we may have killed Arhats, disrupted the harmony of the Saṃgha, harmed those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed Bodhicitta, or severed the seeds of the Buddha so that the Way could not prevail."

Some may cease their practice of the Path and whip or interrogate śramaṇas, beating them with whips and staffs, forcing them into labor, and assailing them with bitter words and slander; some may break the precepts, violate the rules of purity, and neglect dignified deportment; some may encourage others to abandon the holy life (brahmacarya) and instead indulge in the five desires; or some may feign the outward appearance of practitioners while secretly spying on their dwellings.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we repent with a heart of sincere shame. "We disciples!

From beginningless time until this day, we have sometimes stood naked or in single garments before the scriptures and images; we have placed our impure feet or sandals upon the terraces and stupas; we have entered monasteries wearing straw sandals; we have spat and snotted in the halls and rooms, defiling the grounds of the Buddhas and the Sangha; we have slept together with the monks, defiling their Dharma robes; and we have ridden in carriages or spurred horses, jostling and pushing against the temple buildings."

Such offenses as these, the immeasurable and boundless karmic obstructions arising in relation to the Triple Gem, I now sincerely confess before the Buddhas, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Sangha of the ten directions, taking refuge in them.

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit arising from this confession of all karmic obstructions regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, vow that in every birth and every life we shall always encounter the Triple Gem, honoring and revering them without ever feeling satiety; and with celestial silks, exquisite fabrics, jeweled canopies and platforms, hundreds of thousands of musical performances, and rare flowers and incense—things not found in the mundane world—we shall constantly make offerings."

If I have not yet attained Buddhahood, may I go before you first to entreat you to open the gate of the nectar of immortality; if you enter nirvana, may I always be permitted to present the final offering. Among the assembly of monks, may I cultivate the six points of harmonious respect, attain the power of mastery, and cause the Triple Gem to flourish—propagating the Buddha-way above and transforming sentient beings below.
In the *Mahāyāna-padma-ratnagati-praśnavyākaraṇa-sādhūpāya-phala-sūtra*, Ratnagati entered the Hell of Burning Feet a short while ago.
Why is it called the Hell of Burning Feet?

That hell is seventy yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded by iron walls and an iron city, with an iron net covering its interior. Fierce, blazing fires come to burn the offenders, while some iron spikes as sharp as the points of awls come to pierce them; the ground is ablaze with fire, leaving no empty space between the flames.
Within the western gate were eight thousand śramaṇas who cried out these words:
"What sin have we committed that we must enter this place?

The horse-headed rākṣasa grasped an iron mallet in his hand and struck them on the head, driving the sinners forward; he then kicked them with his feet, piercing them with iron spurs so that they fell down at every step.

In a single day and night, they undergo ten thousand forms of suffering; through a thousand births and deaths, a myriad births and deaths, when they emerge from hell, they may be reborn among humans with incomplete physical faculties.
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept bitterly and asked,
"What karmic actions did this person commit to enter here?
"These śramaṇas received the pure precepts of the Buddha but did not maintain them with purity; they came upon the grounds of the Buddha and the Saṃgha with unclean feet;
or they rode donkeys and horses past the gates and doors of the Buddha’s images, their minds devoid of shame or remorse. Because of these transgressions, they have fallen into this hell."
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with grief and departed.

Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Sumana; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Śona; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Riju; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Upāju; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Puṣya; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Gomakha; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Kṣīṇāsrava; Namo to the Pratyekabuddha Antimadehadhara. I take refuge in these and all other immeasurable and boundless Pratyekabuddhas."
"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we now proceed to repentance.

Disciples! As previously stated, we have already repented for all light and heavy offenses committed in relation to the Triple Gem; as for our remaining evils, we shall now repent of them in successive order."
In the sutras, the Buddha said:
"There are two kinds of brave men:
the first is one who does not commit offenses himself;"
"Second, being able to repent after having committed [an offense].
"There are two kinds of pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) that can eliminate all obstacles for sentient beings:"
One who feels shame does not commit evil themselves; one who feels remorse does not cause others to do so. Only those possessed of shame and remorse can be designated as "human."

"If one lacks shame and remorse, one is no different from birds and beasts; 'shame' (hrī) is to feel abashed before the heavens, and 'remorse' (apatrāpya) is to confess the transgressions one has committed to others.
Therefore, disciples today, with utmost sincerity, feel shame and remorse as they take refuge in the Buddha.

“Homage to the Buddha Adorned with a Single Jewel in the eastern direction; homage to the Buddha Sandalwood Virtue in the southern direction; homage to the Buddha Brahma-Sound King in the western direction; homage to the Buddha Jewel-Wisdom Chief in the northern direction; homage to the Buddha Lion-Mark in the southeastern direction; homage to the Buddha Jewel-Canopy Illuminating the Void King in the southwestern direction; homage to the Buddha Joyful Progress in the northwestern direction; homage to the Buddha Mani-Purity in the northeastern direction; homage to the Buddha Supreme King of Jewel Incense in the downward direction; homage to the Buddha Great Renown in the upward direction. I take refuge in all the Triple Gem throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space.”

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, some have believed in heterodox and inverted views, slaughtering sentient beings to offer as sacrifices to *chimei* (goblins), *wangliang* (sprites), ghosts, and spirits, hoping thereby to prolong their lives, yet they were never able to achieve this; or they spoke falsely of having seen ghosts and feigned the utterances of deities."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we confess and repent them. Furthermore, disciples!

From time immemorial until this day, we have sometimes acted with arrogance and haughtiness, exalting ourselves; or, relying on our lineage, we have looked down upon all others, using our nobility to deceive the lowly and our strength to oppress the weak; leaning on wealth, we have slighted the poor, and relying on official positions, we have been insolent toward subordinates; or, drinking wine and inciting strife, we have shown no regard for kin or stranger, remaining intoxicated all day long and failing to distinguish between the honorable and the humble.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I confess and repent them.

"Whether through gluttony, laziness, or a lack of shame, I greedily craved food and drink, disregarding all hardships; I drank wine, ate meat, and engaged in song, dance, and music, without restraint or sense of moderation, never knowing when to rest."

Some eat raw minced fish and consume the five pungent roots; they defile scriptures and images with their foul odors, and push aside those of pure conduct. They indulge their minds and follow their whims without regard for ultimate principle, distancing themselves from virtuous people while becoming intimate with evil companions.

Some are arrogant and hypocritical, stubborn and self-willed; they are coarse and insolent, lacking understanding of human nature. They affirm themselves while disparaging others, praising their own virtues and condemning the faults of others. Upon seeing the transgressions of others, they launch mutual attacks and fabricate words and phrases in the hope of gaining some advantage.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with a sincere heart, I take refuge and repent.
"Whether in the face of wealth I failed to yield, lacking integrity and shame; or engaged in slaughtering meat and selling liquor to live by deception;

or in lending and borrowing at interest, calculating time and selling days; or hoarding and being stingy, greedily seeking more without satiety; or accepting offerings from others without giving rise to a sense of shame or remorse."
Some, lacking moral conduct, vainly receive the offerings of the faithful;
some beat their slaves and servants and drive their children into labor, regardless of hunger or thirst and oblivious to cold or heat;
others tear down bridges and block the paths of travelers.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, I take refuge and repent.

Whether through negligence, self-indulgence, or neutral mental wandering and distraction—playing *chūbǔ*, *báidǎ*, *shuāngliù*, or *wéiqí*; gathering in crowds and drinking wine or eating meat; or mutually mocking one another and engaging in idle chatter—I now repent.

The treatise states that throughout the world, from month to year, people waste their days in vain; during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, they do not cultivate meditation or recitation, but remain idle, indolent, and lie like corpses all day long.

Failing to cultivate the mind through the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), they give rise to envy upon seeing the superior achievements of others; harboring malice and poison, they fully arouse the afflictions (*kleśa*). Consequently, the fierce winds of various evils blow upon the fuel of wickedness, causing the fires to blaze without ceasing. All subtle virtues of the three karmas are utterly consumed by these flames; with wholesome dharmas exhausted, they become icchantikas, falling into the fire hells with no prospect of escape.

Therefore, disciples! Today, with utmost sincerity, we prostrate ourselves before all the Buddhas and the assembly of holy ones throughout the ten directions, repenting for all the various transgressions we have committed heretofore.

Whether light or heavy, coarse or subtle; whether committed by oneself, caused to be done by others, or rejoiced in as being done; whether performed through the compulsion of power or even through praising those who practice unwholesome dharmas—I now, with a sincere heart, confess and repent for all such acts. May they all be extinguished.

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this confession of all evils, pray that in birth after birth we may be compassionate, harmonious, loyal, filial, humble, and self-effacing; that we may know integrity and recognize shame; that we may anticipate others' needs with greetings; that we may be compliant, excellent, steadfast, prudent, pure, righteous, and yielding; that we may distance ourselves from evil friends and constantly encounter favorable conditions; that we may restrain the six sense faculties and reverently protect the three karmas; that we may endure toil and suffering without our resolve ever faltering; and that we may establish the aspiration for Bodhi and take up the burden of all sentient beings."
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Regarding Retribution for Śramaṇas by Padma-ratna-udaya*, it is said that after a short while, Ratna-udaya entered the Hell of Fiery Spears.
Why is it called the Hell of Fiery Spears?
That hell is one hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by iron walls blazing with fierce and great flames.

From that ground, spikes emerge to pierce the offenders; they enter through the soles of the feet and emerge from the tops of the insteps, while the offenders wail and cry out in myriad ways of suffering and pain.
In the midst of the southern gate, five thousand śramaṇas cried out these words:
"By what sin have we now come to enter this place?
The horse-headed rākṣasa, grasping a three-pronged iron fork in his hand, struck them from behind so that it pierced through their chests and emerged on the other side.

When the sinner enters the prison, iron spikes come to pierce his feet, and flames of smoke and fire blaze upward, burning through his chest and heart. Day and night he undergoes ten thousand forms of suffering; he dies and is reborn a thousand times, dies and is reborn ten thousand times, and even if he should obtain a human body, it shall be incomplete.
Bao Da asked the Hayagrīva Rākṣasa,
"What evil karma did these śramaṇas commit that they have come here to undergo such suffering?
The Hayagrīva Rākṣasa replied to the Bodhisattva Bao Da:

"In this regard, there are śramaṇas who, having received the pure precepts of the Buddha, do not guard their dignified deportment; they wear boots and shoes when entering the latrine without removing them, and they tread upon the ground of the Buddha or the grounds of the Saṃgha with their feet, or even step on the shadows of images of the Buddha or of sacred stūpas. By these causes and conditions, they incur such offenses."
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with grief and departed.
