homage to the Bodhisattva Dīrghāyurāja. I take refuge in all such great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, immeasurable and boundless, throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"Homage to all the worthy sages, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we shall next perform repentance.
Now, one who wishes to repent must first revere the Triple Gem."

Why is this so? The Three Jewels are the true friends and fields of merit for all sentient beings; if one can take refuge in them, immeasurable sins will be extinguished and immeasurable blessings will increase, enabling the practitioner to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of liberation.
Therefore, disciples such as I, [Name] and others!

We take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space; we take refuge in all Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space; we take refuge in all Great Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space; and we take refuge in all Noble Sanghas throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.

“Disciple! The reason for your confession today is that, since beginningless time, while remaining in the stage of an ordinary person, regardless of whether one is noble or lowly, one’s transgressions have naturally been immeasurable.”

Either sins are produced through the three karmas, or transgressions arise from the six sense organs; or they stem from one's own internal perverse reflections, or from defiled attachments triggered by external objects. In this way, even down to the ten evil deeds, the eighty-four thousand gates of worldly affliction (*kleśa*) increase.
Although the characteristics of these offenses are indeed immeasurable, when stated in broad terms, they do not exceed three.
The second is the obstacle of karma;
the third is the obstacle of retribution.
These three types of dharmas can obstruct the Noble Path as well as the superior and wondrous blessings of humans and devas; therefore, they are designated as the "three obstacles" in the sutras.

Therefore, when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the expedient means of repentance to eliminate these three obstructions, then the six sense faculties, the ten evil deeds, and even the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction will all become completely pure.

Today you have brought forth this superior and excellent resolve to repent of the three obstructions. If you wish to extinguish the offenses of these three obstructions, what kind of mind must you employ to cause these offenses to be eliminated?"
First, one should give rise to seven kinds of mental states as a preliminary means; only then can these offenses be extinguished.
The first is shame and remorse.
fourth, the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Fifth, to regard enemies and kin with equanimity;
sixth, to mindfully repay the Buddha’s kindness;
seventh, to contemplate the emptiness of the nature of offenses.

"First, regarding shame and remorse: I reflect that I and the Śākya Tathāgata were once fellow ordinary beings; yet while the World-Honored One has already attained the Way for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, we have instead remained immersed in and defiled by the six sense objects, wandering through birth and death with no end in sight. This is truly something for which one should feel shame, remorse, embarrassment, and disgrace before the world."

"The second fear is this: being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one's actions of body, speech, and mind are constantly associated with transgression. For this reason, after the end of life, one ought to fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) to undergo immeasurable suffering; such a thing is truly something to be startled by, to be afraid of, to be terrified of, and to be fearful of."

"Third, regarding weariness and detachment: you should together contemplate that within birth and death there is only impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, and falsity. It is like bubbles upon water, arising and ceasing swiftly; its coming and going and circulation is like a turning wheel. Birth, aging, sickness, and death—these eight sufferings burn one together, with no moment of respite. You all should together observe your own bodies from head to foot and see that within them there are only thirty-six things: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, the sac of pus, mucus, saliva, the two internal organs (the raw and the cooked), the large intestine, small intestine, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, stomach, mesentery, fat, grease, sinews, membranes, veins, arteries, marrow, bones, and the constant flow from the nine orifices of excrement and urine."
"This body is a collection of manifold sufferings; everything within it is impure.
What person of wisdom would take pleasure in this stinking flesh-body?"
"Since birth and death already possess such various evil dharmas, they are truly to be dreaded and weary of.
Regarding the fourth [type of] arousal of the bodhicitta, the Sūtra says:
'One should take pleasure in the Buddha-body.'"

It is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom; it is born from the six pāramitās; it is born from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; it is born from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The body of the Tathāgata is born from such various merits and wisdom."

Those who wish to attain this body should give rise to the bodhicitta and seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), the fruit of omniscience (sarvajñatā) characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; they should purify buddha-fields, bring sentient beings to maturity, and be without stinginess regarding their body, life, or wealth.
"The fifth [point], 'equanimity toward enemies and kin,' means giving rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings without the notion of 'other' or 'self.

Why is this so? If one perceives an enemy as distinct from a relative, that is discrimination. Because of discrimination, various attachments and perceptions arise; with attachments and perceptions as conditions, various afflictions are produced; with afflictions as conditions, various evil karmas are created; and because of evil karma as a condition, one reaps bitter fruits."

"Sixth, regarding the repayment of the Buddha's kindness: throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, the Tathāgata sacrificed his head, eyes, marrow, brain, limbs, joints, hands, and feet, as well as his kingdoms, cities, wives, children, elephants, horses, and the seven treasures. For our sake, he practiced various ascetic austerities; this kindness and this virtue are truly difficult to repay."
"Even if one were to carry [the Buddha] upon the crown of one's head or on both shoulders for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges, one could never repay [his kindness].

Those of us who wish to repay the grace of the Tathāgata should, in this world, be valiant and diligent, enduring toil and suffering, and without begrudging our bodies or lives, establish the Triple Gem, propagate the Mahāyāna, and extensively transform sentient beings so that they may all enter the Right Path.

"Seventh, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of offenses: they possess no real characteristic; they arise from inverted conditions and exist through them. Since they arise from conditions, they can likewise be extinguished by means of conditions."
That which arises from causes and conditions refers to associating closely with evil friends and engaging in groundless actions.
That which ceases through causes and conditions refers to purifying the mind and repenting today.
"The characteristics of this sin are not within, not without, and not in between; thus one knows that this sin is fundamentally empty."

"Having given rise to these seven kinds of mind, one contemplates the Buddhas and sages of the ten directions. With hands joined in prayer and palms pressed together, one lays bare one's heart with utmost sincerity, feeling shame and remorse to undergo transformation. One pours out one's very heart and liver to cleanse the intestines and stomach. Through such repentance, what sin would not be extinguished, and what hindrance would not be dissolved?"
If, moreover, you continue to drift aimlessly and indulge your thoughts with negligence, what benefit is there in merely exhausting yourself in worldly affairs?

Furthermore, human life is impermanent, like a flickering candle; if one breath does not return, one immediately turns to dust and earth. The retribution of suffering in the three miserable realms must be endured by the body itself; it cannot be escaped by entrusting oneself to money, wealth, or treasures. In the profound and dark abyss, there is no hope for pardon; one alone must suffer this misery, with no one to take its place.
Do not say, "In this present life, I have committed no such offenses," and therefore you cannot repent with utmost sincerity.
As it is said in the sutras:
"For an ordinary person, every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step is nothing but an offense."

Furthermore, throughout past lives, you have all accomplished immeasurable evil karma that pursues you like a shadow follows a form; if you do not repent today, your sins will deepen daily. Therefore, to conceal one's blemishes and defects is not permitted by the Buddha’s teachings.
Confessing past transgressions is what the *Vimalakīrti* esteems; thus we know that long immersion in the sea of suffering truly arises from concealment and suppression.
Therefore, disciples, today we openly confess and repent, not daring to hide anything.
What are called the three obstructions are:
Third is the obstacle of karmic retribution.
These three types of phenomena depend upon one another: because of afflictions, evil karma arises; and due to the conditions of evil karma, one obtains bitter fruits.
"Therefore, disciples! Today, with the utmost sincerity, you should first of all repent of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, these afflictions have been rebuked in various ways by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones who have entered into the principle; they also designate these afflictions as enemies."
Why is this? Because they sever the life-root of the wisdom of sentient beings;
furthermore, these afflictions are designated as "thieves," for they can plunder the various wholesome dharmas of sentient beings.
Furthermore, these afflictions are termed "fierce rivers," for they can sweep sentient beings into the great ocean of suffering within birth and death;
they are also termed "fetters and locks," for they bind sentient beings in the prison of birth and death, preventing them from escaping;
and they are also termed "pythons," for they devour the *tathatā* buddha-nature of sentient beings.

Therefore, the six realms are interconnected and the four modes of birth are never-ending; evil karma is inexhaustible and the fruits of suffering do not cease. One should know that all of this is the fault and affliction of the *kleśas*.
Today, generating this superior mind of goodness, I take refuge in the Buddha: Homage to the Buddha Golden Light in the East.

Homage to the Buddha Great Sumeru in the South. Homage to the Buddha Sublime Joy in the West. Homage to the Buddha Possessing Dignified Wisdom in the North. Homage to the Buddha Honored One of the Dharma-Lineage in the Southeast. Homage to the Buddha Banner of Truth in the Southwest. Homage to the Buddha Awakening Bodhisattvas in the Northwest. Homage to the Buddha Wisdom-Vigor in the Northeast. Homage to the Buddha Whose Hair Does Not Stand on End in the Nadir. Homage to the Buddha Infinite Vigor and Abundant Prosperity in the Zenith. I pay homage to all the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space.

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this day, whether receiving retribution within the six realms of existence as humans or devas, this mind-consciousness has constantly harbored ignorance and delusion, filling the breast with abundance. Whether it was due to the three poisons that created all manner of offenses, or due to the three outflows that created all manner of offenses, or due to the three perceptions that created all manner of offenses, or due to the three feelings that created all manner of offenses, or due to the three sufferings that created all manner of offenses, or conditioned by the three provisional designations that created all manner of offenses, or through craving for the three realms of existence that created all manner of offenses."

Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; they have disturbed and troubled all beings within the six realms and the four modes of birth. Today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent.

From beginningless time until this very day, one may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the four abodes of consciousness; or due to the four floods; or due to the four graspings; or due to the four attachments; or due to the four conditions; or due to the four great elements; or due to the four bonds; or due to the four nutriments; or due to the four modes of birth.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; they have troubled and disturbed all sentient beings throughout the six realms. Today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent.

From time immemorial until this day, one may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the afflictions of the five stages of abiding; or due to the five faculties of sensation; or due to the five hindrances; or due to the five forms of stinginess; or due to the five views; or due to the five mental states.
Afflictions such as these are immeasurable and boundless, vexing and disturbing all beings of the four modes of birth throughout the six realms. Today, we reveal them, take refuge, and repent.

From time immemorial until this very day, one may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), or all manner of transgressions due to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), or all manner of transgressions due to the six perceptions (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā*), or all manner of transgressions due to the six feelings (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*), or all manner of transgressions due to the six volitional formations (*ṣaḍ-saṃskāra*), or all manner of transgressions due to the six cravings (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā*), or all manner of transgressions due to the six doubts (*ṣaḍ-vicikitsā*).
Afflictions such as these are immeasurable and boundless, tormenting all beings of the four modes of birth throughout the six realms. Today, with shame and remorse, I take refuge and repent.

From time immemorial until this day, one may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven outflows (*āsrava*), or due to the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), or due to the eight inversions (*viparyāsa*), or due to the eight impurities (*mala*), or due to the eight sufferings (*duḥkha*).
Afflictions such as these are immeasurable and boundless, tormenting all beings of the four modes of birth within the six realms. Today, we reveal them, take refuge, and repent.

From time immemorial until this very day, one may have committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine afflictions (*nava-kleśa*); or due to the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*); or due to the nine superior objects (*nava-adhyālambana*); or due to the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*); or due to the ten envelopments (*daśa-paryavasthāna*); or due to the eleven pervasive proclivities (*ekādaśa-anuśaya*); or due to the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*); or due to the sixteen false views (*ṣoḍaśa-dṛṣṭi*); or due to the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*); or due to the twenty-five notions of self (*pañcaviṃśati-ātman*); or due to the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*). Or, due to the ninety-eight proclivities and one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*)—both those abandoned through the vision of the truths and those abandoned through cultivation—which blaze fiercely day and night, opening the gates of the outflows (*āsrava*), one has committed all manner of transgressions.

Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless; they vex and disturb the worthy and the holy, as well as those of the four modes of birth. They pervade the triple world and extend throughout the six realms of existence, leaving no place to hide and no place to escape.
Today, having arrived before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly, we confess with shame and remorse all our transgressions.

"We pray that by virtue of the merit arising from this confession of all afflictions, such as the three poisons, may our disciples, in birth after birth, possess the clarity of the three types of wisdom, the brilliance of the three forms of omniscience, the cessation of the three sufferings, and the fulfillment of the three vows."

“May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this confession of all afflictions such as the four consciousnesses, vow that in birth after birth we shall broaden the four immeasurable minds, establish the karma of the fourfold faith, extinguish the four evil destinies, and attain the four fearlessnesses.”

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced through this confession of the five hindrances and all other afflictions, pray that in birth after birth we may cross over the five realms of existence, plant the five faculties, purify the five eyes, and perfect the five aggregates."

"May we disciples, by virtue of the merit arising from this confession of the six cravings and all other afflictions, in every birth and lifetime be fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, fulfill the karma of the six perfections, remain unconfused by the six sense objects, and constantly practice the six sublime conducts."

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this confession of all afflictions—the seven outflows, the eight impurities, the nine fetters, the ten entanglements, and so forth—vow that in life after life we shall sit upon the flowers of the seven purities, wash away the dust with the eight waters, possess the nine knowledges of abandonment, and accomplish the practices of the ten stages."

By means of the merit produced from this elevenfold confession of transgressions regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and all other afflictions, I vow that in every birth and lifetime, I shall constantly wash my mind with the understanding of the eleven emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), attain mastery in turning the wheel of the twelve modes of conduct, be fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and bring all immeasurable merits to complete perfection.
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning Retribution for Śramaṇas*, when Bao Da had just entered the Fire-Ball Upside-Down-Mouth Hell,
why is it called the Fire-Ball Upside-Down-Mouth Hell?

That hell is eighty *yojana*s in length and breadth. Its iron city and netting are set ablaze by flames rising together to burn the sinners. From the four corners of the city, fierce winds blow against this iron city, causing it to vibrate and disperse, transforming into iron balls that fly and stream downward. These balls, as sharp as the points of awls on all eight sides, are filled with flames; they clash and strike one another in the void with sounds like thunder.
Within the southern gate were hundreds of thousands of sinners; when the śramaṇa entered therein, he cried out these words:
"For what crime have I now come into this place to undergo such suffering?"

He let out a great cry, and his body split apart; smoke and fire both issued forth from within it. Fire-balls from the air entered through his mouth and emerged from the soles of his feet; all the pores of his body were likewise ablaze, as he endured immeasurable suffering for one day and one night.
Bao Da asked the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa,
"What sins did these śramaṇas commit to undergo such suffering?

"These śramaṇas received the pure precepts of the Buddha yet do not fear transgression; they pluck fruits from the Saṃgha with their own hands, eating them themselves and giving them to others without any sense of shame or remorse.
Because of these causes and conditions, they have fallen into this hell."
"Upon emerging from hell, if one obtains a human birth, one will be mute and unable to speak.
Hearing this, Bodhidharma wept with sorrow and departed.
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Names of Buddhas*, Scroll Seventeen.

At that time, the bhikṣu Upamāna rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One! How many Buddhas have passed away? The Buddha—

Suppose there were worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, from the bottom reaching down to the water's edge and up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), filled completely with fine motes of dust."
Suppose a person were to take that many atoms from among them, and drop one atom in a world-system beyond as many *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges] worlds as there are.
Having thus dropped another atom in a world-system beyond as many *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds, he continues in this manner until all those atoms are exhausted.”
Whether those atoms were heaped together or not heaped together, could the number of those atoms be known by counting?"
The number of those atoms may be known, but the number of those past Buddhas named Śākyamuni who have already entered parinirvāṇa cannot be calculated.”
“Monks! I know those past Buddhas as if seeing them before my eyes.
Those Buddhas all had mothers named Mahāmāyā, fathers named King Śuddhodana, and cities named Kapilavastu.”
The foremost śrāvaka disciples of those Buddhas were all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and their attendant disciples were all named Ānanda.
How much more so for various other names for mothers, fathers, or cities?
Are they attendants with different names?
Regarding those various worlds, in which of them would that person place a mote of dust, and in which would he not?
Whether a mote of dust is placed or not placed in all those worlds, from the lowest limit of the waters up to the pinnacle of existence (bhavāgra).

"Monks! Furthermore, suppose there is a second person who takes a single mote of dust and, having passed beyond as many worlds as there are motes of dust, takes a single step for every hundred thousand million billion nayutas of Buddha-lands and world-systems equal in number to those."

"Monks! That person takes as many worlds as there are atoms as a single step. In this manner, after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he places down a single atom; in this way, he exhausts all those atoms."
"Monks! Suppose there were as many worlds as these motes of dust filling this many worlds, and one were to further place them throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Monks!"
Furthermore, beyond these worlds, one places a mote of dust; in those worlds, from the water's edge below up to the peak of existence above, they are filled with motes of dust.
Can the number of those atoms be known?

"The number of those atoms may be known, but the number of those who share the same name as my mother, the same name as my father, the same name as my city, the same name as my disciples, the same name as my attendants, and the same name as Śākyamuni Buddha cannot be known."
As it is with Śākyamuni, so it is with Anabhibhūdhvaja Buddha;
as it is with Rocana Buddha,
so it is with Vimalajayacakṣus Buddha.
The Buddha Victorious King of Boundless Accomplished Merit was also like this;
the Buddha Jewel Radiance was also like this;
the Buddha Tranquil Cultivation was also like this.
The Buddha Samantaratnacchattra is also like this. Bhikṣus!
You should take refuge in such incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddhas who share the same name.

“Homage to the Buddha Candana-viśeṣa of the world Nanda. If there are good sons or good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite the names of these Buddhas, they will ultimately attain a pure mind.”

“Homage to the Buddha Śāntarañjana in the world Bhadra; homage to the Buddha Mārabalabhañjaka in the world Manojñaketu; homage to the Buddha Aśoka in the world Pūrṇacandra; homage to the Buddha Ratnadaṇḍa in the world Ketumanojña; homage to the Buddha Puṣpavijaya in the world Vādanirghoṣavijaya; homage to the Buddha Samādhiprārambhita in the world Kṣema; homage to the Buddha Drumarājajaya in the world Vipula; homage to the Buddha Vajraguṇakāya in the world Candravijaya; and homage to the past Buddha Sāgaravijaya, immeasurable and boundless. If any son of good family invokes the names of these Buddhas, they shall attain a bodhicitta that is ultimately non-retrogressive.”
"Namo to the Buddha Meruśikhararāja. When that Buddha first attained enlightenment, his first assembly consisted of eighty billion hundred thousand million nayutas of śrāvakas;
the second assembly consisted of seventy billion hundred thousand million nayutas;
and the third assembly consisted of sixty billion hundred thousand million nayutas."
In the fourth assembly, there were twenty-five billion, one hundred thousand million, nayutas of them;
likewise, there were immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas.
“Homage to the Buddha Siṃhaghoṣarāja! In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were nine hundred and ninety million śrāvakas;
in the second assembly, nine hundred million;
and in the third assembly, nine hundred and thirty million.”
In the fourth assembly, there were ninety-nine billion;
thus, the multitude of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas was immeasurable and boundless.
"Homage to the Buddha Puṣpavijaya. In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were eight billion śrāvakas, and the community of Bodhisattvas was likewise.
“Homage to the Buddha Subhācāra. In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were eight billion śrāvakas; the assembly of bodhisattvas was likewise.
“Homage to the Buddha Aparimitamahāvyūha. In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were eight billion śrāvakas;
in the second assembly, seven billion, and so on, up to the tenth assembly, which was likewise.”
The assembly of Bodhisattvas is likewise immeasurable and boundless.

"Homage to the Buddha Radiant Flame. In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were nine billion Śrāvakas; it was the same for the second through the tenth assemblies, and the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas was immeasurable and boundless.
“Homage to the Buddha Sarvālokakara! In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were *nayuta* of billions of śrāvakas, and the community of bodhisattvas was likewise.
Homage to the Buddha Amitābhāsa! In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were nine hundred and sixty billion śrāvakas;
in the second assembly, nine hundred and forty billion.”
In the third assembly, there were nine hundred and thirty million; the assembly of bodhisattvas was likewise.
"Homage to the Buddha Śabdaguṇa. In that Buddha’s first assembly, there were eight hundred million śrāvakas;
in the second assembly, seven hundred million.
In the third assembly, there were sixty billion [monks], and the assembly of bodhisattvas was likewise; one should take refuge in all such Buddhas and bodhisattvas.

One should pay homage to the Bodhisattvas and Buddhas of the southern world-realm, Pure and Stainless (Vimalā), namely Mañjuśrī, who currently resides within the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin.
You should pay homage to the four great bodhisattvas:
the first is named Prabhāketu, who currently resides within the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Abhaya in the eastern direction;..."
The second is Jñānavijaya, currently residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Jñānaskandha in the south;
the third is Śāntendriya, currently residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Jñānaparvata in the west;
the fourth is Abhiprāyasaṃpādana, currently residing in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Nārāyaṇa in the north.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu Mahānāman again questioned the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One:
"How many Buddhas of the past have entered parinirvāṇa?
I shall speak for you, bhikṣu."

In worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the east, worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the south, worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the west, worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the north, and worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the four intermediate directions and above and below.
"Monks, suppose all those worlds, from the bottom reaching down to the water's edge and up to the very peak of existence (bhavāgra), were filled with motes of dust.
“In this same way, the number of Śākyamuni Buddhas who entered parinirvāṇa in the past is beyond calculation.”
I know those past Buddhas as if they were present before me.

Those Buddhas had mothers all named Mahāmāyā, fathers all named King Śuddhodana, and cities all named Kapilavastu. The foremost śrāvaka disciples of those Buddhas were all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and their attendant disciples were all named Ānanda."

"How much more so, Bhikṣu, regarding the various different names— different names for the mother, different names for the father, different names for the city, different names for the disciples, and different names for the attendants."
Regarding those various worlds, in which of them would that person place the motes of dust,
and in which worlds would he not place them? Those worlds—
both those where motes of dust are placed and those where they are not— extend from the water's edge below up to the Peak of Existence above.

"Monks! Furthermore, suppose there were a second person who took those atoms; and for as many worlds as there are in that number of atoms—that is, as many Buddha-fields as there are in incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds—he would take a single step past all those worlds."

"Monks! That person takes a single step across as many worlds as there are atoms; in this manner, after traveling for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he sets down a single atom, and continues until all those atoms have been exhausted."

"Monks! Suppose there were as many worlds as these, both those upon which fine dust has settled and those upon which it has not; suppose they were filled with such fine dust, and then further [dust] were added to the worlds of the ten directions."

"Monks! Furthermore, beyond these worlds—whether those places where atoms are placed or where they are not—fill all those worlds, from the water's edge below up to the Peak of Existence above, with atoms."
Could the number of those atoms be known?"

“One might be able to know the number of those atoms, but one cannot know the number of those Buddhas named Śākyamuni, whose mothers were all named Mahāmāyā, whose fathers were all named King Śuddhodana, whose cities were all named Kapilavastu, and whose foremost śrāvaka disciples were all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and whose attendant disciples were all named Ānanda.”

Suppose there is a third person who takes those aforementioned world-dust atoms, and for every such number of world-dust atoms, he takes a single step across that many worlds. After passing through as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he sets down a single dust atom; in this manner, he exhausts all the dust atoms."

Furthermore, there is a fourth person who takes as many worlds as there are atoms in those [previous] quantities, and whether they are filled with atoms or not, fills them all with atoms from the bottom, reaching down to the water’s edge, up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Is it possible to know the number of those atoms?"

"The number of those various atoms may be known; however, the number of those Buddhas who share the same name Śākyamuni—sharing the same name for their mothers, the same name for their fathers, the same name for their worlds, the same name for their disciples, and the same name for their attendants—is unknowable."
“Monks! In this way there is a fifth person, a sixth, a seventh, an eighth, a ninth, and a tenth person.

Furthermore, there is an eleventh person who takes one mote of dust from among those various motes of dust and breaks it into as many parts as there are motes of dust in worlds throughout the ten directions; just as that one mote of dust is broken into as many parts, so too are all the remaining motes of dust each broken into as many parts as there are motes of dust in worlds throughout the ten directions.
Is it possible to know the number of those atoms?"

"Furthermore, suppose there is a person who takes a single step for as many buddha-fields as there are atoms [in those fields]. Traveling through the eastern worlds with such swift supernatural power for immeasurable and boundless kalpas, he deposits a single atom in each of the eastern worlds. Continuing in this manner until the eastern direction is exhausted—with atoms both where they were placed and where they were not—filling the space from the bottom of the water realm up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra) with these atoms."
In this way, from the south up to the ten directions, filling everything from the bottom of the water to the peak of existence with motes of dust—
“Can the number of those atoms be known?
“The number of particles in a certain amount of dust may be known; however, the number of present-day Śākyamuni Buddhas who have entered nirvāṇa cannot be known.”

Their mothers were all named Mahāmāyā; their fathers were all named King Śuddhodana; their cities were all named Kapilavastu; their foremost śrāvaka disciples were all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; and their attendant disciples were all named Ānanda—how much more so for various other names?
“Bhikṣus! Even if I were to remain in the world for as many eons as there are atoms in a great many worlds, I could not exhaustively describe even a single Buddha named Śākyamuni.

In this same way, there are Buddhas with the same name Dīpaṃkara, the same name Devānām-indra, the same name Pradīpaprabha, the same name Sarvābhibhū, the same name Yaśodhararāja, the same name Padmottara, the same name Vipaśyin, the same name Śikhin, the same name Viśvabhū, the same name Krakucchanda, the same name Kanakamuni, and the same name Kāśyapa. For all such Buddhas with various names—whether it be their mothers, their various attendants, or their entry into nirvana—I know those Buddhas as if they were standing right before me; one should pay homage to all such Buddhas.”
The bhikṣu Upamāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
How many Buddhas will there be in the future?”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Upamāna:

"Monks! In the future Star-Constellation Kalpa, there shall appear three hundred Buddhas in the world, all sharing the same name, Mahāketu; furthermore, there shall be ten thousand others, all sharing the same name, King Adorned Buddha."
"In the Flower-Made Kalpa, one billion hundred thousand million Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Bodhi-Buddha-Kusuma;
furthermore, in another kalpa, eight thousand *bimbara* Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Buddha Free from Attachment."
“In the Tāḷopama kalpa, six thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Saṃkusumita.
In the Jayasvara kalpa, within the world-system Śālendrarājocchrayadhvaja, ten thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Vimalapadmagandhaśikhara.”
"In the Samantakusuma kalpa, one thousand eight hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Vimala;
furthermore, in another kalpa, one thousand three hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Brahmaghoṣa;
and again, in another kalpa, thirty billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Śākyamuni."
Furthermore, in another kalpa, eight thousand Buddhas named Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world;
in yet another kalpa, sixty thousand Buddhas named Nanda appeared in the world;
and in another kalpa, three hundred million Buddhas appeared, all sharing the name Puṣya.
Furthermore, in another kalpa, eighty thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Śālendrarāja;
in another kalpa, three hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Padmottara;
and in another kalpa, five hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Bhadra.
“Furthermore, there was an eon in which a thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Jambūnada;
again, there was an eon in which twelve trillion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Sarvārthadarśin;
and again, there was an eon in which a thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Kruñca.”
Furthermore, there was an eon in which nine thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Kāśyapa;
another eon in which eighteen Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Indraketu;
and another eon in which fifteen Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Sūryabuddha.
Furthermore, in another kalpa, sixty billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Mahāvyūha;
in yet another kalpa, sixty Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Indradhvaja.
Furthermore, in another kalpa, five hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Sun Buddha;
in another kalpa, sixty billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Great Adornment;
and in another kalpa, six thousand two hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Tranquil Conduct.
Furthermore, in another kalpa, sixty billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Śālarājendra;
and in yet another kalpa, eight thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Dṛḍhavīrya.
"Furthermore, in another kalpa, ten billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, *Niyata-prabhāsa*;
in another kalpa, eight billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, *Tattva-dharma-niyata*;
and in another kalpa, six billion two hundred million Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, *Vairocana*."
Furthermore, in another kalpa, sixty thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Wondrous Padma Buddha;
in another kalpa, forty thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Adorned by Vows;
and in another kalpa, five hundred Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, King of Flower Victory.
Furthermore, in another kalpa, forty billion nayutas of Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Wondrous Sound;
in another kalpa, one thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Sovereign King of Peaceful Stability and Merit-Covering;
and in another kalpa, sixty thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, all sharing the same name, Firmly Cultivated Gentleness.
Furthermore, in another eon, there appeared as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten Buddha-lands—countless, ineffable, and beyond description—all named Samantabhadra;
and in yet another eon, seven thousand Buddhas appeared, all named Dharmavyūharāja.
“Bhikṣus! To state the essentials: the future Buddhas are immeasurable and boundless, unspeakably, unspeakably many, and inexhaustible.
"One should single-mindedly take refuge in all such Buddhas as these.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Śāriputra said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
I now truly see the Buddha’s body.”

"I now see, in the immeasurable, boundless, unspeakably unspeakable worlds of the ten directions, those Buddhas named Śākyamuni who currently dwell in the world; they are no different from me as you see me."

In this way, there were Buddhas with the same name as Dīpaṃkara, the same name as Vipaśyin, the same name as Śikhin, the same name as Viśvabhū, the same name as Krakucchanda, the same name as Kanakamuni, and the same name as Kāśyapa.

“Śāriputra! To speak briefly, even if I were to spend an eon, or hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of nayutas of eons, speaking of the Buddhas who share the same name, I could not reach their end.”
How much more so for Buddhas with other names?
All such Buddhas as these were first taught by Mañjuśrī to resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! You all should with one mind take refuge in such Buddhas as these. Śāriputra!”

In the present eon, there are five hundred Buddhas of the same name, Jñānaketu; furthermore, there is an eon with five hundred Buddhas of the same name, Dharmaketu; furthermore, there is an eon with sixty-two Buddhas of the same name, Jvalanolkā; furthermore, there is an eon with sixty-two Buddhas of the same name, Śikhin;

furthermore, there is an eon with one thousand Buddhas of the same name, Jvalanacandrasvaramaheśvararāja; furthermore, there is an eon with two thousand Buddhas of different names, some named Jñānavijaya, some named Dīpaṃkararāja, some named Dharmavijaya, and some named Brahmanvijaya.
“Śāriputra! You all should with one mind take refuge in these and all other such Buddhas. Śāriputra!”
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Suvarṇasvaravibhūṣitabuddha. Śāriputra,
the lifespan of that Buddha Suvarṇasvaravibhūṣitabuddha will be a full sixty hundred years.
Beyond that, in the eastern direction, there is the Two-legged Honored One named Jñāneśvara; the lifespan of that Tathāgata Jñāneśvara is a full twelve thousand years.
Beyond that World-Honored One Jñāneśvara, there is another Buddha named Ojaseśvara, the Two-legged Honored One; the lifespan of that Buddha Ojaseśvara is a full seventy-six thousand years.
Beyond that World-Honored One, Vīryeśvara, there is another Buddha named Maheśvara; the lifespan of that Buddha Maheśvara is a full one hundred million years.
Beyond that Buddha Mahesvara, there was another Buddha named Brahmaghoṣa; the lifespan of that Buddha Brahmaghoṣa was a full ten billion years.
Beyond that World-Honored One Brahmaghoṣa, there was another Buddha named Mahāgaṇeśvara; the lifespan of that Buddha Mahāgaṇeśvara was a full sixty thousand years.
Beyond that World-Honored One, Sovereign of the Great Assembly, there is another Buddha named Sovereign of Sound; the lifespan of that Buddha, Sovereign of Sound, is a full one hundred million years.
Beyond that World-Honored One, Lord of Sound, there was another Buddha named Supreme Sound; the lifespan of that Buddha Supreme Sound was a full ten billion years.
Beyond that World-Honored One, Lord of Supreme Sound, there was a Buddha named Moon Face; the lifespan of that Buddha Moon Face was a full day and night.
Beyond that World-Honored One Moon-Face, there was another Buddha named Sun-Face; the lifespan of that Buddha Sun-Face was a full eighteen hundred years.
Beyond that World-Honored One Sun-Face, there was another Buddha named Brahma-Face; the lifespan of that Buddha Brahma-Face was a full twenty-three thousand years.
Beyond that World-Honored One Brahmamukha, there was another Buddha named Brahmasvabhāva; the lifespan of that Buddha Brahmasvabhāva was a full eighteen hundred years.
"Śāriputra! You all should with one mind take refuge in these and other such Buddhas. Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, during another kalpa, two hundred Buddhas appeared in the world; I shall recite their names for you to take refuge in:
Homage to the Buddha Pure Voice.
Homage to the Buddha Victorious Wisdom.
Homage to the Buddha Liberated Wisdom.
Homage to the Buddha Wisdom Valiant;
homage to the Buddha Pure Supreme;
homage to the Buddha Brahmā Heaven.
Homage to the Buddha Good Brahmā.

homage to the Buddha Well-Pacified and Valiant;
homage to the Buddha Well-Pacified Abiding in Excellence.

Homage to the Buddha Emitting Exquisite Fragrance.

Homage to the Buddha Dharmarati-niścaya. "Homage to the eighty billion Buddhas named Niścaya who appear during one eon of the Real Dharma; homage to the eighty billion Buddhas likewise named Niścaya who appear during the second eon; and to the Buddha named Atiniścaya and the Buddha named Viśeṣasiddha—one should also pay respectful homage to them with a single mind."
Homage to the Buddha Fine Eye.
Homage to the Buddha Wondrous Eye.
Homage to the Buddha Good Vision.
Homage to the Buddha Wondrous Departure.

homage to the Buddha of Great Merit;
Homage to the Buddha Pure Virtue.
Homage to the Buddha Pure Abiding.

Homage to the Buddha Subsequently Exalted Śākyamuni.
“Namo to Kāśyapa Buddha. The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
“In the present world-realm of Abhirati in the eastern direction dwells the Buddha named Akṣobhya; you all should pay him homage with single-minded devotion.”
Homage to the Buddha Dragon’s Joy;
homage to the Buddha Renowned Radiance.
Homage to the Buddha Renowned Sovereign King.
Homage to the Buddha Renowned for the Practice of Dharma.
Homage to the Buddha Primordial Wisdom.
Homage to the Buddha Supreme on the High Mountain.
Homage to the Buddha Treasury of Merit.
Homage to the Buddha Fearless Sovereignty.

Homage to the Buddha Accomplishment of Wisdom.

Homage to the Buddha Mountain of Merit.
Homage to the Buddha Decisive Renown.
Homage to the Buddha King of Boundless Contemplation.

Homage to the Buddha Unobstructed Peace;
homage to the Buddha Gate of Tranquility;
homage to the Buddha Vigorous in the Power of Merit.

Homage to the Buddha King of the Increasing Banner of Dharma.
Homage to the Buddha Light of Candana-pāra.
Homage to the Buddha Renowned for Sustaining Merit;
homage to the Buddha Firm Resolve and Diligence;
homage to the Buddha Lamp that Illuminates the Dust.
Homage to the Buddha King of Supreme Adornment;
homage to the Buddha Well-Seated on the Lion Throne;
homage to the Buddha King Who Radiates Moonlight Flowers. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
To the Buddhas of the present in the southern direction, you should single-mindedly take refuge:
Homage to the Buddha Sarabha First-Arousing-the-Mind Fragrance-Sovereign.

Homage to the Buddha Sovereign Dragon King Sound.

Homage to the Buddha King of Liberation;
homage to the Buddha King of the Lightning of Sovereign Power. Next, pay homage to the Great Dharma Wheel of the Treasury of the Honored Scriptures of the Twelve Divisions.
"Homage to all the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the ten directions.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Supreme Jewel Moon;
homage to the Bodhisattva Dignified Conduct;
homage to the Bodhisattva Non-Vain Virtue.
Homage to all the courageous and powerful Bodhisattvas.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Darkness.

homage to the Bodhisattva Free from Evil Realms;
homage to the Bodhisattva Cloud Shadow.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māra.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Samādhi.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dharma.
Homage to the Dharma Prince Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
homage to the Dharma Prince Maitreyarāja;
homage to the Dharma Prince Brahmaghoṣa.
Homage to the Dharma Prince Wondrous Form;
homage to the Dharma Prince Sandalwood Forest;
homage to the Dharma Prince Lion’s Roar Sound.
Homage to the Dharma Prince Wondrous Sound.
Homage to the Dharma Prince Wondrous Form and Appearance.
Homage to the Dharma Prince Various Adornments.
Homage to the Dharma Prince Śakraketu;
homage to the Dharma Prince Mūrdhaja. I take refuge in all such great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, immeasurable and boundless, throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
"I pay homage to all the worthy sages, both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, I shall next perform repentance.
Now, as for what is called repentance, its essence is to reform the past and cultivate the future, to extinguish evil and promote goodness."

In this world, who among those living their lives can be without transgression? Even a student on the path of learning gives rise to afflictions when mindfulness lapses; even an Arhat manifests physical and verbal karma through the movement of residual habits—how much more so, then, could an ordinary person be without faults?

However, the wise perceive this first and are thus able to repent and reform; the foolish conceal their faults, allowing them to spread and entangle like creeping vines. Consequently, through long habituation, they remain in the dark night of ignorance with no hope of awakening.

If one can, with a sense of shame and remorse, reveal and repent of one's transgressions, it will not only serve to extinguish offenses, but will also increase immeasurable merit and establish the wondrous fruit of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.

"If one wishes to practice this dharma, one should first externally solemnize one's physical demeanor and gaze upon the honored image with veneration; internally, one should give rise to a respectful mind and focus upon the characteristics of the dharma, reaching a state of profound sincerity and generating two kinds of minds."
First, one reflects to oneself: "This life of mine is difficult to preserve forever; it may perish in a single morning, and I do not know when this body might be restored.

If I do not encounter the Buddhas and the worthy sages, and should suddenly fall into the company of evil friends to create various sinful karmas, I shall again fall into deep pits and perilous realms."

Second, one should reflect: "In this life, although we have encountered the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and become his disciples—wherein the duty of a disciple is to perpetuate the lineage of the Sages and abide in the wholesome dharmas of purity in body, speech, and mind—we have instead collectively committed evils and concealed them. We claim that others do not know and that they do not see, hiding these deeds in our hearts with arrogance and shamelessness. This is indeed the height of folly and delusion in the world."

Furthermore, there currently exist the Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas of the various stages, and the devas and immortals; how could they ever fail to behold our committed evils with their pure divine eyes?
Furthermore, the spirits of both the hidden and the manifest record every detail of one's sins and blessings without the slightest error.

"Now, regarding those who commit transgressions, after their lives have ended, the ox-headed jailers will seize their spirits and bring them before King Yama to interrogate them thoroughly on their right and wrong."
At that time, all those who had been his enemies came forward as witnesses, each saying:
"In the past, you slaughtered my body, roasting, boiling, steaming, and grilling me.
"You previously plundered all my wealth and treasures and separated me from my kin; it is only now that I have finally found my opportunity against you.

At that time, with such evidence manifest before one's eyes, how could one dare to deny it? One should simply accept the retribution for past misdeeds with a willing heart, for as the sutras clarify, the hells do not punish the innocent.
"If, during his lifetime, he has lost his composure regarding the multitude of sins he habitually committed, then all the images of the places where he created those evils will appear before him."
"In the past, you committed such offenses in our presence; how can you now seek to conceal them?
This is what is meant by having no place of concealment for the commission of offenses.
Thereupon, King Yama gnashes his teeth in reproach and consigns them to hell, where they must pass through kalpas and years with no means of escape.

This matter is not far off and does not concern others; it is precisely my own body that acts and receives its retribution. Even between father and son, who are most intimate, when the moment arrives, there is no one to take their place. All of you, while your forms are still intact and your bodies free from ailment, each should exert yourselves and vie with your very lives to cultivate great dread. When death is about to arrive, it will be too late for regret.
Therefore, disciples! With a sincere heart, take refuge in all the Buddhas of the ten directions:

Homage to the Buddha Golden Ocean in the East. Homage to the Buddha Surpassing Mount Sumeru in the South. Homage to the Buddha Immeasurable Banner in the West. Homage to the Buddha Practice-Wisdom in the North. Homage to the Buddha Ultimate Wisdom in the Southeast. Homage to the Buddha Unsurpassed Wisdom in the Southwest. Homage to the Buddha Sovereign Wisdom in the Northwest. Homage to the Buddha Luminous Wisdom in the Northeast. Homage to the Buddha Brahma-Wisdom in the Nadir. Homage to the Buddha Subduing-Enemy Wisdom in the Zenith. I take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions.

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, you have accumulated ignorance that obscures the mind and eyes, and following the nature of the afflictions, you have committed sinful karmas throughout the three periods of time."

Whether it be the affliction of greed arising from indulgence, attachment, and craving; the affliction of malice and resentment harboring anger and intent to harm; the affliction of dullness, stupor, and lack of clarity; the affliction of arrogance and haughtiness born of self-conceit; the affliction of hesitation and doubt regarding the Right Path; the affliction of false views that deny cause and effect; the affliction of clinging to a self through ignorance of dependent origination; the affliction of grasping at permanence or annihilation due to confusion regarding the three periods of time; the affliction of dogmatic adherence to views arising from intimacy with unwholesome dharmas; the affliction of dogmatic adherence to precepts resulting from following heterodox teachers; and even the various afflictions of the four types of grasping and arbitrary conceptualizations—to all these, today we sincerely take refuge and repent.
From beginningless time until this day, we have harbored the affliction of stinginess by guarding and clinging tenaciously to things;
the affliction of dissipation by failing to restrain the six sense-faculties; the affliction of impatience through the practice of an evil mind; and the affliction of indolence."

The affliction of laxity and lack of diligence; the affliction of mental agitation through discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*); the affliction of ignorance and delusion when encountering sensory objects;
the affliction of "self" and "other" arising from the eight worldly winds; the affliction of a crooked mind that flatters and seeks praise;
the affliction of being unharmonious, stubborn, and difficult to approach; and the affliction of being easily provoked to anger and difficult to please.

The afflictions of harboring much resentment; the afflictions of being bound by the thorns of jealousy and being perverse and stubborn; the afflictions of being cruel, violent, harmful, deceitful, and poisonous;
the afflictions of being contrary to the two truths and clinging to signs; the afflictions that give rise to inversions regarding suffering, its origin, cessation, and the path;
the afflictions that follow along with the flow of the twelve links of dependent origination within birth and death; and so forth, up to...

From the beginningless ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), there arise the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; these give rise to the four grounds of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) and construct the fruits of suffering within the triple world.

Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, vexing and disturbing the worthies and sages across the six paths and four modes of birth. Today, we openly confess them before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, taking refuge and repenting.

"May we, the disciples, by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance of all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, in every birth and every life: may we break the banner of arrogance and exhaust the waters of craving; extinguish the fire of anger and shatter the darkness of ignorance; uproot the source of doubt and tear asunder the net of false views. May we deeply realize that the three realms are like a prison, the four elements are like venomous snakes, the five aggregates are like hostile bandits, and the six sense bases are like an empty village where craving feigns intimacy. May we cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to sever the source of nescience, proceeding directly toward Nirvana without ceasing or resting; may the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment be in accord with every thought, and may the ten perfections be ever present before us."

In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning Retribution for Śramaṇas*, as Precious Attainment was about to enter another hell called the Hell of Severed Hands, [the interlocutor] asked:
"Why is it named the Hell of Severed Hands?"

That hell is thirty-six yojanas in length and breadth. Within that hell there is a great iron bed, over fifty paces in length and breadth. Fierce flames and smoke rise together to burn the offenders; when the offenders see it, they are so oppressed by fear that they fall to the ground, unable to endure it.
In the middle of the southern gate, five thousand śramaṇas raised their voices and cried out, "What crime have we committed that we have come to enter this place?

The horse-headed rākṣasa, grasping a three-pronged iron fork in his hand, thrust it through their chests so that it emerged from their backs; he then led them to an iron bed, upon which fire blazed and smoke and flames both issued forth to burn the sinners.

Furthermore, there are iron axes that chop the hands of the offenders, shattering them inch by inch; throughout a single day and night, they undergo myriad forms of suffering, unable to seek life nor able to seek death.
Bao Da asked the horse-headed rākṣasa,
"What sinful karma did these śramaṇas commit to come here?

"These śramaṇas receive the pure precepts of the Buddha yet are unable to uphold them; they do not purify themselves by rinsing their mouths with *śītalā* twigs, nor are their hands clean, being covered in much filth. Sometimes they grasp male or female genitals, or grasp impure objects; while having foul odors and filth within their bellies that they have not removed, they then grasp scriptures and images."

"Because of these causes and conditions, one falls into this hell, remaining there for thousands of millions of kalpas without being able to escape; even if one subsequently attains a human body, it will be incomplete.
Upon hearing this, Bodhidharma wept with grief and departed.

fourth, observing the body of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the first observation of causes and conditions: one knows that these transgressions of mine are based on ignorance and unwholesome reflection; lacking the power of right contemplation, I failed to recognize my faults and remained far removed from virtuous friends, the Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas.

Following the path of Māra, they travel along crooked and perilous ways; like a fish swallowing a hook without knowing its danger, like a silkworm spinning a cocoon to entangle and bind itself, or like a moth rushing into a flame to burn and rot itself, by these causes and conditions they are unable to escape on their own.

"Second, regarding the contemplation of karmic retribution: all evil and unwholesome deeds result in the endless suffering of transmigration throughout the three periods of time. One sinks into the vast ocean of the great night of boundlessness, devoured by the rākṣasas of the afflictions; future births and deaths are dark and shoreless."

Even if one were to obtain the retribution of becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four continents with sovereign power of flight and possessing the seven treasures, one would still not escape death and falling into the evil realms after the end of life.

The retribution of the four formless attainments is the most exalted within the three realms; yet when one's merit is exhausted, one returns to become a worm in a cow's head. How much more so for others who possess no merit and further fail to exert themselves in repentance? This is like clutching a stone and sinking into a deep abyss—difficult indeed to seek deliverance.

"Third, I contemplate my own person: although I possess the nature of the numinous awakening which is the direct cause, it is shrouded by the dense forest of the darkness of afflictions; lacking the power of the revealing cause, it cannot manifest."

I should now give rise to the supreme mind, shatter the heavy obstructions of ignorance and perversion, sever the causes of the false suffering of birth and death, manifest the great luminous wisdom of the Tathāgata, and establish the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

"Fourth, one contemplates the body of the Tathāgata: unconditioned, tranquil, and luminous, transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations; replete with all virtues, it abides in profound stillness and permanence. Although he enters parinirvāṇa through skillful means, his compassionate salvation never ceases for even a moment."
To give rise to such a mind may be called an excellent ford for extinguishing transgressions and an essential practice for removing obstacles.
Today, with a sincere heart, we bow our heads and take refuge in the Buddha.

"Disciples! From beginningless time until this very day, our afflictions have been nurtured, growing deeper and thicker, flourishing and spreading daily. They shroud the eye of wisdom so that nothing may be seen; they sever all roots of goodness so that they cannot continue, creating obstacles to their arising. We fail to see the Buddhas, hear the True Dharma, or meet the Holy Sangha because of the obstacles created by afflictions. We do not perceive the good and evil karmic actions throughout all worlds of the past and future because of the obstacle of afflictions. We face the obstacle of afflictions regarding the reception of noble rewards as humans, devas, or honored beings. We face the obstacle of afflictions regarding the meditative concentrations and meritorious joys of the form and formless realms. And we face the obstacle of afflictions that prevents us from attaining sovereign supernormal powers—such as flying, appearing and disappearing at will, and traveling everywhere to the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions to listen to the Dharma."

"One studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the counting of *ānāpāna* and the contemplation of impurity; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the causal conditions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the meaning of the seven expedients and the three contemplations; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the World-Transcending Dharma within the four foundations of mindfulness; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the first dharma of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the liberation through emptiness, equality, and the Middle Way; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the manifestation of signs within the Eightfold Noble Path; one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the non-manifestation of signs within the seven factors of enlightenment; and one studies the hindrances of affliction regarding the contemplation of the causal conditions of the factors of the path."

The afflictive hindrances to studying the eight liberations and nine emptinesses; the afflictive hindrances to studying the ten knowledges and samādhis; the afflictive hindrances to studying the three clarities, six supernormal powers, and four unhindered understandings; the afflictive hindrances to studying the six perfections and four immeasurables; the afflictive hindrances to studying the four means of attraction for the sake of extensive transformation; the afflictive hindrances to studying the Mahāyāna mind and the four great vows; the afflictive hindrances to studying the ten insights and ten practices; and the afflictive hindrances to studying the ten dedications and ten vows.

"The afflictive hindrances clearly understood in the first, second, third, and fourth stages; the afflictive hindrances regarding various knowledge and views in the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages; the afflictive hindrances regarding the dual illumination while training in the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages; and likewise, the afflictive hindrances above the millions of *asaṃkhyeya* practices that obstruct the attainment of the Buddha-fruit—such hindrances to practice are immeasurable and boundless."

Today, having arrived here, I prostrate with utmost sincerity before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly. With shame and remorse, I repent and pray that all [obstructions] may be extinguished.
"By virtue of this repentance, may the obstacles of afflictions regarding all conditioned phenomena be forever exhausted without remainder."

May the disciple, wherever they may be, attain birth with sovereign mastery, no longer subject to the turning of karmic fetters. Through the supernormal power of *ṛddhi*, may they reach all ten directions in a single thought-moment, purifying Buddha-lands and gathering and transforming sentient beings. May they penetrate without obstruction the profound realms of various meditative concentrations as well as all forms of knowledge and vision. May their mind universally encompass all phenomena, delighting in inexhaustible eloquence without becoming stained or attached. May they attain mastery over the mind, mastery over the Dharma, mastery over wisdom, and mastery over skillful means (*upāya*). May these afflictions and the habitual tendencies of ignorance be utterly and permanently severed so that they never again continue; may the untainted noble path shine forth clearly like the sun.
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning Retribution for Śramaṇas*, the Jewel-Attainer (Ratnada) entered the Rain-of-Fire Hell a short while ago.
Why is it called the Rain-of-Fire Hell?

That hell is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its iron walls are circular and surrounded by blazing fires. Beneath it lies a floor of iron blades with their edges pointing upward. At the four corners of the city, winds arise and blow against the walls, causing the fires within the city to blaze even more fiercely.

In the four corners are copper dogs with fangs protruding upward; fire issues from their mouths and eyes, and they move as swiftly as the wind. From the mouths of these copper dogs, billowing and dense clouds of vapor emerge; water flows from their noses like falling rain, and within each drop, flames arise simultaneously. Descending from the sky, the fire is like chariot wheels; it strikes the bodies of the offenders, and their entire bodies burst into flame. Day and night they undergo immeasurable suffering, dying and being reborn a thousand times, ten thousand times, even a hundred thousand times.
Bao Da asked the Hayagrīva Rākṣasa,
"What karmic actions did these śramaṇas perform to undergo such suffering?

"These śramaṇas have received the pure precepts of the Buddha, yet they do not guard or cherish their dignified deportment; though they have fashioned saṃghāṭī robes, they are unwilling to wear them, entering villages with empty bodies and exposed forms, like withered trees devoid of luster."
If they do so on the grounds of the Buddha or the Sangha, it is likewise;
the devas will cry out, "A mad thief of a bhikṣu has entered a human village!
Due to these causes and conditions, one falls into this hell.
"Having emerged from hell, one shall constantly be reborn as an animal for thousands of millions of kalpas.
Upon hearing this, Bodhidharma wept with sorrow and departed.
