At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "To speak in brief, the present Buddhas are inexhaustible in number.
Śāriputra! It is as if, for example, there were worlds in the eastern direction as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise in the southern direction..."

In worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—worlds in the west as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, worlds in the north as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and worlds in the zenith, nadir, and the four intermediate directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—in all those worlds, from the bottom to the water’s edge and from the top to the Peak of Existence, they were filled with motes of dust.
Is it possible to know the number of those atoms?

"In this way, as for those Tathāgatas named Śākyamuni who currently exist in the world, I see them all before my eyes. Their mothers are all named Mahāmāyā; their fathers are all named King Śuddhodana; their cities are all named Kapilavastu. Among those Buddhas, their foremost śrāvaka disciples are all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and their attendant disciples are all named Ānanda."
How much more so for various names of mothers,
Are they disciples under different names?
Are they attendants under different names? “Śāriputra!
Regarding those various worlds, in which of them would that person place a mote of dust, and in which would he not?
Whether those worlds have motes of dust placed upon them or not, they extend from the water’s edge below up to the Peak of Existence above.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, suppose there were a second person who took those atoms of dust; for as many Buddha-fields as there are in that number of atoms—namely, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds—he would take a single step for every such world passed.

Śāriputra! That person takes as many worlds as there are atoms as a single step; in this manner, after traveling for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he sets down a single atom, continuing until all the atoms are exhausted.
Śāriputra! Suppose these many worlds—both those where atoms have been placed and those where they have not—are filled with atoms, and then further atoms are added to the worlds of the ten directions.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, beyond these worlds—whether those places where atoms are placed or where they are not—fill all those worlds, from the water’s edge below up to the Peak of Existence above, with atoms.

“Śāriputra! Furthermore, there is a third person who takes that many atoms of dust and, having passed as many worlds as there are atoms, takes a single step. After traveling for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he sets down a single atom; in this manner, he exhausts all the atoms.”
"Furthermore, there is a fourth person who takes as many worlds as there are atoms in those [previous] quantities.
Whether they are occupied by atoms or not, from the bottom limit of the waters up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), he fills them entirely with atoms."
Is it possible to know the number of those atoms?

“One might be able to know the number of those various atoms; however, as for those Buddhas all named Śākyamuni, their mothers all named Mahāmāyā, their fathers all named King Śuddhodana, their cities all named Kapilavastu, their foremost disciples all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and their attendant disciples all named Ānanda—the number of those Buddhas cannot be known.”
Śāriputra! It is the same for the fifth person, the sixth, the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, and the tenth person. Śāriputra!

Furthermore, there is an eleventh person who takes one atom from among those many atoms and breaks it into as many parts as there are atoms in as many worlds of the ten directions; he likewise breaks all the remaining atoms into as many parts as there are atoms in as many worlds of the ten directions.
Can the number of those minute particles be known?

"Furthermore, suppose there were a person who took as many Buddha-lands as there are particles of dust as a single step; with such swift supernatural power, they travel through the worlds of the eastern direction, dropping a single particle of dust at the end of every immeasurable and boundless kalpa until the eastern direction is exhausted by such particles."
Whether they occupy space or not, suppose that from the bottom of the water-world up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), the space were filled with these atoms.
Likewise, in the southern direction, and so on throughout the ten directions, from the bottom of the water-world up to the peak of existence, the space were filled with these atoms.
Can the number of those atoms be known?

"One might be able to know the number of those various particles of dust; however, the number of present-day Buddhas in the world named Śākyamuni—whose mothers are all named Mahāmāyā, whose fathers are all named King Śuddhodana, whose cities are all named Kapilavastu, whose foremost disciples are all named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, and whose attendant disciples are all named Ānanda—is impossible to know."
How much more so for those with various different names for Buddhas,
Are they different names for the city?
“Śāriputra! Even if I were to remain in the world for as many eons as there are atoms in a certain number of worlds, I could not exhaustively describe even a single instance of the name Śākyamuni.

In this same way, there are those with the same name as Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the same name as Dīpaṃkara Buddha, the same name as Pradyota-prabha Buddha, the same name as Sarvābhibhū Buddha, the same name as Mahāyaśas Buddha, the same name as Padmottara Buddha, the same name as Vipaśyin Buddha, the same name as Śikhin Buddha, the same name as Viśvabhū Buddha, the same name as Krakucchanda Buddha, the same name as Kanakamuni Buddha, and the same name as Kāśyapa Buddha.”
All those who bear such names, even down to their various alternative names, as well as those who exist in the present age—I now know them all; you should pay them single-minded homage.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“If sons or daughters of good family seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should first repent of all their transgressions.”
If a bhikṣu commits one of the four pārājika offenses, a bhikṣuṇī commits one of the eight pārājika offenses, a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera,
or śrāmaṇerī commits a fundamental offense of the renunciant life, or if an upāsaka commits a grave precept of an upāsaka,
or an upāsikā commits a grave precept of an upāsikā— should they wish to repent, [they must proceed as follows].
One should bathe until clean, put on new, pure garments, and abstain from pungent-smelling vegetables.
One should prepare the interior of the room in a quiet place, adorning the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) with various banners and flowers.
One should smear it with fragrant mud, hang forty-nine banners, adorn the Buddha’s seat, install the image of the Buddha, and burn various incenses such as sandalwood and aloeswood.
With frankincense, tagara, and kastūrikā, as well as various powdered incenses and unguents, he burned such diverse and wondrous perfumes and scattered various flowers.
Raising great compassion, he vowed to rescue suffering sentient beings:
to enable those not yet crossed over to cross over, those not yet liberated to be liberated, and those not yet at peace to find peace. Those who had not yet attained...
Nirvāṇa is that which brings about the attainment of nirvāṇa.

Day and night he contemplates the Tathāgata’s original practices and ascetic austerities; throughout immeasurable kalpas, he underwent all manner of suffering and affliction without ever giving rise to weariness or aversion. For the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, he spontaneously gave rise to a humble mind toward all sentient beings, like the heart of a servant.

"If a bhikṣu repents for the four grave offenses, he should, for forty-nine days and nights, confess his transgressions before eight pure bhikṣus. He should confess them once every seven days, with a sincere and earnest heart repenting of his past deeds, single-mindedly taking refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions, calling their names and prostrating according to his means and ability. If he maintains such sincerity for the full forty-nine days, his offenses will certainly be extinguished; when this person attains purity, signs shall appear."
Whether in the waking state or in a dream, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions bestowing upon them predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

Or one sees Bodhisattvas bestowing predictions, coming to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as companions, or placing their hands upon one’s head to demonstrate the signs of the purification of transgressions.

Or they may see themselves entering a great assembly and taking their place among the multitude; or they may see themselves preaching the Dharma within the assembly; or they may see various teachers and śramaṇas of pure conduct leading them to the site of enlightenment to show them the Buddhas.

“Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu, when repenting of his offenses, sees such signs as these, you should know that this person’s defilements of offense have been extinguished, except in cases where there was a lack of sincere intent.”

If a bhikṣuṇī confesses the eight grave offenses (pārājika), she shall follow the rules for bhikṣus: after completing forty-nine days, she shall attain purification, except in cases where she lacks a sincere mind.

"If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī confesses a fundamental grave offense, they must do so before four pure bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; according to the aforementioned method, after completing twenty-one days, they should be known as pure, except in cases where they lack a sincere heart."

"If a layman or laywoman seeks to repent and extinguish their transgressions, they should with a sincere heart revere the Triple Gem. Upon seeing a śramaṇa, they should pay respectful homage and conceive the thought that such a person is difficult to encounter. They should invite him to a place of practice and provide various offerings. Furthermore, they should invite a bhikṣu whom they hold in deep respect, and before him, confess all the offenses they have committed with a sincere heart. With single-minded devotion, they should take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions, reciting their names and prostrating. If they continue in this manner for seven full days, they will certainly attain purity, provided they do not harbor insincerity."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Having attained Bodhi and subdued Māra, He dwells with mastery beneath the tree of enlightenment;
Realizing the unobstructed eye and body, The Dharma-realm is equal to empty space.”
Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattva disciples as numerous as the atoms within ten billion lands,
they have attained a mind of universal tranquility and dwell skillfully within all the practices of Samantabhadra.
The Buddha’s body is wondrously adorned with the primary and secondary marks;
He emits various kinds of immeasurable light, universally illuminating all lands in the ten directions.
By the inconceivable power of all Buddhas, one sees that all lands are entirely free from defilement, Filled with infinite sublime colors and pure clarity.
All the supreme and wondrous deeds of the Buddhas, Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, one beholds the great assembly.
In the eastern world named Ratnaketu, Far removed from all defilements and exquisitely adorned,
The Buddha Ratnapradīpa-vibhu currently dwells In that world at this very time.
In the southern land of Sphāṭikadīpa, Pure and adorned with exquisite colors,
The Tathāgata Maṇivimalamegha Currently dwells in the world, preaching the sublime Dharma.
In the west lies the stainless and pure land, Known as the wondrous world of Sukhāvatī;
There dwells the sovereign Amitāyus Buddha, Surrounded by his bodhisattva disciples.
In the northern world named Fragrant Lamp, The land is pure and most exquisitely adorned.
It is the transformation of the Buddha Unstained Light Banner, Who now dwells at ease beneath the tree of the site of enlightenment.
With the wondrous color of lapis lazuli radiance, The land is pure and supremely magnificent.
The Tathāgata Unobstructed Light Cloud Buddha now dwells in the northeastern direction,
within the world-realm Illuminated by the Banner of Radiance, where he is seen manifesting and bringing all bodhisattvas to fulfillment.
The Buddha Svatantra-ghoṣa currently resides there in the southeastern direction,
in the world-realm of Citra-sukha-saṃbhava, which is exquisitely pure and adorned with mani jewels.
The Victorious and Sublime Moon of Wisdom, like Mount Sumeru, currently resides in the southwest;
in the northwest, one beholds the Tathāgata of the Realm of Equal Radiance of Mount Meru.
There, the Great Sage, the Buddha Sovereign, is surrounded by a host of disciples and bodhisattvas.
In the world below is the realm Sovereign Light, A pure land named Treasury of Jewel Flames;
The Buddha Amoghadarśin dwells within that wondrous realm, Surrounded by a sublime wheel of radiance.
In the world above, the Treasury of Radiant Flames, That world is named Pure and Stainless;
From clouds of light of the merit of the Universal Eye, He appears seated beneath the Bodhi tree.
At that time, Śāriputra and the great assembly, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, beheld the infinite and boundless Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions.
At that time, Śāriputra, weeping with tears streaming down his face in the midst of the great assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
If good sons or good daughters do not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they shall not achieve Buddhahood.”
"We have been like withered grass from time immemorial; though we have experienced the warmth of spring, we have had no hope for the fruit of autumn.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We pray that you would further expound at length the names of all the Buddhas throughout the ten directions; we long to hear them.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“You should listen with a sincere mind and attend closely; I shall speak for you.”
Śāriputra! To the east of this world, passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, there is a buddha-world named Rocaṇa.
In that world there is a Buddha named Ratnasaṃcaya, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha and wholeheartedly receive, uphold, and mindfully recollect it, these good sons and good daughters will ultimately attain the samādhi of the seven factors of enlightenment, achieve non-retrogression from the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and transcend sixty kalpas of the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In the eastern realm of Dīpaṃkara, There is a Buddha named Ratnasaṃbhava;
If anyone hears his name, They shall transcend sixty kalpas of worldly existence."
“Śāriputra! In the eastern direction there is a world named Ratnasamcaya. In that world there is a Buddha named Ratnaśrī, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears the name of that Buddha, receives and upholds it with a sincere heart, recites it, and joins their palms in prostration;

and if there were another son of good family or daughter of good family who were to give away as alms the precious treasures filling a trichiliocosm, doing so day after day for a full hundred years—the merit of such giving would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, nor any numerical fraction, nor any calculable fraction, nor any illustrative analogy of the merit of the former’s sincere prostration.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In the world-system Ratnasaṃcaya, there is a Buddha named Ratnavijaya. If a person hears his name, even a gift [given elsewhere] would not equal one-sixteenth of it."

“Śāriputra! To the east from here, passing through eight hundred worlds, there is a buddha-world named Gandhavatī. There dwells a Buddha named Siddhalokeśvararāja Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”
If a person hears the name of that Buddha, upholds it, recites it, remembers it, and pays homage to it, they will transcend five hundred kalpas of worldly existence.
"Śāriputra! From this world, passing through a thousand worlds to the east, there is a world named Śuddhavati."
In that world there is a Buddha named Vairocana-Bimba Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma.

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha, uphold, read, and recite it, and mindfully remember him with a sincere heart, revering and prostrating before him, they shall be liberated from the three evil realms.
“Śāriputra! To the east of here, passing through two thousand worlds, there is a buddha-field named Immeasurable Radiance and Merit.
In that world there is a Buddha named Vairocana-prabha Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

If a son or daughter of good family hears the name of that Buddha, prostrates themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, and with a deeply reverent heart upholds, recites, and respectfully worships it, this person shall transcend twenty kalpas of worldly existence.
“Śāriputra! To the east, beyond a thousand worlds, there is a buddha-field named Ramanīya; the Buddha there is named Akṣobhya, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and pay homage with reverence, such persons will ultimately never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and no demons whatsoever shall be able to move them.
“Śāriputra! To the east, beyond a thousand worlds, there is a buddha-field named Immeasurable.
There dwells a Buddha named Mahāprabha, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently teaching the Dharma.”

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha Prabhāsa, uphold, read, recite, revere, and pay homage to it, such persons shall never be separated from all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and will ultimately attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Śāriputra! To the east of this buddha-field, passing through sixty worlds, there is a buddha-field named Dīpapradyota. There dwells a buddha named Aparimitasvara, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”

If a son or daughter of good family hears the name of that Amitābha Buddha and recites "Namo to the Tathāgata Immeasurable Sound" three times—Namo to the Tathāgata Immeasurable Sound, Namo to the Tathāgata Immeasurable Sound, Namo to the Tathāgata Immeasurable Sound—that person will ultimately never fall into the three evil realms and will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, beyond those worlds, crossing over a thousand Buddha-lands, there is a Buddha-world named Dustless (Vimalā).
There dwells a Buddha of the same name as Amitābha—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who is currently preaching the Dharma.”

If a good man or a good woman hears the name of that Buddha, and with a profound mind of reverence upholds, recites, and respectfully worships it, this person shall transcend twelve kalpas of the world.
“Śāriputra! Beyond twenty thousand buddha-fields, there is a buddha-world named Durjayā. There dwells a buddha named Mahāyaśas, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
If a son or daughter of good family hears the name of that Buddha and joins their palms,
saying these words: "Namo to Mahāyaśas Tathāgata," and if there were another person who,

for a full hundred years, daily gave as alms the seven treasures equal in measure to Mount Sumeru, the merit of hearing this Buddha's name and prostrating before him would exceed that [merit], such that the former does not equal even one-hundredth part of it, nor even one part in any calculation or numerical fraction.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, beyond three thousand Buddha-fields, there is a world named Prabhāsa; the Buddha there is named Ratnaprabhāsa, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
If good sons or good daughters uphold the name of that Buddha, they shall transcend one hundred kalpas of the world and attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"If there are those who do not believe that hearing this name brings such merit, these people shall fall into the Avīci Hell for a full hundred kalpas. Śāriputra!"

To the east, beyond ten thousand buddha-fields, there is a world named Prabhāsvarāloka. There dwells a Buddha named Mahāvīraprāpta, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there preaching the Dharma.

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha, uphold it, read and recite it, and pay respectful homage, these people will ultimately attain great fearlessness and gather an immeasurable and boundless mass of merit.
“Śāriputra! Beyond seven thousand buddha-fields there is a world named Maṇiprabhā. There dwells a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently teaches the Dharma.”

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha and, with a sincere heart, pay respectful homage, receive and uphold it, and recite it, such persons will attain the ten powers of the Tathāgata.

“Śāriputra! Furthermore, beyond eight thousand buddha-lands, there is a world named Reality (Tattva). In that world there is a Buddha, titled Real Sound (Tattvasvara) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma.”

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha, uphold, read, recite, and with a sincere heart pay homage to it, these people will ultimately attain the Four Noble Truths and ultimately attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

“Śāriputra! Beyond twenty thousand buddha-fields, there is a buddha-world named Prabhāsa; the Buddha there is named Anantavimala, an Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”

If a son or daughter of good family hears the name of that Buddha and, with a sincere heart, believes, accepts, upholds, recites, and reverently worships it; and if there were another person who were to give as an offering the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm, the merit of the latter would not equal even one ten-millionth part of the merit of hearing, upholding, and reciting the name of the Buddha Vimala, nor would it reach even a calculable fraction thereof.
Why is this? If sentient beings have meager roots of goodness, they will be unable to hear the name of the Buddha Vimala.

If there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Tathāgata Anantavimala, these people have not planted roots of goodness under only one Buddha, nor have they planted roots of goodness under a thousand Buddhas; rather, these people have planted roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, and these people shall transcend forty-eight kalpas of the world.

“Śāriputra! To the east, passing through nine thousand buddha-lands, there is a world named Wonderful Sound. There, a Buddha named Moon Sound Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”

If good sons or good daughters hear the name of that Buddha, and are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it while paying homage with a sincere heart, all the merit they obtain will be complete in a hundred qualities like the full moon, and they will ultimately attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Śāriputra! Beyond ten thousand buddha-lands, there is a world named Abhaya; the Buddha there is named Anantayaśas, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears the name of that Buddha, upholds it, recites it, and with palms joined speaks these words:
"Namo to the World-Honored One of Boundless Renown."

"Furthermore, if there were someone who gave away the seven treasures in quantities equal to Mount Sumeru, doing so every day for a full hundred years, this mass of merit would not equal even one-hundredth part of the merit of upholding the Buddha’s name; it would not even be reached by calculation or analogy."
“Śāriputra! Beyond another fifteen hundred buddha-fields, there is a world named Dīpaṃkara. There, a Buddha named Candrasūryaprabhāsa Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears the name of that Buddha and upholds, recites, and reads it, then kneeling with palms joined and the right knee touching the ground, they shall three times speak these words:
"Namo to the World-Honored One Sun-Moon Radiance; Namo to the World-Honored One Sun-Moon Radiance; Namo to the World-Honored One Sun-Moon Radiance."
Śāriputra, beyond thirty thousand Buddha-lands, there is a world named Vimalā; there dwells a Buddha named Vimalaprabhā Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma."

If good sons, good daughters, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or humans and non-humans hear these names of the Buddhas, they will ultimately never regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall not enter the evil realms.
“Śāriputra! Ten thousand Buddha-lands to the east, there is a world named Hundred Radiances. There dwells a Buddha named Pure Radiance Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”

If devas, nāgas, yakṣas, or non-humans hear this name, they will certainly attain a human body and remain far removed from the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion; however, if any person hears it and does not believe, they shall fall into the great hells for sixty thousand kalpas.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, beyond a hundred buddha-fields, there is a world named Śubhakṛt, where a Buddha named Sūryaprabha Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”

If a person, with a mind of ultimate purity, invokes the name of this Buddha, the merit they obtain will be as complete as the orb of the sun; they will ultimately be able to subdue all demons and non-Buddhists, and transcend thirty kalpas of the world.

“Śāriputra! Beyond sixty thousand Buddha-lands further away, there is a world named Abiding in the Seven Factors of Enlightenment; there dwells a Buddha named Anantaratna Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.”

If a person hears the name of that Buddha, they will fully attain the seven factors of enlightenment; they will be able to establish sentient beings within the midst of supreme jewels, ultimately accomplishing an immeasurable mass of merit.

“Śāriputra! Beyond five hundred buddha-fields, there is a world named Flower Mirror Image; the Buddha there is named Flower Victorious Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”

If a person hears the name of that Buddha and, with faith and reverence, honors it, that person will achieve all wholesome dharmas like a flower in full bloom and transcend fifty-five kalpas of worldly existence.

“Śāriputra! Beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of buddha-fields, there is a world named Free from All Sorrow and Affliction. There, a Buddha named Sublime Body Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.”

If a person hears the name of that Buddha and with a sincere heart reveres, prostrates to, and makes offerings to him, that person will ultimately remain far removed from all obstacles, shall not enter the evil realms, and will transcend immeasurable kalpas of the world.

“Śāriputra! Beyond that, past nayutas of buddha-fields, there is a world named Samatā. There resides a Buddha, titled Dharmaprabhāsa-viśuddha-praphulla-padma Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently teaches the Dharma.”
If anyone hears the name of that Tathāgata, receives and upholds it without forgetting, they shall forever be free from the three evil realms.

If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās wish to repent of their various transgressions, they should bathe and purify themselves, put on new, clean robes, thoroughly cleanse the interior of the room, arrange a high seat, and install an image of the Buddha. They should hang twenty-five banners, make offerings of various flowers and incense, and recite the names of these twenty-five Buddhas while repenting during the six periods of the day and night. Upon completing twenty-five days, they will extinguish the four grave offenses, the eight grave offenses, and other such sins. This applies equally to śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the names, surnames, and the lengths of the lifespans of the seven Buddhas of the past; we delight in hearing this.”
I shall explain it for you, Śāriputra.
Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata.
In the past, thirty kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Śikhin Tathāgata.
Within that same kalpa, there was also a Buddha named Viśvabhū Tathāgata; from that time onward, immeasurable and boundless kalpas passed by empty, without any Buddhas.
In the present Bhadrakalpa, there are four Buddhas:
Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and I, Śākyamuni Buddha.

“Vipaśyin Buddha’s lifespan was eighty thousand kalpas; Śikhin Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand kalpas; Viśvabhū Buddha’s lifespan was two thousand kalpas; Krakucchanda Buddha’s lifespan was fourteen minor kalpas; Kanakamuni Buddha’s lifespan was thirty minor kalpas; Kāśyapa Buddha’s lifespan was two minor kalpas; and my own present lifespan is the shortest, being one hundred years.”
“Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, and Viśvabhū Buddha were born into kṣatriya families.
Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha were born into brāhmaṇa families.”
Śāriputra, I, Śākyamuni Buddha, was born into a Kṣatriya family.
The three Buddhas—Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū—were all of the Kauṇḍinya clan.
The Buddhas Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa—these three Buddhas have the clan name Kāśyapa.

"The foremost śrāvaka disciples of Vipaśyin Buddha were first named Kiṃśuka and second named Khaṇḍa.

The foremost śrāvaka disciples of Viśvabhū Buddha were first named Nakṣatra and second named Uttara.
The foremost śrāvaka disciples of Krakucchanda Buddha were first named Tvarita and second named Bala.
The first two śrāvaka disciples of Konākamuni Buddha were, first, Jīvaka and second, Vīra.
The first two śrāvaka disciples of Kāśyapa Buddha were, first, Śuna and second, Phalada.
I, Śākyamuni Buddha, have two foremost śrāvaka disciples: the first is named Śāriputra, and the second is named Maudgalyāyana.
Of these two, as mentioned above, the former is foremost in wisdom, and the latter is foremost in supernormal powers.

“The attendant of Vipaśyin Buddha was named Aśoka; the attendant of Śikhin Buddha was named Vigatabhaya; the attendant of Viśvabhū Buddha was named Śānta; the attendant of Krakucchanda Buddha was named Jñāna; the attendant of Kanakamuni Buddha was named Priya; the attendant of Kāśyapa Buddha was named Kāśyapa; my attendant is named Ānanda.”

The abbreviated repentance for the afflictive hindrances is now complete; we shall now proceed in order to repent for the karmic hindrances.
For karma is that which adorns the various realms of existence, appearing everywhere and in every place; therefore, one should contemplate and seek liberation from the world.

Therefore, one should know that the various and distinct forms and categories of the retributive fruits within the six realms of existence are all produced by the power of karma; thus, among the ten powers of a Buddha, the power of karma is most profound.
Ordinary people frequently give rise to doubts and suspicions regarding this matter. Why is this so?
It is because we see in the world that those who practice virtue meet with misfortune and adversity, while those who commit evil encounter success and favorable circumstances at every turn.
To say that there is no distinction between good and evil in the world—
such a calculation arises from an inability to deeply penetrate the principles of karma. Why is this so?
First, retribution in the present life;
second, retribution in the next life;
Karma to be experienced in the present life refers to performing good or evil deeds in the present and receiving their retribution in the present body.
Karma to be experienced in the next life refers to performing good or evil deeds in this life and receiving their retribution in the life to come.

Regarding karma that ripens later: it may be wholesome or unwholesome deeds performed during immeasurable past lives that are experienced either in this life, or their retribution is experienced only during immeasurable future lives in the present or the future.

"As for those who previously committed evil deeds yet appear to experience good fortune in the present, this is because the ripening of wholesome karma from past lives—whether as a result in the present life or a subsequent life—is now maturing; thus, they enjoy these pleasant fruits in the present. How could this possibly be related to performing various evil deeds in the present and receiving a favorable retribution!"

When a person who practices virtue experiences suffering in the present life, it is because the retributions from evil karma—whether from past lives as birth-retribution or subsequent-retribution—have ripened; since the power of their current roots of goodness is weak and cannot dispel them, they receive this bitter retribution. How could this possibly be related to performing good deeds in the present and thereby inviting an evil retribution?
How is this known to be so?
We observe in the world that those who perform wholesome deeds are praised by others and held in high esteem; therefore, we know that they will inevitably bring forth pleasant fruits in the future.

Since one possesses such evil karma from the past, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct one to draw near to virtuous friends and practice repentance together; for a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is of complete benefit in the attainment of the Way.
Therefore, disciples! Today we take refuge with utmost sincerity in the Buddha. Homage to the Buddha Pure Treasury of the East (Pūrva-vimalagarbha).

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, you have accumulated evils as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and committed sins that fill the heavens and the earth; yet, when casting off one body and receiving another, you were neither aware nor did you know."

Some commit the grave offenses of the five heinous crimes, bound by deep and turbid entanglements; some create the karma of an icchantika who severs their roots of goodness; some engage in the karma of slandering the Buddha’s words and denigrating the Vaipulya sutras; some perform the karma of destroying the Triple Gem and subverting the True Dharma; some lack faith in sin and merit, giving rise to the ten evil deeds; some commit the karma of delusion that turns one away from the truth and toward perversity; some commit the karma of filial impiety toward both parents and perverse rebellion; some commit the karma of slighting and insulting teachers and elders, lacking propriety and respect; and some commit the karma of being untrustworthy toward friends and violating principles of righteousness.

Or they may create karma that constitutes fourfold, sixfold, or eightfold obstructions to the Noble Path; they may violate the five precepts and destroy the practice of the eightfold fast; or they may commit many transgressions and omissions regarding the five categories and seven groups of offenses.

The grave and light defiled karmas of an upāsaka; or the inability to maintain the purity of the bodhisattva precepts as prescribed in their practice; the defilement of the brahmacarya through preparatory and subsequent actions; and the karma of negligence regarding the six fast days each month.

Throughout the three long fasts of the year, one does not constantly cultivate practice; one fails to act in accordance with the dharma regarding the three thousand codes of deportment; one commits the subtle offenses of the eighty thousand rules of discipline; one does not cultivate the karma of body, precepts, mind, and wisdom; during the eight royal festivals of spring and autumn, one creates manifold sinful karmas; one engages in the sixteen kinds of evil non-disciplinary practices; toward suffering sentient beings, one lacks the karma of compassion; and one lacks the karma of pity, mindfulness, or mercy.

Karma that neither uproots nor delivers, providing no protection; karma characterized by envy and jealousy, lacking the means to transcend others; karma that is partial toward enemies and kin; karma of indulgence in the five desires without weariness or renunciation; karma of dissipation arising from clothing, food, gardens, groves, ponds, or pools; karma of committing manifold transgressions through unrestrained pursuit of sensual desires during one's prime years; or karma of dedicating wholesome yet out-flowing (*sāsrava*) merit toward the three realms of existence, thereby obstructing the supramundane.
Such karmas as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we reveal them before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly, taking refuge and repenting.

"We pray that by virtue of the merit and goodness arising from this confession of the sins of the immediate retribution and other offenses, our disciples may, in birth after birth, extinguish the five heinous crimes and eliminate the delusions of icchantikas. From this day forth until we reach the site of enlightenment, we vow never again to commit such light or heavy transgressions. We shall constantly practice the supramundane, pure, and wholesome dharmas, diligently uphold the disciplinary conduct, and guard our dignified demeanor."

Like one crossing the sea who cherishes a life-preserving float, may the six perfections and four immeasurables always be the foremost of their practices; may the categories of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom become increasingly bright and clear; and may they swiftly achieve the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, great compassion, the three types of mindfulness, and the constant delight in wondrous wisdom and the eightfold self-mastery.
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning Retribution for Śramaṇas*, the Jewel-Attainer (Ratnada) entered a Hell of Boiling Excrement a short while ago.
Why is it called the Hell of Boiling Excrement?

That hell is sixty yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded by iron walls and covered above with an iron net. Excrement flows from east to west and from south to north; fire issues from within, and smoke and flames rise together like clouds and rain. It is exceedingly foul and filthy; there is no stench more offensive than this.
Within the northern gate were six hundred śramaṇas who entered therein; they wailed and wept with fire erupting from their mouths and eyes without ceasing.

They entered this pit of filth to drink excrement and urine; as they entered the excrement and urine, flames and fire issued forth from their mouths, and it was likewise for their mouths, eyes, and the other six sense organs. Thus they died and were reborn a thousand times, ten thousand times, dying and being reborn again and again.
Bao Da asked the Horse-Headed Rākṣasa,
"For what causes and conditions have these śramaṇas fallen into this hell?
"These śramaṇas received the pure precepts of the Buddha but did not maintain them with purity; being greedy for wine and meat and consuming the five pungent roots, they have fallen into this hell.
Upon hearing this, Bodhidharma wept with sorrow and departed.

"Homage to all the worthy and holy ones, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next perform repentance. Disciples!..."
Now, having performed this general repentance for all karmas, we shall now proceed to repent each one individually according to their specific characteristics.
Whether general or specific, coarse or subtle, light or heavy, spoken or unspoken—may all these categories of karma, following their respective types, be completely extinguished.

Regarding the repentance of distinct characteristics (*betsō zange*): first repent for the three actions of the body, then the four of the mouth, and subsequently prostrate for all other obstacles in their proper order.

As for the three karmas of the body, the first is killing; as clarified in the sutras, one may take oneself as a metaphor: do not kill, do not wield the staff. Although there is a distinction between humans and animals, the fact that all cherish life and fear death is one and the same.

If one investigates these sentient beings from time immemorial, they may have been one's own parents, brothers, or members of one's six types of kin; yet, due to the causes and conditions of karma, they have transmigrated through the six realms, passing through birth and death, changing forms and receiving retributions until they no longer recognize one another. To now give rise to malice and devour their flesh is to sever the seed of great compassion.
"Even if one obtains leftover food, one should regard it as if eating the flesh of one's own child during a time of famine;
how much more so regarding the eating of this fish and meat?"
"To kill sentient beings for profit, or to purchase the flesh of sentient beings with money—both are evil karmas; upon death, one will fall into the Raurava Hell."
Thus we know that the sins of killing and eating [flesh] are as deep as rivers and seas, and more grievous than hills and mountains.
Yet, from time immemorial, we disciples, failing to encounter virtuous friends, have all engaged in these karmic acts.
"The sin of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or among the hungry ghosts to undergo suffering.

If they are born among animals, they may receive the bodies of tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, hawks, or falcons; or they may receive the bodies of venomous snakes, vipers, or scorpions, constantly harboring evil intentions; or they may receive the bodies of deer, bears, or brown bears, constantly harboring fear."
"If one is born among humans, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, being frequently ill; second, having one's life cut short.
Since the slaughter and consumption [of living beings] result in such immeasurable and various retributions as these, therefore, disciples!"
"Today we have arrived; with bowed heads and utmost sincerity, we take refuge in the Buddha.

Namo to the Buddha Dharmapadajñāna of the East. Namo to the Buddha Dharmottama of the South. Namo to the Buddha Vairocanavyūha of the West. Namo to the Buddha Jñāneśvaranāman of the North. Namo to the Buddha Varṣasvareśvaradharmma of the Southeast. Namo to the Buddha Prabhāvasenarāja of the Southwest. Namo to the Buddha Prathamacittotpādika of the Northwest. Namo to the Buddha Yaśaḥprasaradaśadiś of the Northeast. Namo to the Buddha Dharmapratigrahaka of the Nadir. Namo to the Buddha Candramaṇipuṣpaśrī of the Zenith. We take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space."

"Disciples! From beginningless time until this very day, within this mind-consciousness we have constantly harbored cruelty and poison, lacking a heart of compassion. Whether through greed, hatred, delusion, or pride, we have committed killing; or we have employed evil means—vowing to kill, wishing to kill, or using incantations to kill; or by damming and dredging lakes and ponds, burning mountains and wilds, hunting and fishing; or by fanning fires with the wind, releasing hawks, or setting dogs—thereby harassing and harming all sentient beings throughout the six realms."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with a sincere heart, I take refuge and repent.

Whether by using snares, traps, spears, halberds, pikes, bows, or crossbows to shoot and strike birds and wild beasts, or by using nets, weirs, and hooks to scoop up aquatic creatures such as fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, crocodiles, shrimp, clams, and bivalves that dwell in the moisture—causing those who live on land, in water, or in the air no place to hide or flee.

Some raise chickens, pigs, cattle, sheep, dogs, swine, geese, ducks, and the like to provide for their own kitchens; others sell them to slaughterers. Thus, before their cries of distress have ceased, their feathers and fur are stripped away, their scales and shells are mangled, and their bodies and heads are severed. Their flesh and bones are minced and torn apart, roasted, steamed, boiled, or grilled—subjected to such agonizing and piercing cruelty against the innocent. Yet the flavor gained by the mouth is extremely meager, lasting no longer than the root of a three-inch tongue.
Yet the retribution for such offenses will persist through eternal kalpas; for these and other sins, I today sincerely take refuge and repent.

Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, I may have raised armies to wage war, contending over territory with rival forces facing one another and slaughtering each other; I may have killed others myself, incited others to kill, or rejoiced upon hearing of killings; I may have practiced butchery and carving, served as an executioner, or slaughtered the lives of others, committing acts of unbearable cruelty; I may have indulged in rage, brandishing halberds and grasping blades, cutting, piercing, or pushing beings into pits and trenches; I may have drowned them in water, blocked their burrows or destroyed their nests, crushed them with earth and stones, or run over and trampled all sentient beings with chariots and horses.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we reveal them, take refuge, and repent.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, we have irrigated dry fields, caused abortions and miscarriages, shattered eggs and destroyed nests, used poisons and sorcery to injure and kill sentient beings, tilled the soil and dug the earth to plant gardens and orchards, raised silkworms and boiled cocoons, and kept cats to catch mice—our acts of injury and killing have been exceedingly great.

Or they strike and crush mosquitoes, gadflies, horseflies, bees, scorpions, fleas, and lice; or they burn away refuse, dig up ditches and canals, and thereby cause the wrongful harm of all living beings; or they eat fruits, or use parched rice, water, or vegetables, and thus kill sentient beings by accident; or they light firewood or expose lamps and candles, burning various types of insects; or they consume sauces and vinegars without checking for moving life; or they pour out hot water and drown insects and ants.

In this manner, even throughout the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—they constantly injure and kill subtle beings, whether flying through the air or dwelling upon the ground.
Because the consciousness of an ordinary person is darkened, they fail to perceive or know [this]; today, I reveal it, take refuge, and repent.

From time immemorial until this very day, we have used various evil means to afflict sentient beings—such as with whips, staves, shackles, fetters, and stocks; by pressing them down, torturing, beating, throwing, kicking with hands and feet, trampling, binding, confining in cages, and depriving them of water and grain."
Today, with utmost sincerity, we turn toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages; we take refuge and repent.

"We pray that by the merit arising from this repentance for the sins of killing and other offenses, may we, throughout all our lives, attain a vajra-body with infinite lifespan; may we forever be free from enmity and hatred, harbor no intent to kill, and attain the stage of regarding all sentient beings as one's only child."

If one sees those in peril, distress, or urgent calamity, one should not begrudge one’s own body or life, but employ skillful means to rescue and liberate them; thereafter, one shall expound the subtle and wondrous True Dharma, so that all sentient beings who behold one’s form or shadow receive peace and happiness, and all whose names are heard or voices are listened to have their terrors entirely dispelled.
In the *Mahāyāna Padma-ratna-bodhi-praśna-vyākaraṇa-sārdhaṃ-śramaṇa-sūtra*, Bodhi entered a Hell of Dissolving Bodies (Kāya-vilaya-naraka) shortly thereafter.
Why is it called the Hell of Dissolving Bodies?

That hell is thirty yojanas in length and breadth; it is surrounded by an iron city with an iron net covering it above. Within, fierce fires blaze with intense brilliance, and iron spikes are spread across its ground.
Furthermore, flying spears come to pierce the offenders, and there are great iron frames upon which the bodies of the offenders are suspended, their limbs and joints being torn asunder.
At that time, within the eastern gate, countless offenders behold this from afar; weeping and wailing, they throw their entire bodies to the ground and cry out these words:
"By what sin have I now entered here?"

The yakṣa wardens of hell, holding great axes, struck at his head; they further bound his body with iron chains, while fierce fires scorched his frame and flying spikes pierced him in chaotic profusion.

At that time, the sinner falls at every step until he reaches the foot of the gallows. The yakṣa jailers shove and shove the sinner, dismembering him limb by limb with great iron saws. Blood flows across the ground as he suffers ten thousand kinds of agony. Then, creatures in the forms of sheep, oxen, donkeys, horses, and various other species of insects, birds, and beasts come to drink his blood and devour his flesh; for all these animals seek from the sinner his original life-force and his original flesh.
At that time, the sinner was unable to utter a word in reply, while all the various animals tore and bit him.
The pain and agony were unbearable; the sinner groaned and shrieked as blood flowed from his mouth and eyes, his mournful wailing and sobbing reaching up to the heavens.

Thus, for one day and one night, they undergo immeasurable suffering and retribution, dying and being reborn a thousand times, ten thousand times; though they pass through thousands of millions of kalpas, there is no time of escape.
Even if they later manage to emerge, they shall fall among the animals, where for hundreds of billions of lifetimes they will be devoured by their enemies.
"What karma did these śramaṇas perform that they now undergo such suffering?

"These sinful persons, having received the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, do not seek the unsurpassed, truly correct, and wondrous Dharma; instead, they look only to what is before their eyes, believing in heterodox and inverted views. Arrogant, boastful, and self-indulgent, their hearts harbor cruelty and poison, and lacking compassion, they kill and harm sentient beings, severing the limbs of those who belong to the lineage of the Buddhas."

Because of these causes and conditions, they undergo such punishments; later, even when born as humans for hundreds or thousands of lifetimes, their faculties will be incomplete—they will be deaf, blind, mute, or have impaired limbs—and their bodies will be covered in many sores that constantly flow with pus and blood. Because they took the lives of others, they shall receive this short lifespan as retribution.
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with grief and departed.

"If good sons and good daughters wish to extinguish all sins, they should bathe thoroughly, put on new and clean clothes, and invoke the names of these Buddhas while making offerings and prostrating. They should speak these words:

'From beginningless worlds until now, I have committed unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, even including slandering the Vaipulya sutras and committing the five heinous crimes; may they all be extinguished.'"

“Śāriputra! A son or daughter of good family who wishes to fulfill the practice of the six pāramitās, who wishes to dedicate [their merit] toward unsurpassed bodhi, and who wishes to fulfill all the pāramitās of the bodhisattvas, should speak these words:

‘I shall study the past, future, and present bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, practicing great relinquishment, tore open their chests and gave their hearts to sentient beings, such as the Bodhisattva Jñānavijaya and King Kāśī.’”
One gives away one's wife, children, and so forth to those who are destitute, as did the Bodhisattva Avinivartanīya, King Aśokarāja, Sudāna, King Śobha, and others.
They enter the hells to rescue suffering sentient beings, such as the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika and the Devaputra Sunetra;
they rescue sentient beings who commit evil deeds, such as the Bodhisattva Sucarita and King Vijayacaryā.
He gave away his jeweled celestial crown upon his head and even flayed his scalp, as did the Bodhisattva Uttaptavīrya, the Devaputra Ratnaśikhin, and others;
he gave his eyes in alms, as did the Bodhisattva Maitreya, King Candraprabha, and others.
They gave away their ears and noses in alms, such as the Bodhisattva Aśoka and the Devaputra Vijayagāmin;
they gave away their teeth in alms, such as the Bodhisattva Puṣpadanta and the Six-Tusked Elephant King.
They gave up their tongues, such as the Bodhisattva Avinivartana and King Sumukha;
they gave up their hands, such as the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta and King Dṛḍhamati;
they gave up their blood, such as the Bodhisattva Dharmakāra and the Devaputra Candracintin.
They gave away their flesh and marrow, like the Bodhisattva An-yin (Anuruddha) and King Sarvamdada;
they gave away their large intestines, small intestines, liver, lungs, spleen, and kidneys, like the Bodhisattva Shan-de (Kalyāṇakārin) and King Svayamyāpita-sarvapāpa.
They sacrificed all their major and minor limbs, such as the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara and the Devaputra Jyotiṣprabha;
they sacrificed their skin, such as the Bodhisattva Viśuddhagarbha, the Devaputra Suvarṇa, and the Golden Deer King.
They gave up their fingers and toes, such as the Bodhisattva Drdhavīrya and King Suvarṇavarṇa;
they gave up their fingernails and toenails, such as the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati and the Devaputra Dharmakāma.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, they enter great pits of fire, such as the Bodhisattva Vīrya and King Candraprabha;
for the sake of seeking the Dharma, they sell their bodies, cut them open, break their bones, and extract their marrow, such as the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and King Suvarṇabāhu.
They undergo all manner of suffering and affliction, such as the Bodhisattva Seeking the Sublime Dharma and the Great King Swift Traveler;
they relinquish the four continents, the great earth, and all their adornments, such as the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta and the Devaputra Supreme Merit.
They sacrifice their bodies, like the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and King Mahābhara;
they serve as attendants and servants to all impoverished and suffering sentient beings, like King Śibi.
"To state the essentials: may I likewise accomplish all the practices of the *pāramitās* of all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present;

with all the exquisite incense, flowers, garlands, and sublime music throughout the worlds of the ten directions, I rejoice in making offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and further dedicate this merit to bestow upon all sentient beings."

By virtue of this merit, may they fulfill the eighty-four thousand practices of the *pāramitās*, swiftly receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression, and swiftly achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.

“Śāriputra! If there are good men or good women—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—who believe my words and receive, uphold, read, and recite the names of these Buddhas, they should bathe and put on fresh, clean clothes. During the first, middle, and last watches of the day, and during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, they should rise from their seats, bare their right shoulders, place their right knees upon the ground, and with single-minded devotion invoke the names of these Buddhas, making offerings and prostrating while saying:
‘I now pay homage to all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as known by the Tathāgata.’”
“Śāriputra! These sons and daughters of good family, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who thus make offerings and pay homage shall obtain immeasurable merit.”
If one wishes to attain the stage of a śrāvaka, the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one should pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and all shall be attained.

Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next perform repentance. Disciples!..."
Next is the repentance for the karma of stealing.
"If an object belongs to another and is guarded by another, one should not take even a single blade of grass or a single leaf from it without being given; how much less so should one commit theft?"
However, because sentient beings see only immediate benefit, they seize property through various unrighteous means, thereby causing them to suffer these calamities and burdens in the future.
"The sin of robbery can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or as hungry ghosts to undergo suffering."
If they are born among animals, they take on the forms of oxen, horses, donkeys, mules, camels, and the like, repaying their past debts with the physical strength, blood, and flesh of those bodies.

"If one is born among humans as a slave or servant to others, with clothing that does not cover the body and food that does not sustain life, one suffers the poverty and hardship of human existence to its very limit.
Since robbery and theft bring such bitter retributions, therefore, disciple!
Having arrived here today, I bow my head and take refuge in the Buddha. Homage to the Buddha of Great Wisdom in the East. Homage to the Buddha of the Great Assembly in the South.

Homage to the Buddha of Pure Wisdom in the West. Homage to the Buddha Renowned for Wisdom in the North. Homage to the Buddha King of Upholding Precepts in the Southeast. I take refuge in all such Triple Gems throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space in the ten directions.

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, you may have stolen others' wealth and treasures by raising blades to seize them by force; or, relying on your own physical strength, you may have coerced and taken from others; or, depending on official authority or feigning power, you may have used high stocks and heavy shackles to unjustly oppress the virtuous, swallowing bribes and torturing the upright to make them appear guilty. For these causes and conditions, your bodies have been ensnared in the net of the law."

Or they may govern with perverse methods, seizing the property of others; they encroach upon the public for private gain or encroach upon the private for public benefit; they harm others to profit themselves or profit others at their own expense; they deprive others to enrich themselves, while their speech and heart remain stingy.
Or we may have secretly embezzled taxes and assessments, stolen customs duties, or concealed public levies by hiding them away;
such offenses are immeasurable and boundless. Today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent.

"Whether it be taking without being given property belonging to the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; or property of scriptures and images; or property for the maintenance of stupas and temples; or property intended for offerings to the resident monastics (*sāṃghika*); or property designated for the *cāturdisa-saṃgha*; or stealing and misusing such items, failing to return them despite having the power to do so; or borrowing from others oneself; or again, exchanging, lending, or using them with negligence or deceit; or confusing and mixing the property of the Three Jewels for various uses; or taking at will and according to one's own whims the monastic community’s grain, rice, firewood, ginger, fermented soybeans, sauces, vinegar, vegetables, fruits, money, silk, bamboo, wood, brocades, banners, canopies, incense, flowers, oil, or candles."

Perhaps they deceive those who have offered property to the Triple Gem by not giving it back; or they use it for themselves or give it to others; or they pluck flowers or fruits from the Buddha’s offerings and use items belonging to the Sangha’s treasury, thereby privately benefiting themselves with the wealth of the Triple Gem.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we reveal and repent them.

From beginningless time until this day, whether acting as friends, associates, preceptors, teachers, fellow students, parents, brothers, or members of our six kinds of kinship and relatives, dwelling and residing together in hundreds and thousands of places, we have repeatedly deceived one another.

Or, among neighbors and those living nearby, they shift fences and expand walls, encroaching upon and seizing land and dwellings, altering boundaries and enclosures, and plundering fields and gardens; under the guise of public business yet driven by private motives, they seize the shops and marketplaces of others, as well as their lands and wilderness holdings.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today we reveal them, take refuge, and repent.

From beginningless time until this day, we have perhaps besieged cities, destroyed towns, burned villages, and demolished stockades; we have stolen and sold free citizens, or enticed away the servants of others.

Furthermore, some may have innocent people pinned down by pillars, their bodies mangled by blades and their limbs bound in fetters; their households and livelihoods are ruined and scattered, their kin torn apart and separated, divided between different cities with life and death set apart.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we reveal and repent them.

From time immemorial until this day, whether engaged in trade as merchants, or dealing in goods at shops and markets, we have used light scales and small measures, reduced dimensions, and stolen fractions of a grain. We have deceived others regarding weights and volumes, exchanging coarse goods for the fine, or short items for the long, employing a hundred clever ruses in hopes of gaining the slightest profit.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we take refuge and repent.

From time immemorial until this day, we have breached walls and overstepped boundaries, waylaid travelers and plundered them, resisted debts and interest, defaulted on obligations, and deceived others through our faces, speech, and hearts.

Or they may plunder and seize by unrighteous means the beings of the four births—gods, ghosts, spirits, and animals; or they may falsely rely on divination and physiognomy to take people's wealth and treasures; and so on, even seeking profit through profit, pursuing evil gains and excessive desires without satiety or contentment.

Such offenses as these are immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be fully described; today, I come before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Holy Assembly, to take refuge and repent.

“May we disciples, by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance for the sins of robbery and so forth, in every birth and every life obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel; may the seven treasures, exquisite garments, the nectar of a hundred flavors, and various medicinal decoctions rain down constantly. May whatever is required according to one’s wishes arrive as soon as it is needed. May all sentient beings be free from the intent to steal or plunder; may they all be able to have few desires and know contentment, neither being addicted to nor stained by worldly things. May they always delight in practicing generosity and the path of urgent succor, regarding their own heads, eyes, marrow, and brains as discarded mucus or spittle, dedicating these merits toward the fulfillment of the *dānapāramitā*.
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Concerning the Retribution of Śramaṇas*, as Precious Attainment was about to enter the Hell of Bleating Cries,
he beheld that hell where fierce fires blazed and smoke and flames erupted together, and wherein the sinners entered to undergo ten thousand forms of suffering.
Within the western gate, various śramaṇas arrive and enter, groaning and wailing so that the earth trembles.

The horse-headed rākṣasas seize iron mallets in their hands and strike them upon the head; the offenders cry out with bleating sounds as they flee, while the yakṣa jailers compete with one another to beat them.

Having no place to flee to, he runs toward the eastern gate, but it is closed; the southern, western, and northern gates are likewise so. For one day and one night he undergoes the agony of punishment, seeking life but unable to find it, seeking death but unable to find it.
Bao Da asked the horse-headed rākṣasa,
"What sins did these śramaṇas commit to receive such retribution?

"These śramaṇas, though they have received the pure precepts of the Buddha, lack compassion in their hearts; they beat animals with clubs and possess no mercy, and by these causes and conditions, they undergo such retribution."
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with grief and departed.

"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, we next proceed to repentance.
Disciples! With a sincere heart, we repent for the sins of greed and desire."
"It is solely because they are shut in by craving within the prison of delusion that sentient beings are submerged in the river of birth and death, unable to emerge.
For the sake of these five desires, sentient beings have wandered through birth and death since time immemorial.

Within a single eon, the bones accumulated by each and every sentient being would equal Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha; the breast milk they have drunk equals the waters of the four oceans; the blood shed from their bodies exceeds even this; and the tears shed by parents, brothers, and six kinds of kinsmen while wailing at their deaths upon the passing of life would equal the ice of the four oceans.
"Where there is craving, there is birth; where craving is exhausted, there is cessation. Thus, one knows that craving is the root of birth and death.
For this reason, the Sūtra says:

"The sin of sexual desire can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or as hungry ghosts to undergo suffering; if they are born among animals, they will take the form of sparrows, finches, mandarin ducks, and the like; if they are born among humans, their spouses will not be chaste, and they will obtain followers who do not accord with their wishes."
"Since sexual desire possesses such evil karma as this, for this reason, disciples! Today, with a sincere heart, we prostrate ourselves and take refuge in the Buddha:

Namo to the Buddha Light-Wheel in the East; Namo to the Buddha Opening the Radiance in the South; Namo to the Buddha Practicing Wisdom in the West; Namo to the Buddha Great Lapis Lazuli in the North; Namo to the Buddha Joyful Lotus-Crest in the Southeast; Namo to the Buddha Harmony of Wisdom in the Southwest; Namo to the Buddha Unsurpassed Victorious Honored One in the Northwest; Namo to the Buddha Pure Eye Free from Stain in the Northeast; Namo to the Buddha Endowed with Complete Radiance below; Namo to the Buddha Supreme Purity of Immeasurable Banner above. We take refuge in all the Triple Gem throughout the entirety of the ten directions and the realm of empty space."

"Disciples! From time immemorial until this very day, you may have violated the wives and concubines of others or abducted the women of others; you may have assaulted the chaste or defiled *bhikṣuṇīs*, thereby destroying their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) through improper coercion; you may have looked upon others with turbid minds and evil glances, engaging in mocking and derisive speech; or you may have brought shame upon the families of others, tarnishing the reputations of the virtuous and good; or you may have committed impure acts toward the five kinds of men."
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we take refuge and repent.
"Disciples! From beginningless time until this day, we may have received a female body; our minds were like wild horses, constantly wandering and dissolute, never for a single moment at rest."

Constantly harboring perverse thoughts and perpetually giving rise to lustful desires, they may, at monasteries or assembly halls, have no intention of listening to the Dharma but instead gaze greedily with their eyes; or, out of love for desire, they corrupt other men who are śramaṇas.

They do not honor the Buddha-dharma but indulge their lustful passions at will, causing their minds to drift upon the great ocean, darkly losing the shore; they may defile the three robes and Dharma garments of the Sangha, or engage in impure acts within the courtyards and chambers of the vihāras, groping about together in debauchery.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and a sincere heart, we repent. Furthermore, disciples!

From time immemorial until this day, some have taken female form and constantly harbored lustful desires; others have violated the husbands of others or deluded men; some have used talismans, incantations, or sorcery to afflict the wives of others. When people possess little merit, they become possessed by malevolent spirits, and various disease-demons take advantage of this. Failing to encounter a skilled physician, they ultimately meet their death.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with shame and remorse, we reveal and repent them. With utmost sincerity, we prostrate ourselves and take refuge in repentance.

From time immemorial until this very day, my eyes have been captivated by forms—whether by being stained by the attachment to dark and yellow, red and green, crimson and purple, or by precious playthings and jeweled ornaments; or by grasping at the features of men and women, whether tall or short, black or white, and giving rise to improper thoughts.

My ears have craved pleasant sounds—the notes of the *gong* and *shang*, the lutes and pipes, and the singing and music of courtesans; or by grasping at the voices and speech of men and women, their weeping and laughter, and giving rise to improper thoughts.
My nose has relied upon famous fragrances—musk, orchids, saffron, and *suhak*—and given rise to improper thoughts.

Or, the tongue craves delicious flavors—fresh, savory, sweet, and rich—and since the flesh and blood of sentient beings nourish the four great elements, one further increases the root of suffering by giving rise to unrighteous thoughts;
or, the body delights in flowers, finery, brocades, silks, and gauzes, as well as all fine textures and beautiful garments of the seven treasures, giving rise to unrighteous thoughts;
or, the mind is filled with many distracted thoughts that turn toward what is contrary to the Dharma. When these six types of thoughts arise, one commits transgressions most severely.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we take refuge and repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages.

"We pray that by the merit arising from this repentance for the sins of lust and other transgressions, our disciples may, in life after life, be born spontaneously without passing through a womb; may we be pure and radiant, with majestic features and brilliant countenances; may our six sense-faculties be clear and sharp, perceiving with distinct clarity; and may we fully comprehend that affection and attachment are like shackles."

Contemplating these six sense objects as being like illusions and transformations, one becomes resolutely weary of and detached from the realms of the five desires; such that even in dreams no perverse thoughts arise, and internal or external causes and conditions can never move them.

"By the merit of this repentance of the eye-faculty, I vow that these eyes may see through to the ten directions, perceiving the pure Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas without dualistic characteristics."

By the merit of this repentance regarding the faculty of hearing, I vow that these ears shall constantly hear the true Dharma expounded by the Buddhas and sages of the ten directions, and that I shall practice in accordance with their teachings.

By the merit of this repentance regarding the faculty of the nose, may this nose always perceive the fragrance of the Accumulated Merit that enters the station of the Dharma, and may it abandon the impure stench and filth of birth and death.

By the merit of this repentance of the faculty of the tongue, may this tongue always partake of the food of the joy of Dharma and the rapture of dhyāna, never again craving the flavors of the flesh and blood of sentient beings.

By the merit of this confession of the faculty of the body, may this body be clothed in the robes of the Tathāgata, don the armor of patience, lie upon the bed of fearlessness, and sit upon the seat of the four dhyānas.

By the merit of this repentance of the mental faculty, may this mind achieve the ten conceptions and penetrate the five sciences; may it deeply contemplate the principle of the equality of emptiness within the two truths; may it give rise to the ten sublime practices from skillful means and wisdom; may it enter the stream of Dharma, increasing in clarity with every thought-moment, and manifest the Tathāgata’s great patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
In the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions and Answers Regarding Retribution for Śramaṇas*, as Precious Attainment was about to enter the Hooked-Shadow Hell, it was asked:
"Why is it called the Hooked-Shadow Hell?"
That hell is thirty yojanas in length and breadth; within it, streams of fire flow and pour, spreading across the ground, while its four walls are no different from those described above.

In the meantime, countless sinners have the hell-warden yakṣas seize them with iron hooks aimed at their private parts; the fire burning within the hooks ascends into their chests and hearts, and the fire burning upon their hearts penetrates through both their bellies and backs.
Because of the karma of desire, he transforms himself into a woman, exactly as she appeared when he first saw her in his previous life.

Once he has seen her, the fire of lust is ignited and he runs toward her. That woman’s body is composed of vajra and iron, blazing with heat; having reached her, he embraces the sinner, but upon being embraced, he is shattered to pieces. He then approaches her mouth, whereupon his lips are devoured and his body is likewise consumed. When he is entirely finished, he is born again, and once born, he is devoured once more.
It is likewise with those women who love men: their desire is unstable and the fire of lust is constantly burning; such bitter and agonizing pain is difficult to endure.

At that time, the multitude of sinners still do not repent; they undergo immeasurable suffering for one day and one night, dying and being reborn a thousand times, ten thousand times—indeed, ten million times—passing through immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of kalpas before they finally attain liberation.

Due to the remaining fruit of that karma, he was born among animals as an impure worm; after two hundred thousand lifetimes, he obtained birth among humans, yet died in the womb for five hundred lifetimes, and was born [only to die] again for another five hundred lifetimes.

Unable to distinguish male from female, their vision is impaired; they suffer from poverty and exposure, and their lifespans are short. At times, their wives are violated by others, or they themselves lust after the wives of others; unable to restrain themselves, they perpetually sever their lineage.
Bao Da asked the horse-headed rākṣasa,
"What kind of conduct did these śramaṇas perform to receive such punishment?
"These śramaṇas received the pure precepts of the Buddha but were unable to maintain them purely; therefore, they engaged in sexual desire and gave free rein to their six sense-faculties.
By reason of these causes and conditions, they have incurred such offenses."
Upon hearing this, Baoda wept with grief and departed.

"The transgressions of verbal karma can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo suffering; if they are born among animals, they take the form of owls, crows, vultures, or eagles, such that no one who hears their cries fails to loathe them."

"If one is born among humans, one's breath will always be foul-smelling; whatever one says will not be trusted or accepted by others; and one's kin and followers will be discordant, constantly prone to quarreling and strife.
Since the karmic results of verbal actions are thus evil, therefore, disciple!

Today, with utmost sincerity, I take refuge in the Buddha: Homage to the Buddha Star-Host Renown in the East. Homage to the Buddha Moon-Light Lamp in the South.
